## 5.5 Polar $\leftrightarrow$ Rectangular Transformations in the Complex Domain

In AC circuit and RF analysis, we constantly switch between two views of the same complex number: **rectangular form** ($\mathbf{z} = x + iy$, which makes series addition effortless) and **polar phasor form** ($\mathbf{z} = r\angle\theta = r e^{i\theta}$, which reveals the physical voltage/current magnitude $r$ and phase angle $\theta$):
$$r = |z| = \sqrt{x^2 + y^2}, \quad \theta = \operatorname{atan2}(y, x), \qquad x = \operatorname{Re}(z) = r\cos\theta, \quad y = \operatorname{Im}(z) = r\sin\theta$$

| Transformation | Key Sequence | Stack Input ($Y, X$) | Stack Output ($Y, X$) | Mathematical Mapping |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **Cartesian to Polar** | `[↰] [▸θ,r]` | $Y = y$ (Vertical / Imaginary)<br>$X = x$ (Horizontal / Real) | $Y = \theta$ (Phase angle)<br>$X = r$ (Modulus / Magnitude) | $r = \operatorname{hypot}(X, Y), \quad \theta = \operatorname{atan2}(Y, X)$ |
| **Polar to Cartesian** | `[↱] [▸y,x]` | $Y = \theta$ (Phase angle)<br>$X = r$ (Modulus / Magnitude) | $Y = y$ (Vertical / Imaginary)<br>$X = x$ (Horizontal / Real) | $x = r\cos\theta, \quad y = r\sin\theta$ |

### 5.5.1 The `[x⇄y]` Bridge & Three-Phase Symmetrical Components

Look closely at the table above and notice one subtle detail: in Chapter 4, the Euclidean vector keys `[↰] [▸θ,r]` and `[↱] [▸y,x]` placed the vertical component $y$ in Register $Y$ and the horizontal component $x$ in Register $X$. In Gaussian complex arithmetic ($\mathbf{z} = Y + Xi$), however, the Real part ($x$) sits in Register $Y$ and the Imaginary part ($y$) sits in Register $X$. Therefore, **pressing `[x⇄y]` is the one-keystroke bridge between Gaussian complex $(Y = \text{Real}, X = \text{Imag})$ order and Euclidean $(Y = y, X = x)$ polar conversion**:

- **From Complex $(Y = \text{Real}, X = \text{Imag})$ to Polar $(\theta, r)$:** Press `[x⇄y] [↰] [▸θ,r]`.
- **From Polar $(Y = \theta, X = r)$ to Complex $(Y = \text{Real}, X = \text{Imag})$:** Press `[↱] [▸y,x] [x⇄y]`.

Let us trace a round-trip conversion of $\mathbf{z} = 3 + 4i$ on the stack:

| Step | Keystroke | Register T | Register Z | Register Y | Register X | Notes & State Analysis |
| :---: | :--- | :---: | :---: | :---: | :---: | :--- |
| 1 | `3 [ENTER] 4` | $0.0000$ | $0.0000$ | $3.0000$ | $4.0000$ | Gaussian complex coordinates $(Y=\text{Real}, X=\text{Imag})$ |
| 2 | `[x⇄y] [↰] [▸θ,r]` | $0.0000$ | $0.0000$ | $0.927295$ | **$5.000000$** | Polar conversion: $\theta$ in $Y$, magnitude $r$ in $X$ |
| 3 | `[↱] [▸y,x]` | $0.0000$ | $0.0000$ | $4.000000$ | **$3.000000$** | Rectangular conversion: horizontal $x$ in $X$, vertical $y$ in $Y$ |
| 4 | `[x⇄y]` | $0.0000$ | $0.0000$ | **$3.000000$** | **$4.000000$** | Realign to Gaussian complex format: Real in $Y$, Imag in $X$ |

This `[↱] [▸y,x] [x⇄y]` polar-to-Gaussian bridge answers a classic question of electrical power engineering: why can a high-voltage three-phase transmission tower carry megawatts of power across three phase wires without needing a fourth neutral return cable? In 1918, Charles LeGeyt Fortescue introduced **symmetrical components** using the $120^\circ$ complex phase rotator $a = e^{i 120^\circ} = \cos(120^\circ) + i\sin(120^\circ) = -0.5 + 0.866025i$ and $a^2 = e^{i 240^\circ} = -0.5 - 0.866025i$. Because the three unit phasors $1$, $a$, and $a^2$ point $120^\circ$ apart like the three spokes of a Mercedes star, their vector sum vanishes identically ($1 + a + a^2 = 0$), meaning balanced three-phase currents cancel at the neutral point:

$$a = -0.5 + 0.866025i, \quad a^2 = -0.5 - 0.866025i \implies 1 + a + a^2 = \mathbf{0.000000 + 0.000000i}$$

In Degrees mode (`[DEG]`), we project the two unit phasors $1\angle 120^\circ$ and $1\angle 240^\circ$ into Gaussian complex coordinates via `[↱] [▸y,x] [x⇄y]`, sum them via `[↰] [CMPLX] [+]`, and add the reference phase $1 + 0i$ to verify exact zero-sequence cancellation:

| Step | Keystroke | Register T | Register Z | Register Y | Register X | Notes & State Analysis |
| :---: | :--- | :---: | :---: | :---: | :---: | :--- |
| 1 | `120 [ENTER] 1 [↱] [▸y,x] [x⇄y]` | $0.0000$ | $0.0000$ | $-0.500000$ | $0.866025$ | Polar to Gaussian: $a = -0.5 + 0.8660i$ |
| 2 | `240 [ENTER] 1 [↱] [▸y,x] [x⇄y]` | $-0.500000$ | $0.866025$ | $-0.500000$ | $-0.866025$ | Polar to Gaussian: $a^2 = -0.5 - 0.8660i$ |
| 3 | `[↰] [CMPLX] [+]` | $-0.500000$ | $-0.500000$ | $-1.000000$ | $0.000000$ | Complex sum: $a + a^2 = -1.0 + 0.0i$ |
| 4 | `1 [ENTER] 0 [↰] [CMPLX] [+]` | $-1.000000$ | $-1.000000$ | **$0.000000$** | **$0.000000$** | Add $+1$ reference: $1 + a + a^2 = 0 + 0i$ |

## 5.6 AC Circuit Analysis: Series, Parallel & Bridge Impedance Networks

Returning to Radians mode (`[RAD]`), in an alternating-current network driven at angular frequency $\omega = 2\pi f$, every passive component maps to a point in the complex impedance plane: a **resistor** ($R$) sits on the positive real axis at $\mathbf{Z}_R = R + 0i\,\Omega$; an **inductor** ($L$) points straight up the positive imaginary axis at $\mathbf{Z}_L = 0 + j\omega L\,\Omega$ (because Faraday's law $v = L\,di/dt$ multiplies by $j\omega$, advancing voltage $90^\circ$ ahead of current); and a **capacitor** ($C$) points straight down the negative imaginary axis at $\mathbf{Z}_C = 0 - j/(\omega C)\,\Omega$ (dragging voltage $90^\circ$ behind current).

### 5.6.1 Complex Series Impedance Addition

When two AC branches are wired in series—say, an inductive coil $\mathbf{Z}_1 = 8.0 + 4.0i\,\Omega$ followed by a capacitive load $\mathbf{Z}_2 = 4.0 - 8.0i\,\Omega$—the same current flows through both, so their impedances add component by component:
$$\mathbf{Z}_{\text{series}} = \mathbf{Z}_1 + \mathbf{Z}_2 = (8.0 + 4.0) + (4.0 - 8.0)i = 12.0 - 4.0i\,\Omega$$

Loading $\mathbf{Z}_2$ into $(T, Z)$ and $\mathbf{Z}_1$ into $(Y, X)$ and summing in the complex plane via `4 [ENTER] 8 [+/-] [ENTER] 8 [ENTER] 4 [↰] [CMPLX] [+]` resolves both components simultaneously:

| Step | Keystroke | Register T | Register Z | Register Y | Register X | Notes & State Analysis |
| :---: | :--- | :---: | :---: | :---: | :---: | :--- |
| 1 | `4 [ENTER]` | $0.0000$ | $0.0000$ | $4.0000$ | $4.0000$ | Real part of $\mathbf{Z}_2$ pushed |
| 2 | `8 [+/-] [ENTER]` | $0.0000$ | $4.0000$ | $-8.0000$ | $-8.0000$ | Imag part of $\mathbf{Z}_2$ pushed |
| 3 | `8 [ENTER]` | $4.0000$ | $-8.0000$ | $8.0000$ | $8.0000$ | Real part of $\mathbf{Z}_1$ pushed |
| 4 | `4` | **$4.0000$** | **$-8.0000$** | **$8.0000$** | **$4.0000$** | Complete 4-register setup |
| 5 | `[↰] [CMPLX] [+]` | $4.0000$ | $4.0000$ | **$12.000000$** | **$-4.000000$** | $\mathbf{Z}_{\text{total}} = 12.0 - 4.0i\,\Omega$ |

The display immediately shows **Real $= 12.0\,\Omega$ in Register $Y$** and **Imaginary $= -4.0\,\Omega$ in Register $X$**.

### 5.6.2 Parallel Complex Impedance: Admittance Inversion vs. Direct `CMPLX x∥y`

What if two reactive branches—$\mathbf{Z}_1 = 20.0 + 15.0i\,\Omega$ and $\mathbf{Z}_2 = 10.0 - 25.0i\,\Omega$—are wired in *parallel* across the same voltage source? Now their currents add, which means their reciprocal **complex admittances** ($\mathbf{Y} = 1/\mathbf{Z} = G + jB$, measured in Siemens) add directly:
$$\mathbf{Y}_{\text{parallel}} = \mathbf{Y}_1 + \mathbf{Y}_2 = \frac{1}{\mathbf{Z}_1} + \frac{1}{\mathbf{Z}_2} \implies \mathbf{Z}_{\text{parallel}} = \frac{1}{\mathbf{Y}_{\text{parallel}}}$$

Across AC circuit analysis, RF impedance matching, and electro-acoustics, the SC-32's transient `[↰] [CMPLX]` prefix gives you two complementary ways to evaluate parallel complex impedances in Registers $(Y, X)$. When you want to inspect the physical **conductance $G$ and susceptance $B$** of each parallel branch ($\mathbf{Y}_k = 1/\mathbf{Z}_k = G_k + jB_k$), use **Reciprocal Admittance Summation (`[↰] [CMPLX] [1/x]`)**:

1. **Invert Branch 1 in $(Y, X)$:** Key `20 [ENTER] 15 [↰] [CMPLX] [1/x]` $\rightarrow$ **`-0.024`**. This converts $\mathbf{Z}_1 = 20 + 15i\,\Omega$ into its inductive admittance $\mathbf{Y}_1 = 0.032000 - 0.024000i\,\text{S}$ in $(Y, X)$.
2. **Load and Invert Branch 2 (Automatically Lifting $\mathbf{Y}_1$ into $(T, Z)$):** Key `10 [ENTER] 25 [+/-] [↰] [CMPLX] [1/x]` $\rightarrow$ **`0.0344827586`**. Typing `10 [ENTER] 25 [+/-]` lifts $\mathbf{Y}_1$ cleanly into the upper registers $(T = 0.032000,\; Z = -0.024000)$, and pressing `[↰] [CMPLX] [1/x]` inverts $\mathbf{Z}_2$ in place into capacitive admittance $\mathbf{Y}_2 = 0.013793 + 0.034483i\,\text{S}$ in $(Y, X)$ without disturbing $(T, Z)$!
3. **Sum Admittances and Invert Back to Ohms:** Key `0.045793 [ENTER] 0.010483 [↰] [CMPLX] [1/x] [x⇄y]` $\rightarrow$ **`20.749994624`**. `[↰] [CMPLX] [+]` adds the two admittances into $\mathbf{Y}_{\text{parallel}} = 0.045793 + 0.010483i\,\text{S}$, and `[↰] [CMPLX] [1/x]` inverts that total admittance back into the equivalent parallel impedance $\mathbf{Z}_{\text{parallel}} = \mathbf{20.7516 - 4.7507i\,\Omega}$:

| :---: | :--- | :---: | :---: | :---: | :---: | :--- |

| 2 | `10 [ENTER] 25 [+/-] [↰] [CMPLX] [1/x]` | $0.032000$ | $-0.024000$ | $0.013793$ | $0.034483$ | $\mathbf{Y}_1$ lifts to $(T, Z)$; $\mathbf{Y}_2$ in $(Y, X)$ |

Admittance inspection is especially illuminating when audio engineers wire a **Zobel impedance-compensation network** ($R - jX_C$) in parallel with an inductive loudspeaker voice coil ($R + jX_L$) so that the amplifier sees a purely resistive load. Consider the parallel combination of conjugate branches $Z_1 = 3 + 4i\,\Omega$ and $Z_2 = 3 - 4i\,\Omega$:

$$\frac{1}{Z_{\text{parallel}}} = \frac{1}{3+4i} + \frac{1}{3-4i} = \frac{3-4i}{25} + \frac{3+4i}{25} = \frac{6}{25} \implies Z_{\text{parallel}} = \frac{25}{6} = \mathbf{4.166667\,\Omega}$$

Because the opposite susceptances $\mp 4/25 = \mp 0.16i\,\text{S}$ cancel identically when the two conjugate admittances are added, we only need to invert $Z_1 = 3 + 4i$ (`3 [ENTER] 4 [↰] [CMPLX] [1/x]` $\to Y = 0.120000,\; X = -0.160000$), swap the real conductance $G = 0.12\,\text{S}$ into Register $X$ (`[x⇄y]`), double it (`2 [×]`), and invert (`[1/x]`) via `3 [ENTER] 4 [↰] [CMPLX] [1/x] [x⇄y] 2 [×] [1/x]` to obtain $Z_{\text{parallel}} = \mathbf{4.166667\,\Omega}$ (or in one stroke via `3 [ENTER] 4 [ENTER] 3 [ENTER] 4 [+/-] [↰] [CMPLX] [x∥y]`):

### 5.6.3 Active Filter Gain & Loudspeaker Crossover Networks

Complex impedance ratios and complex polynomials also govern the frequency response of analog audio filters. In 1930, British engineer Stephen Butterworth designed the "maximally flat" low-pass filter $H(s) = 1 / (s^2 + \sqrt{2}s + 1)$ so that passband ripple vanishes completely. At the normalized cutoff frequency $s = j\omega/\omega_c = 0 + 1i$ (e.g., $f_c = 2,500\text{ Hz}$), the $s^2 = -1$ term and the $+1$ constant in the denominator $B_2(j) = s^2 + \sqrt{2}s + 1$ cancel identically, leaving only the damping term $0 + j\sqrt{2}$:

$$s^2 = -1 + 0i, \quad \sqrt{2} s = 0 + 1.414214i \implies B_2(j) = (-1 + 1) + 1.414214i = 0 + 1.414214i$$
$$H(j) = \frac{1}{0 + 1.414214i} = 0 - \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}i = 0 - 0.707107i \implies |H| = \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \approx -3.01\text{ dB}$$

Loading $B_2(j) = 0 + 1.414214i$ into $(Y, X)$ and inverting in place via `0 [ENTER] 1.414214 [↰] [CMPLX] [1/x]` (or exact `0 [ENTER] 2 [√x] [↰] [CMPLX] [1/x]`) directly evaluates the complex transfer function $H(j) = \mathbf{0.000000 - 0.707107i}$—showing both the $-3.01\text{ dB}$ half-power attenuation ($|H| = 1/\sqrt{2}$) and the $-90^\circ$ phase lag at crossover.

Why, then, do studio monitor loudspeakers rarely use a single 2nd-order Butterworth crossover? Because at the crossover frequency $s = j$, the low-pass output lags by $-90^\circ$ ($-i/\sqrt{2}$) while the high-pass output leads by $+90^\circ$ ($+i/\sqrt{2}$)—a $180^\circ$ phase opposition that causes a deep acoustic cancellation null! In 1976, Siegfried Linkwitz and Russ Riley solved this by cascading *two* 2nd-order Butterworth filters in series (`LR4`), squaring the transfer function so both drivers sit at $-6.02\text{ dB}$ ($|H| = 0.5$) and are in phase at $-180^\circ$, summing acoustically back to unity gain ($0.5 + 0.5 = 1.0$, $0\text{ dB}$):

$$H_{\text{LR4}}(j) = [H_{\text{Butter2}}(j)]^2 = \left(-\frac{i}{\sqrt{2}}\right)^2 = -0.500000 + 0.000000i \implies 20 \log_{10}(0.5) = -6.02\text{ dB}$$

Constructing $-i/\sqrt{2}$ in $(Y, X)$ with full precision and squaring in place via `0 [ENTER] 2 [√x] [1/x] [+/-] [↰] [CMPLX] [↰] [x²]` lands on exact Real **`-0.500000`** and Imag **`0.000000`**, from which `[x⇄y] [ABS] [↰] [LOG] 20 [×]` confirms the $-6.0206\text{ dB}$ crossover attenuation:

| Step | Keystroke | Register T | Register Z | Register Y | Register X | Notes & State Analysis |
| :---: | :--- | :---: | :---: | :---: | :---: | :--- |
| 1 | `0 [ENTER] 2 [√x] [1/x] [+/-]` | $0.0000$ | $0.0000$ | $0.0000$ | $-0.707107$ | Construct exact Butterworth response $0 - i/\sqrt{2}$ |
| 2 | `[↰] [CMPLX] [↰] [x²]` | $0.0000$ | $0.0000$ | **$-0.500000$** | **$0.000000$** | Evaluate $[H_{\text{Butter2}}]^2$; Real in $Y$, Imag in $X$ |
| 3 | `[x⇄y] [ABS]` | $0.0000$ | $0.0000$ | $0.0000$ | $0.500000$ | Inspect Real component magnitude $\lvert H\rvert = 0.5$ |
| 4 | `[↰] [LOG] 20 [×]` | $0.0000$ | $0.0000$ | $0.0000$ | **$-6.020600$** | Calculate $-6.02\text{ dB}$ acoustic crossover attenuation |

When implementing active audio filters with operational amplifiers, complex impedance ratios determine the stage gain. Suppose an inverting active bandpass filter uses a parallel RC feedback network $Z_f = 10\text{ k}\Omega \parallel 10\text{ nF}$ and a series RC input network $Z_{\text{in}} = 1\text{ k}\Omega + 100\text{ nF}$. At the center angular frequency $\omega = 10,000\text{ rad/s}$ ($f = 1,591.55\text{ Hz}$), where $1/(\omega C_f) = 10\text{ k}\Omega$ and $1/(\omega C_{\text{in}}) = 1\text{ k}\Omega$, the feedback and input impedances are $Z_f = 5000 - 5000i\,\Omega$ and $Z_{\text{in}} = 1000 - 1000i\,\Omega$, giving a complex voltage gain $A_v = -Z_f / Z_{\text{in}}$ of:

$$Z_f = \frac{10000}{1 + j} = 5000 - 5000i\,\Omega, \quad Z_{\text{in}} = 1000 - 1000i\,\Omega \implies A_v = -\frac{Z_f}{Z_{\text{in}}} = -\frac{5000(1 - i)}{1000(1 - i)} = -5.0 + 0i$$

Because both networks share the exact same $-45^\circ$ phase angle at $\omega_0 = 10,000\text{ rad/s}$, executing `5000 [ENTER] 5000 [+/-] [ENTER] 1000 [ENTER] 1000 [+/-] [↰] [CMPLX] [÷] [↰] [CMPLX] [+/-] [x⇄y]` cancels their reactive phase shifts completely via complex division and negation, yielding pure inverting gain $A_v = \mathbf{-5.000000}$ + **`-5`** $i$ ($13.98\text{ dB}$):

| :---: | :--- | :---: | :---: | :---: | :---: | :--- |
| 1 | `5000 [ENTER] 5000 [+/-] [ENTER]` | $0.0000$ | $5000.0000$ | $-5000.0000$ | $-5000.0000$ | Feedback impedance $Z_f$ pushed |

## 5.7 RF Transmission Lines, Reflection Coefficient ($\Gamma$), VSWR & Smith Chart

When an electromagnetic wave travels down a coaxial cable of characteristic impedance $Z_0$ (typically $50\,\Omega$) and strikes an antenna whose load impedance $\mathbf{Z}_L = R_L + jX_L$ does not match $Z_0$, boundary conditions for voltage and current cannot be satisfied by a forward wave alone. Part of the incident wave bounces back toward the transmitter—just like a beam of light partially reflecting off a glass window when the refractive index jumps.

In 1939, Bell Labs engineer Phillip H. Smith showed that the entire semi-infinite right half of the complex impedance plane ($R_L \ge 0$) can be mapped inside the unit circle via a bilinear Möbius transformation, defining the complex **voltage reflection coefficient** $\mathbf{\Gamma}$ (whose polar plot is the famous **Smith Chart**):
$$\mathbf{\Gamma} = \frac{\mathbf{Z}_L - Z_0}{\mathbf{Z}_L + Z_0} = \frac{\mathbf{z} - 1}{\mathbf{z} + 1}, \quad \text{where } \mathbf{z} = \frac{\mathbf{Z}_L}{Z_0} = r + jx$$
When the load is perfectly matched ($\mathbf{Z}_L = Z_0$), $\mathbf{\Gamma} = 0$ sits at the exact bullseye center of the Smith Chart and $100\%$ of power enters the antenna. When a mismatch is present ($0 < |\mathbf{\Gamma}| \le 1$), the interfering forward and reflected waves set up a stationary interference pattern along the coax whose peak-to-trough voltage ratio is the **Voltage Standing Wave Ratio (VSWR)**, while the reflected power fraction $|\mathbf{\Gamma}|^2$ determines the **Return Loss ($RL$)** and **Mismatch Loss ($ML$)**:
$$\text{VSWR} = \frac{1 + |\mathbf{\Gamma}|}{1 - |\mathbf{\Gamma}|}, \qquad RL = -20 \log_{10} |\mathbf{\Gamma}|\;\text{(dB)}, \qquad ML = -10 \log_{10} \left(1 - |\mathbf{\Gamma}|^2\right)\;\text{(dB)}$$

### 5.7.1 Antenna Feedline Mismatch, VNA $S_{11}$ & Quarter-Wave Matching

Suppose a dipole antenna with measured feedpoint impedance $\mathbf{Z}_L = 75.0 + 40.0i\,\Omega$ is connected to a $Z_0 = 50.0\,\Omega$ coaxial feedline. Subtracting and adding the real $50\,\Omega$ characteristic impedance gives the complex numerator $\mathbf{Z}_L - Z_0 = 25 + 40i\,\Omega$ and denominator $\mathbf{Z}_L + Z_0 = 125 + 40i\,\Omega$:
$$\mathbf{\Gamma} = \frac{(75 + 40i) - 50}{(75 + 40i) + 50} = \frac{25 + 40i}{125 + 40i}$$

We load the numerator into $(T, Z)$ (`25 [ENTER] 40 [ENTER]`), the denominator into $(Y, X)$ (`125 [ENTER] 40`), and press `[↰] [CMPLX] [÷]` to obtain $\mathbf{\Gamma} = \mathbf{0.274311 + 0.232221i}$. Swapping to polar coordinates via `[x⇄y] [↰] [▸θ,r]` immediately reveals the reflection magnitude $|\mathbf{\Gamma}| = \mathbf{0.359406}$ in Register $X$ and phase angle $\theta_\Gamma = 0.702494\text{ rad}$ ($40.25^\circ$) in Register $Y$. From $|\mathbf{\Gamma}| = 0.359406$, the standing wave ratio follows as `0.359406 [ENTER] [ENTER] 1 [+] [x⇄y] 1 [x⇄y] [-] [÷]` $\implies \text{VSWR} = \mathbf{2.1221}$, and the return loss as `0.359406 [↰] [LOG] 20 [×] [+/-]` $\implies RL = \mathbf{8.89\text{ dB}}$ ($8.8883\text{ dB}$):

When an RF engineer characterizes a microwave filter or cellular antenna on a Vector Network Analyzer (VNA), the instrument measures this reflection coefficient directly as the input **scattering parameter** $S_{11}$. Suppose a port exhibits $S_{11} = 0.25 - 0.40i$. What is its **Return Loss ($\text{RL}$)** in decibels (how many dB the reflected wave is suppressed below the incident carrier)?

$$|S_{11}| = \sqrt{0.25^2 + (-0.40)^2} = \sqrt{0.0625 + 0.1600} = \sqrt{0.2225} \approx 0.471699, \qquad \text{RL} = -20 \log_{10}(0.471699) = 6.527\text{ dB}$$

Loading $S_{11}$ via `0.25 [ENTER] 0.40 [+/-]` and bridging to polar coordinates with `[x⇄y] [↰] [▸θ,r]` leaves phase $\theta = -1.012197\text{ rad}$ ($-58.0^\circ$) in Register $Y$ and reflection magnitude $|S_{11}| = 0.471699$ in Register $X$. Completing the sequence `0.25 [ENTER] 0.40 [+/-] [↰] [▸θ,r] [↰] [LOG] 20 [×] [+/-]` converts that magnitude directly into Return Loss $\text{RL} =$ **`6.5266998468`** $\text{dB}$ (and if you also need the standing wave ratio $\text{VSWR} = (1+|S_{11}|)/(1-|S_{11}|) = 2.786$, pressing `[↰] [LASTX]` right after `[↰] [LOG]` recovers $|S_{11}|$).

Once a reflection mismatch is measured, how do you match a $Z_L = 100\,\Omega$ patch antenna to a $Z_0 = 50\,\Omega$ transmitter feedline without lumped inductors or capacitors? A transmission line segment of length $\ell = \lambda/4$ ($90^\circ$ of electrical phase shift one way, or $180^\circ$ round-trip across the Smith Chart) acts as a hardware **impedance inverter** $Z_{\text{in}} = Z_{\text{line}}^2 / Z_L$. Choosing the quarter-wave section's characteristic impedance as the geometric mean $Z_{\text{line}} = \sqrt{Z_0 Z_L} = \sqrt{50 \times 100} \approx 70.7107\,\Omega$ transforms the $100\,\Omega$ load into an exact $50\,\Omega$ input match:

$$Z_{\text{in}} = \frac{70.7107^2}{100.0} = \frac{5000.0}{100.0} = 50.00\,\Omega$$

Squaring $Z_{\text{line}} = 70.7107\,\Omega$ in place and dividing by $Z_L = 100\,\Omega$ via `70.7107 [↰] [x²] 100 [÷]` confirms the **$50.0000\,\Omega$** impedance match:

| Step | Keystroke | Register T | Register Z | Register Y | Register X | Notes & State Analysis |
| :---: | :--- | :---: | :---: | :---: | :---: | :--- |
| 1 | `70.7107` | $0.0000$ | $0.0000$ | $0.0000$ | $70.7107$ | Enter line characteristic impedance $Z_0$ |
| 2 | `[↰] [x²]` | $0.0000$ | $0.0000$ | $0.0000$ | $5000.0031$ | Square characteristic impedance $Z_0^2$ |
| 3 | `100 [÷]` | $0.0000$ | $0.0000$ | $0.0000$ | **$50.0000$** | Divide by load resistance $Z_L$; matched $Z_{\text{in}} = 50.0\,\Omega$ |

### 5.7.2 Lossy Telegrapher's Equations & Complex Characteristic Impedance

In an ideal lossless coaxial cable ($R' = G' = 0$), the characteristic impedance $Z_0 = \sqrt{L'/C'}$ is a pure real resistance ($50\,\Omega$). In a real physical cable with series copper resistance $R' = 0.1\,\Omega/\text{m}$, inductance $L' = 0.25\,\mu\text{H/m}$, dielectric shunt conductance $G' = 1\,\mu\text{S/m}$, and capacitance $C' = 100\,\text{pF/m}$ operating at $\omega = 10^7\text{ rad/s}$, Oliver Heaviside's telegrapher's equations yield a **complex characteristic impedance**:

$$Z_0 = \sqrt{\frac{R' + j\omega L'}{G' + j\omega C'}} = \sqrt{\frac{0.1 + 2.5i}{10^{-6} + 10^{-3}i}} \approx \mathbf{50.0095 - 0.9748i\,\Omega}$$

Loading the series impedance per meter $Z' = 0.1 + 2.5i$ into $(T, Z)$, the shunt admittance per meter $Y' = 10^{-6} + 10^{-3}i$ into $(Y, X)$, dividing via `[↰] [CMPLX] [÷]`, and taking the complex square root via `[↰] [CMPLX] [√x]` reveals how copper loss perturbs $Z_0$ to $\mathbf{50.0095 - 0.9748i\,\Omega}$:

| Step | Keystroke | Register T | Register Z | Register Y | Register X | Notes & State Analysis |
| :---: | :--- | :---: | :---: | :---: | :---: | :--- |
| 1 | `0.1 [ENTER] 2.5 [ENTER]` | $0.0000$ | $0.1000$ | $2.5000$ | $2.5000$ | Load series impedance $Z' = 0.1 + 2.5i$ |
| 2 | `1 [E] 6 [+/-] [ENTER] 1 [E] 3 [+/-]` | $0.1000$ | $2.5000$ | $1.0000 \times 10^{-6}$ | $1.0000 \times 10^{-3}$ | Load shunt admittance $Y'$ into $(Y, X)$ |
| 3 | `[↰] [CMPLX] [÷]` | $0.1000$ | $0.1000$ | $2499.9975$ | $-97.4999$ | Complex impedance ratio $Z'/Y'$ |
| 4 | `[↰] [CMPLX] [√x]` | $0.1000$ | $0.1000$ | **$50.0095$** | **$-0.9748$** | Characteristic impedance $Z_0 = \sqrt{Z'/Y'}$ |

## 5.8 Complex Powers, Roots of Unity, Analytic Continuation & Domain Guards

Because Euler's formula writes any complex number in polar form as $z = r e^{i\theta}$, raising a complex number to the $n$-th power simply raises its radius to $r^n$ while multiplying its angle by $n\theta$ (**Abraham de Moivre's theorem**), and taking an $n$-th root divides its angle into $n$ equally spaced spokes around the circle:
$$z = r e^{i\theta} \implies z^n = r^n e^{i n \theta} = r^n (\cos(n\theta) + i\sin(n\theta))$$
$$\sqrt[n]{z} = r^{1/n} \left[\cos\left(\frac{\theta + 2k\pi}{n}\right) + i\sin\left(\frac{\theta + 2k\pi}{n}\right)\right], \quad k = 0, 1, \dots, n-1$$

### 5.8.1 Principal Roots of $i$, Cube Roots of $-8$, and General Complex Powers

When 16th-century algebraists first encountered $i = \sqrt{-1}$, critics feared that taking the square root of $i$ itself ($\sqrt{i}$) would require inventing yet another "more imaginary" dimension outside the complex plane. Carl Friedrich Gauss and Jean-Robert Argand proved that the complex plane is algebraically closed: on the *Unit Circle Volvelle*, $i = 0 + 1i$ is simply a unit vector pointing straight up at $90^\circ$ ($\pi/2\text{ rad}$), so taking its principal square root takes the square root of its unit length ($\sqrt{1} = 1$) while bisecting its angle in half to **$45^\circ$** ($\pi/4\text{ rad}$) in the first quadrant—the exact $45^\circ$ phase angle of Warburg electrochemical diffusion and RF skin-effect impedance:

$$\sqrt{i} = \sqrt{0 + 1i} = e^{i\pi/4} = \cos\left(\frac{\pi}{4}\right) + i\sin\left(\frac{\pi}{4}\right) = \frac{\sqrt{2}}{2} + \frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}i \approx 0.707107 + 0.707107i$$

Entering the pure imaginary unit $0 + 1i$ with `0 [ENTER] 1` (placing Real $= 0$ in $Y$ and Imag $= 1$ in $X$) and executing `0 [ENTER] 1 [↰] [CMPLX] [√x]` evaluates the complex square root in place, leaving $Y = \mathbf{0.707107}$ and $X = \mathbf{0.7071067812}$.

Similarly, on the real number line, the equation $z^3 = -8$ has only the negative root $z = -2$. In the complex plane, however, $-8$ sits on the negative real axis at polar angle $\theta = \pi\text{ rad}$ ($180^\circ$): $z^3 = 8 e^{i\pi}$. By de Moivre's theorem, its three cube roots sit at the vertices of an equilateral triangle on a circle of radius $8^{1/3} = 2$, starting with the **principal root** at one-third of the angle ($\theta_0 = \pi/3 = 60^\circ$):

$$z_0 = 8^{1/3} e^{i\pi/3} = 2 \left(\cos\frac{\pi}{3} + i\sin\frac{\pi}{3}\right) = 2(0.5 + 0.866025i) = 1.0 + 1.732051i$$

Loading the base $z_2 = -8 + 0i$ into $(T, Z)$ (`8 [+/-] [ENTER] 0 [ENTER]`) and evaluating the cube root via `8 [+/-] [ENTER] 0 [ENTER] 0.333333333333 [ENTER] 0 [↰] [CMPLX] [yˣ] [x⇄y]` yields **`1`** in Register $X$, or forming the exact rational exponent $z_1 = 1/3 + 0i$ in $(Y, X)$ via `8 [+/-] [ENTER] 0 [ENTER] 0.333333333333 [ENTER] 0 [↰] [CMPLX] [yˣ]` evaluates the principal branch $e^{(1/3)\ln(-8)} = 2 e^{i\pi/3}$ to full precision, yielding $(Y = \mathbf{1.000000},\; X = \mathbf{1.7320508075})$.

Even more generally, the binary complex power operator `[↰] [CMPLX] [yˣ]` evaluates $\mathbf{z}_2^{\mathbf{z}_1} = e^{\mathbf{z}_1 \ln(\mathbf{z}_2)}$ when *both* the base and the exponent are complex numbers! To evaluate $(1 + i)^{(1 - i)}$, we load the base $\mathbf{z}_2 = 1 + i$ into $(T, Z)$ (`1 [ENTER] 1 [ENTER]`), load the exponent $\mathbf{z}_1 = 1 - i$ into $(Y, X)$ (`1 [ENTER] 1 [+/-]`), and press `[↰] [CMPLX] [yˣ]` to obtain **$2.807879 + 1.317865i$**:

| Step | Keystroke | Register T | Register Z | Register Y | Register X | Notes & State Analysis |
| :---: | :--- | :---: | :---: | :---: | :---: | :--- |
| 1 | `1 [ENTER] 1 [ENTER]` | $0.0000$ | $1.0000$ | $1.0000$ | $1.0000$ | Base $z_2 = 1 + i$ loaded into $(T, Z)$ |
| 2 | `1 [ENTER] 1 [+/-]` | $1.0000$ | $1.0000$ | $1.0000$ | $-1.0000$ | Exponent $z_1 = 1 - i$ loaded into $(Y, X)$ |
| 3 | `[↰] [CMPLX] [yˣ]` | $1.0000$ | $1.0000$ | **$2.807879$** | **$1.317865$** | General complex power $z_2^{z_1}$ evaluated |

Watch what happens when you use `[↰] [CMPLX] [yˣ]` to raise the imaginary unit $i$ to the $i$-th power ($i^i$): because $i = e^{i\pi/2}$, Euler's identity predicts that $i^i = \left(e^{i\pi/2}\right)^i = e^{i^2 \pi/2} = e^{-\pi/2} \approx 0.207880$ is a **purely real number**! Loading $z = 0 + 1i$ into both $(T, Z)$ and $(Y, X)$ and pressing `[↰] [CMPLX] [yˣ]` via `0 [ENTER] 1 [ENTER] 0 [ENTER] 1 [↰] [CMPLX] [yˣ]` immediately lands on $(Y = \mathbf{0.207880},\; X = \mathbf{0.000000})$.

### 5.8.2 Complex Circular Functions & Analytic Continuation ($\sin^2 z + \cos^2 z = 1$)

Stepping from algebraic roots to complex trigonometry reveals an even deeper surprise. For a real angle $x$, $\sin x$ is trapped forever between $-1$ and $+1$. What happens when we feed a complex argument $z = x + iy = 1 + 2i$ into `[↰] [CMPLX] [SIN]`? By Euler's definition $\sin z = (e^{iz} - e^{-iz})/(2i)$, the imaginary component $iy$ becomes a real exponential $e^{\mp y}$, coupling circular oscillation along $x$ with hyperbolic growth ($\cosh y, \sinh y$) along $y$—which is why $\sin(1 + 2i)$ has a magnitude greater than $3.7$!

$$\sin(x + iy) = \sin x \cosh y + i \cos x \sinh y$$
$$\text{Real} = \sin(1)\cosh(2) \approx 0.841471 \times 3.762196 = 3.165779, \quad \text{Imag} = \cos(1)\sinh(2) \approx 0.540302 \times 3.626860 = 1.959601$$

Keying `1 [ENTER] 2` to load $1 + 2i$ into $(Y, X)$ and executing `1 [ENTER] 2 [↰] [CMPLX] [SIN]` evaluates the complex sine in place, producing $(Y = \mathbf{3.165779},\; X = \mathbf{1.9596010414})$. By the same Euler expansion, the complex cosine $\cos(x + iy)$ describes damped standing waves on lossy transmission lines and evanescent waveguide modes:

$$\cos(x + iy) = \cos x \cosh y - i \sin x \sinh y$$
$$\text{Real} = \cos(1)\cosh(2) = 0.540302 \times 3.762196 = 2.032723, \quad \text{Imag} = -\sin(1)\sinh(2) = -0.841471 \times 3.626860 = -3.051898$$

Entering $1 + 2i$ and evaluating the complex cosine via `1 [ENTER] 2 [↰] [CMPLX] [COS]` yields $(Y = \mathbf{2.032723},\; X = \mathbf{-3.051897799})$. Even though $\sin(1+2i)$ and $\cos(1+2i)$ in our complex sine and cosine evaluations above grew far outside $[-1, +1]$, the principle of **analytic continuation** guarantees that the Pythagorean identity $\sin^2 z + \cos^2 z = 1$ still holds across the entire complex plane! Let us square both complex outputs and add them together on the stack:

$$\sin^2(1+2i) + \cos^2(1+2i) = (6.182115 + 12.407147i) + (-5.182115 - 12.407147i) = 1.000000 + 0.000000i$$

Notice how the large $\pm 12.407147i$ imaginary cross-terms cancel each other while $6.182115 - 5.182115$ collapses back to $1.000000$ (and if you chain the calculation directly from $z = 1+2i$ via `1 [ENTER] 2 [↰] [CMPLX] [SIN] [↰] [CMPLX] [↰] [x²] 1 [ENTER] 2 [↰] [CMPLX] [COS] [↰] [CMPLX] [↰] [x²] [↰] [CMPLX] [+]`, it holds to full 64-bit precision):

| Step | Keystroke | Register T | Register Z | Register Y | Register X | Notes & State Analysis |
| :---: | :--- | :---: | :---: | :---: | :---: | :--- |
| 1 | `3.165779 [ENTER] 1.959601` | $0.0000$ | $0.0000$ | $3.165779$ | $1.959601$ | Load $\sin(1+2i)$ from above |
| 2 | `[↰] [CMPLX] [↰] [x²]` | $0.0000$ | $0.0000$ | $6.182115$ | $12.407147$ | Square complex sine $(\sin z)^2$ |
| 3 | `2.032723 [ENTER] 3.051898 [+/-]` | $6.182115$ | $12.407147$ | $2.032723$ | $-3.051898$ | Load $\cos(1+2i)$ from above |
| 4 | `[↰] [CMPLX] [↰] [x²]` | $6.182115$ | $12.407147$ | $-5.182115$ | $-12.407147$ | Square complex cosine $(\cos z)^2$ |
| 5 | `[↰] [CMPLX] [+]` | $6.182115$ | $6.182115$ | **$1.000000$** | **$0.000000$** | Sum squares: $\sin^2 z + \cos^2 z = 1 + 0i$ |

### 5.8.3 Poles, Branch Cuts, and Non-Destructive Complex Recovery

Because complex arithmetic pairs two registers for every operand, the SC-32 firmware enforces strict boundary guards to keep the $(T, Z)$ and $(Y, X)$ register pairs synchronized. Pressing `[↰] [CMPLX]` illuminates the `[↰] [CMPLX]` annunciator in the status bar for the next operation only; if you tap `[↰] [CMPLX]` by mistake, pressing `[C]` cancels the prefix cleanly without displacing or clearing a single stack value. When evaluating a complex quotient $\mathbf{z}_{\text{num}} / \mathbf{z}_{\text{den}}$ via `[↰] [CMPLX] [÷]`, always load the numerator $\mathbf{z}_{\text{num}}$ into Registers $(T, Z)$ first and the denominator $\mathbf{z}_{\text{den}}$ into Registers $(Y, X)$ second; if you ever enter them in reverse order, you do not need to re-type the four components—simply press `[↰] [CMPLX] [1/x]` to take the complex reciprocal of $(Y, X)$ in place!

What happens at a pole or singularity in the complex plane? Attempting complex division by the origin $0 + 0i$ (`0 [ENTER] 0` followed by `[↰] [CMPLX] [÷]` or `[↰] [CMPLX] [1/x]`) halts with `DIVIDE BY 0` (Code 01) and leaves all four stack registers intact; similarly, pressing `[↰] [CMPLX] [LN]` at the origin $0 + 0i$ halts with `DIVIDE BY 0` (Code 01) without corrupting the stack, until you press `[C]` to clear the error banner. Likewise, while the SC-32 supports complex algebraic powers, roots, exponentials, natural logarithms, and direct circular functions (`SIN`, `COS`, `TAN`), attempting an unsupported combination such as `[↰] [CMPLX] [↰] [ASIN]` or `[↰] [CMPLX] [↰] [HYP]` displays `INVALID DATA` (Code 02) non-destructively so you can evaluate the corresponding logarithmic conformal mapping directly on the stack.

## 5.9 Summary & Looking Ahead

Chapter 5 unified complex algebra and alternating current phasor analysis on the operational stack. By treating the physical coordinate pair $(Y, X)$ as real and imaginary components ($Y + Xi$), you executed complex arithmetic, inverted reactive admittances, validated Euler's identity ($e^{i\pi} + 1 = 0$), and solved multi-branch impedance networks in place via `[↰] [CMPLX]`. Without scratchpad bookkeeping or complex-mode matrix software, two-dimensional algebraic quantities flowed through the stack with the speed and certainty of real numbers.

Yet every two-dimensional electromagnetic phasor, Linkwitz-Riley audio crossover wave, and damped mechanical oscillation studied in this chapter must ultimately live inside—and radiate from—a **three-dimensional physical structure**: a bass-reflex loudspeaker cabinet, an extruded aluminum RF heat sink, a titanium pressure hull, or a 3D-printed instrument shell. In **[Chapter 6: Analytic & Solid Geometry, Surface Area & Mensuration](sc32/06-geometry-surface-area.md)**, we step from the 2D complex plane into 3D physical space to calculate the planar areas, enclosed volumes, rotational moments of inertia, and convective cooling boundaries of those enclosures—using the **Surface Area via Stats Mode (`[Σ+]`)** technique to accumulate multi-faceted solids on the hardware statistical bus without scratch paper or parentheses.

# Chapter 6: Analytic & Solid Geometry, Surface Area & Mensuration

## 6.1 The Heat Sink, the Rocket Nozzle & Surface-to-Volume Scaling

In his 1638 treatise *Two New Sciences* (*Discorsi e dimostrazioni matematiche intorno a due nuove scienze*) *([Galilei, 1638](sc32/appendix-e-annotated-bibliography.md#cite-galilei1638))*, **Galileo Galilei** formulated the geometric **Square-Cube Law**: scaling any physical body by a linear factor $\ell$ multiplies its heat-dissipating and load-bearing surface area by the square ($\ell^2$) while multiplying its heat-generating volume and mass by the cube ($\ell^3$). Across biology, thermodynamics, aerodynamic friction, chemical catalysis, and semiconductor cooling, that $A/V \propto \ell^2 / \ell^3 = 1/\ell$ scaling asymmetry is the governing physical bottleneck.

Inside a modern high-performance microprocessor, billions of nanometer-scale transistors switch at gigahertz frequencies, generating localized thermal flux exceeding $100\text{ W/cm}^2$ *([Incropera et al., 2007](sc32/appendix-e-annotated-bibliography.md#cite-incropera2007))*—a power density approaching the heat flux inside a nuclear reactor core. Under Fourier's Law of Thermal Conduction and Newton's Law of Cooling *([Incropera et al., 2007](sc32/appendix-e-annotated-bibliography.md#cite-incropera2007))*, convective heat removal from a solid boundary to an ambient fluid is governed by:

$$\dot{Q} = h \cdot A_{\text{surface}} \cdot (T_{\text{solid}} - T_{\text{fluid}})$$

Because the heat dissipation rate $\dot{Q}$ is directly proportional to exposed surface area $A_{\text{surface}}$, inadequate boundary area causes internal junction temperatures to soar. This physical law links microprocessor pin-fin heat sinks directly to biological thermoregulation across the animal kingdom:
* **Why Hummingbirds Enter Torpor While Elephants Grow Ear-Fins:** A $3\text{-gram}$ **ruby-throated hummingbird** ($\ell \approx 2\text{ cm}$) has a massive surface-area-to-volume ratio ($A/V \propto 1/\ell$), radiating body heat so rapidly relative to its tiny thermal mass that its heart must beat $1,200\text{ times per minute}$ by day and plunge into deep hypothermic **torpor** at night to avoid starving. Conversely, a $5,000\text{-kilogram}$ **African elephant** ($\ell \approx 200\text{ cm}$—a $100\times$ linear scale-up that multiplies heat-producing volume by $100^3 = 1,000,000\times$ while multiplying skin area by only $100^2 = 10,000\times$) has $1/100\text{th}$ the relative cooling surface and would fatally overheat without pumping blood through huge, thin, vascularized **ear-fins**.
* **Extruded Silicon Heat Sinks:** A high-power microprocessor faces the exact elephant bottleneck: machining or extruding aluminum into dozens of parallel fins adds no volume—in fact, it removes material—yet it multiplies the effective convective surface area by more than $2,500\%$.

In real-world aerospace enclosures and consumer instruments, geometry is never composed of tidy textbook cubes. Enclosures feature drafted mold tooling angles, filleted stress-relief radii, cylindrical fastener bosses, and compound chamfers. Rather than scribbling fragile intermediate area calculations across scratch paper, the engineer audits the physical artifact polygon by polygon directly on the RPN stack:
* Primary exterior faces accumulate into the statistical bus via `[Σ+]`.
* Internal mounting apertures, screw countersinks, and display cutouts subtract via `[↰] [Σ-]`.
* The LCD counter ($n = 1, 2, 3 \dots$) tracks every verified face.
* Recalling `[↱] [SUMS]` → `Σx` instantly produces the certified boundary surface area.

## 6.2 From Caliper Datums to the Statistical Accumulator Bus

Every spatial mensuration problem begins with physical geometry: measuring the exterior length, width, height, and wall thickness of a machined enclosure, a truncated cone frustum, or a polyhedral truss with vernier calipers. Rather than transcribing individual face measurements onto paper and keying a fragile chain of parenthesized products, the StackCalc SC-32 maps each physical face directly onto the **Statistical Accumulator Bus (`[Σ+]`)**.

As you compute the area of each boundary face in Register $X$, pressing `[Σ+]` adds that face area into the dedicated $\Sigma x$ summation register while incrementing the face counter $n$ in Register $X$ ($n = 1, 2, 3, \dots$). You can inspect the running face count on the transflective LCD after every step, recall the accumulated total surface area via `[Σx]`, and extend the same 4-register pipeline to three-dimensional Euclidean norms $d = \sqrt{\Delta x^2 + \Delta y^2 + \Delta z^2}$ and parallel-axis moments of inertia $I = I_{\text{cm}} + md^2$.

## 6.3 2D Plane Geometry, Regular Polygons & Conic Sections

Before accumulating three-dimensional bounding surfaces, we establish the planar area and perimeter primitives that govern individual cross-sections, machine flanges, polygon blanks, and conic slices.

### 6.3.1 2D Plane Area Primitives & Difference-of-Squares Annuli
The SC-32 evaluates 2D plane geometric regions using rapid, parenthesis-free RPN keystroke pipelines. In high-speed STEM tournaments and engineering analysis, these primitives collapse multi-step trigonometric and radical reductions into continuous tactile reductions:

| Geometric Region | Analytical Area Formula | Physical & Geometric Motivation | RPN Keystroke Pipeline |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **Rectangle** | $A = l \times w$ | Orthogonal Cartesian product of orthogonal basis vectors. | `l [ENTER] w [×]` |
| **Triangle (Base/Height)** | $A = \frac{1}{2} b \times h$ | Half of the circumscribing parallelogram. | `b [ENTER] h [×] 2 [÷]` |
| **Circle** | $A = \pi r^2$ | Integration of concentric infinitesimal rings ($dA = 2\pi r dr$). | `r [↰] [x²] [↱] [π] [×]` |
| **Circular Sector** | $A = \frac{1}{2} r^2 \theta$ ($\theta$ in rad) | Fractional aperture $(\theta / 2\pi)$ scaled to full circle area $\pi r^2$. | `r [↰] [x²] θ [×] 2 [÷]` |
| **Circular Segment** | $A = \frac{1}{2} r^2 (\theta - \sin\theta)$ | Sector area minus triangular chord core ($\frac{1}{2} r^2 \sin\theta$). | `θ [ENTER] [SIN] [-] r [↰] [x²] [×] 2 [÷]` |
| **Circular Annulus** | $A = \pi (R^2 - r^2) = \pi(R-r)(R+r)$ | Difference of concentric disks; factored via difference-of-squares. | `R [ENTER] r [-] R [ENTER] r [+] [×] [↱] [π] [×]` |
| **Trapezoid** | $A = \frac{1}{2} (a + b) h$ | Average parallel base length multiplied by perpendicular altitude. | `a [ENTER] b [+] h [×] 2 [÷]` |
| **Ellipse** | $A = \pi a b$ | Area under 2D affine scaling of unit circle by semimajor axes $a, b$. | `a [ENTER] b [×] [↱] [π] [×]` |
| **Parabolic Segment** | $A = \frac{2}{3} b h$ | Archimedes' quadrature: segment is exactly $\frac{4}{3}$ of inscribed triangle. | `b [ENTER] h [×] 2 [×] 3 [÷]` |
| **Regular $n$-gon** | $A = \frac{1}{4} n s^2 \cot(\pi/n)$ | Decomposition into $n$ congruent central isosceles triangles. | `[↱] [π] n [÷] [TAN] [1/x] s [↰] [x²] [×] n [×] 4 [÷]` |
| **Cyclic Quadrilateral** | $A = \sqrt{(s-a)(s-b)(s-c)(s-d)}$ | Brahmagupta's formula: 4-term cyclic extension of Heron's formula. | Four stack factors multiplied inside-out $\to$ `[√x]` |

For the master quick-reference tables of all 2D plane sections and perimeter formulas, consult **[Appendix D: Section 7 (Coordinate Geometry, Mensuration & 2D Curved Sections)](sc32/appendix-d-constants-and-equations.md)**.

Notice how factoring a circular ring (annulus) simplifies pipe-flange and pressure-vessel calculations. When bolting together an ASME B16.5 high-pressure flange joint, the required bolt preload depends on the seating contact area of the ring-shaped neoprene gasket—an **annulus** bounded by outer radius $R = 85.0\text{ mm}$ and inner pipe bore radius $r = 50.0\text{ mm}$. Rather than multiplying by $\pi$ twice ($\pi R^2 - \pi r^2$), we factor $\pi$ outside the difference of squares:

$$A = \pi (R^2 - r^2) = \pi (85^2 - 50^2) = \pi (7225 - 2500) = 4725\pi \approx \mathbf{14,844.0253\text{ mm}^2}$$

Keying `85 [↰] [x²] 50 [↰] [x²] [-] [↱] [π] [×]` computes the squared outer radius $R^2 = 7,225$ (`85 [↰] [x²]`), subtracts the squared inner bore $r^2 = 2,500$ (`50 [↰] [x²] [-]`) to leave $4,725.0\text{ mm}^2$ in Register $X$, and scales by `[↱] [π] [×]` to return **`14,844.02529`** (**$14,844.03\text{ mm}^2$**, or $148.44\text{ cm}^2$). Better still, when $R \approx r$ in thin-walled pressure vessel shells, keying `R [ENTER] r [-] R [ENTER] r [+] [×] [↱] [π] [×]` avoids squaring two nearly equal numbers and preserves full floating-point precision.

What if an enclosure cover is a regular polygon rather than a circular flange? How do you find the area of a regular octagonal sheet-metal face plate of edge length $s = 65.0\text{ mm}$ without looking up trigonometric cotangents? Picture a regular octagon as a bounding square of width $(1 + \sqrt{2})s$ with four $45^\circ$ right-isosceles corner triangles of leg $s/\sqrt{2}$ clipped off the four corners. Subtracting those four corner triangles leaves $A = 2(1 + \sqrt{2})s^2 = 2\delta_S s^2$, where $\delta_S = 1 + \sqrt{2} \approx 2.414214$ is the **silver ratio**:

$$A = 2 (1 + \sqrt{2}) s^2 \approx 4.828427 \times 65^2 = 4.828427 \times 4225 = \mathbf{20,400.1047\text{ mm}^2}$$

Entering `2 [√x] 1 [+] 2 [×] 65 [↰] [x²] [×]` builds the octagonal shape multiplier $2(1 + \sqrt{2}) \approx 4.828427$ directly on the stack (`2 [√x] 1 [+] 2 [×]`), squares the edge length $s = 65\text{ mm}$ (`65 [↰] [x²]`), and multiplies (`[×]`) to yield **`20,400.1046`** (**$20,400.10\text{ mm}^2$**).

### 6.3.2 Ramanujan's Ellipse Perimeter & Planetary Oblateness

One of the great surprises of classical geometry is that while the *area* of an ellipse with semi-axes $(a, b)$ is the effortless product $A = \pi a b$ (a circle of radius $b$ stretched along one axis by $a/b$), its *perimeter* has no closed-form expression in elementary functions! Measuring the arc length of an ellipse requires evaluating a complete elliptic integral of the second kind—which is where elliptic integrals got their name.

In 1914, Indian mathematician Srinivasa Ramanujan published a remarkable algebraic approximation that achieves sub-parts-per-million accuracy across nearly all engineering eccentricities by defining the dimensionless flattening parameter $h = \frac{(a - b)^2}{(a + b)^2}$:
$$h = \frac{(a - b)^2}{(a + b)^2}, \qquad P \approx \pi (a + b) \left[ 1 + \frac{3h}{10 + \sqrt{4 - 3h}} \right]$$
On the SC-32 stack, Ramanujan's nested radical evaluates from the inside out without a single parenthesis: form $h = ((a - b)/(a + b))^2$, evaluate $\sqrt{4 - 3h}$ in Register $X$, add $10$ and invert via `[1/x]`, multiply by $3h$, add $1$, and scale by $\pi(a + b)$.

That same axial difference $(a - b)$ governs planetary geodesy. Because the Earth spins once every $23\text{ hr } 56\text{ min}$, centrifugal acceleration bulges the equator to $a = 6,378.137\text{ km}$ compared to the polar semi-minor axis $b = 6,356.752\text{ km}$—an equatorial bulge of $a - b = 21.385\text{ km}$. Geodesists specify this oblateness by the **reciprocal flattening** $1/f = a / (a - b)$:

$$\text{Flattening } f = \frac{a - b}{a} = 1 - \frac{b}{a} = \frac{6378.137 - 6356.752}{6378.137} = \frac{21.385}{6378.137} \approx \mathbf{\frac{1}{298.2572}}$$

Rather than typing the 7-digit equatorial radius `6378.137` twice, the sequence `6378.137 [ENTER] 6356.752 [-] 6378.137 [÷] [1/x]` duplicates $a$ into Register $Z$ on entry: keying `6378.137 [ENTER] [ENTER] 6356.752 [-]` forms $(a - b) = 21.385\text{ km}$ in Register $X$ while $a = 6,378.137\text{ km}$ drops into Register $Y$, and pressing `[x⇄y] [÷] [1/x]` resolves the reciprocal flattening **$298.2572$**—or even more compactly in just 8 keystrokes by rewriting $f = 1 - b/a$ so each radius is entered only once: `6356.752 [ENTER] 6378.137 [÷] 1 [x⇄y] [-] [1/x]` ($\to \mathbf{298.2528}$ for the three-decimal polar radius $b = 6356.752\text{ km}$).

### 6.3.3 Heron's Formula & Right-Triangle Incircles

When a surveyor or structural engineer measures the three side lengths $(a, b, c)$ of a triangular gusset plate or land parcel, finding a perpendicular altitude $h$ by trigonometry takes extra steps. In the 1st century CE, **Heron of Alexandria** showed in his *Metrica* that the area of any triangle follows directly from its **semiperimeter** $s = (a + b + c)/2$ alone:
$$s = \frac{a + b + c}{2}, \qquad A = \sqrt{s(s - a)(s - b)(s - c)}$$

Suppose a triangular parcel has sides $a = 7.0\text{ m}$, $b = 9.0\text{ m}$, and $c = 12.0\text{ m}$. Watch how storing $s$ in Variable `S` lets you build the four-factor product cleanly on the stack:
1. **Compute and store the semiperimeter $s$:** Key `7 [ENTER] 9 [+] 12 [+] 2 [÷]` (`7 [ENTER] 9 [+] 12 [+] 2 [÷]`) to obtain $s = 14.0\text{ m}$ in Register $X$, and store it via `[STO] S`.
2. **Accumulate the three $(s - \text{side})$ factors:** Since $s = 14.0$ is already sitting in Register $X$, simply key `7 [-]` to get $(s - a) = 7.0$; then key `[RCL] S 9 [-] [×]` to multiply by $(s - b) = 5.0$ ($\to 35.0$); then key `[RCL] S 12 [-] [×]` to multiply by $(s - c) = 2.0$ ($\to 70.0$).
3. **Multiply by $s$ and extract the root:** Key `[RCL] S [×] [√x]` to evaluate $\sqrt{14.0 \times 70.0} = \sqrt{980.0} = \mathbf{31.304952\text{ m}^2}$:

| Step | Keystroke | Register T | Register Z | Register Y | Register X | Notes & State Analysis |
| :---: | :--- | :---: | :---: | :---: | :---: | :--- |
| 1 | `7 [ENTER] 9 [+] 12 [+] 2 [÷] [STO] S` | $0.0000$ | $0.0000$ | $0.0000$ | $14.0000$ | Semiperimeter $s = (a+b+c)/2$ stored in `S` |
| 2 | `7 [-]` | $0.0000$ | $0.0000$ | $0.0000$ | $7.0000$ | Factor $(s - a) = 14 - 7 = 7.0$ directly from $X$ |
| 3 | `[RCL] S 9 [-] [×]` | $0.0000$ | $0.0000$ | $0.0000$ | $35.0000$ | Multiply by $(s - b) = 5.0$; subtotal $= 35.0$ |
| 4 | `[RCL] S 12 [-] [×]` | $0.0000$ | $0.0000$ | $0.0000$ | $70.0000$ | Multiply by $(s - c) = 2.0$; subtotal $= 70.0$ |
| 5 | `[RCL] S [×] [√x]` | $0.0000$ | $0.0000$ | $0.0000$ | **$31.304952$** | Multiply by $s$ and take root; Area $= 31.30\text{ m}^2$ |

Once you know the semiperimeter $s$ of a triangle, dividing area by semiperimeter ($r = A/s$) gives the radius of its **incircle**—the largest circle that fits inside the three sides. When the triangle is a right-angled structural channel with orthogonal legs $a = 15.0\text{ cm}$ and $b = 20.0\text{ cm}$, what is the radius $r$ of the largest cylindrical coolant pipe that can be tucked inside it? By the two-tangent theorem of Euclidean geometry, the tangent segments from the $90^\circ$ corner to the incircle form a little square of side $r$, while the remaining tangent segments along the legs—$(a - r)$ and $(b - r)$—fold onto the hypotenuse $c = \sqrt{a^2 + b^2} = 25.0\text{ cm}$ so that $c = (a - r) + (b - r)$. Solving for the inradius $r$ yields a wonderfully clean linear formula:

$$r = \frac{a + b - c}{2} = \frac{15 + 20 - 25}{2} = \frac{10}{2} = \mathbf{5.0000\text{ cm}} \qquad (\text{with circumradius } R = \frac{c}{2} = 12.5\text{ cm})$$

Running `15 [↰] [x²] 20 [↰] [x²] [+] [√x] 15 [ENTER] 20 [+] [x⇄y] [-] 2 [÷]` computes the hypotenuse $c = 25.0\text{ cm}$ in Step 1 (which can also be done via `15 [ENTER] 20 [↰] [▸θ,r]`), sums the legs $a + b = 35.0\text{ cm}$ in Step 2, subtracts $c$, and halves the result to yield the exact inradius **`5.0000`** (**$r = 5.0000\text{ cm}$**):

| Step | Keystroke | Register T | Register Z | Register Y | Register X | Notes & State Analysis |
| :---: | :--- | :---: | :---: | :---: | :---: | :--- |
| 1 | `15 [↰] [x²] 20 [↰] [x²] [+] [√x]` | $0.0000$ | $0.0000$ | $0.0000$ | $25.0000$ | Hypotenuse $c = \sqrt{a^2 + b^2}$ in cm |
| 2 | `15 [ENTER] 20 [+]` | $0.0000$ | $0.0000$ | $25.0000$ | $35.0000$ | Sum of orthogonal legs $a + b$ |
| 3 | `[x⇄y] [-]` | $0.0000$ | $0.0000$ | $0.0000$ | $10.0000$ | Excess tangent span $(a + b - c)$ |
| 4 | `2 [÷]` | $0.0000$ | $0.0000$ | $0.0000$ | **$5.0000$** | Right triangle inradius $r$ in cm |

## 6.4 The Master Surface Area Technique via Stats Mode (`[Σ+]`)

In mechanical CAD, thermal design, and additive manufacturing, finding the total exterior surface area of a 3D part is traditionally a bookkeeping headache. Real-world enclosures have top and bottom lids, side walls, end caps, bosses, and cutout apertures. On an algebraic calculator, summing all those faces requires a fragile string of parenthesized products:
$$A_{\text{total}} = (2 \times L \times W) + (2 \times L \times H) + (2 \times W \times H) + \dots$$
where a single mistyped digit at face #5 forces you to re-key the entire expression from the beginning.

### 6.4.1 Turning the Statistical Accumulator (`[Σ+]`) into a Polygon Tally Bus

On the StackCalc SC-32, the **Statistical Accumulator (`[Σ+]`)** serves as a dedicated hardware summing bus that decouples each face calculation from the running total:

First, press `[CLΣ]` to clear the six internal statistical registers ($\Sigma x = 0, n = 0$). Next, compute the area $A_1$ of your first face (or symmetric face pair) on the stack and press `[Σ+]`. That single keystroke adds $A_1$ into the internal $\Sigma x$ summation register, increments the polygon counter to $n = 1$, displays $1.0000$ in Register $X$ so you can verify how many face groups you have tallied, and arms the stack for your next face calculation! If you need to deduct a window cutout or screw bore—or if you accidentally push a wrong dimension—simply compute that area and press `[↰] [Σ-]` to subtract it from $\Sigma x$ without disturbing any previous faces. Once every boundary face has been tallied, pressing `[↱] [SUMS]` recalls the exact total surface area $\Sigma x$ at full 12-digit precision—with **zero parentheses, zero named memory variables, and zero scratch paper**.

![Fraction Studio Precision Gauge Comparison](../assets/renders/fraction-studio-gauge-comparison.png)
*Figure 6.2: Precision micrometer comparator gauge verification, pairing physical volumetric measurement directly with statistical accumulator face audits on the RPN stack.*

### 6.4.2 Galileo's Square-Cube Law, L-Frame Annuli & Polyhedral Face Decomposition

To see why surface-area-to-volume scaling and the `[Σ+]` statistical bus work together so naturally, combine three physical tools from the StackCalc studio kit:
1. **Counting Tiles & Galileo's Square-Cube Asymmetry:** Dock a single $19.0 \times 19.0 \times 7.0\text{ mm}$ ($1\text{U}$) counting tile on the Snapfinity lid: it has $1$ top unit face, $1$ bottom unit face, and $4$ perimeter side edges ($6$ outer block faces). Now dock eight $1\text{U}$ tiles into a $2 \times 2 \times 2$ block prism (four $2\text{-tile}$ towers docked in a $2 \times 2$ square): doubling the block count along each axis ($\ell \to 2\ell$) multiplies the exposed exterior surface area by $2^2 = 4$ ($6 \to 24\text{ exposed block faces}$), while multiplying the internal volume by $2^3 = 8$ ($1 \to 8\text{ tiles}$)—physically demonstrating Galileo's 1638 Square-Cube Law. Conversely, halving the edge length of a unit cube ($\ell \to \frac{1}{2}\ell$) packs **$2^3 = 8$ half-size cubes into each unit volume** while doubling the total exposed surface area ($A/V \to 2\times$), which is why finely divided catalyst pellets, pulmonary alveoli, and pin-fin heat sinks pack massive active surface area into a compact volume.
2. **The Algebra Factoring L-Frame Stage & Difference-of-Squares Annuli:** When evaluating a flanged pipe gasket or hollow structural tube $A = \pi(R^2 - r^2) = \pi(R - r)(R + r)$, docking an $R \times R$ square flat into the $90^\circ$ L-Frame Stage and removing an $r \times r$ corner square leaves an L-shaped gnomon whose two wings rearrange directly into a single $(R - r) \times (R + r)$ rectangle.
3. **Isohedral Polyhedra & Planar Face Accumulation (`[Σ+]`):** Inspecting the five Platonic polyhedra ($d4$ tetrahedron, $d6$ cube, $d8$ octahedron, $d12$ dodecahedron, and $d20$ icosahedron) among the **Polyhedral Dice** confirms Leonhard Euler's topological invariant ($V - E + F = 2$) and reveals why you never need a monolithic 30-character algebraic formula for surface area: every three-dimensional solid is simply a boundary collection of $F$ planar faces. Computing each planar face (or opposing face pair) on the 4-level stack and pressing `[Σ+]` accumulates the area into $\Sigma x$ while the LCD counter $n = 1, 2, \dots$ verifies that every face of the solid has been accounted for.

### 6.4.4 Stepped Castings, Extruded Heat-Sink Fins & Pyramidal Roofs

What happens when a real-world component is not a single prism, but a stepped casting or an array of cooling fins? To estimate the electroplating bath current for a stepped cast-iron machine bracket consisting of a base block ($120 \times 80 \times 30\text{ mm}$) surmounted by a rectangular boss ($60 \times 40 \times 25\text{ mm}$), we need its total exposed surface area. Look at a geometric shortcut before we even touch a key: the top face of the upper boss ($60 \times 40\text{ mm}$) plus the exposed horizontal ledge of the base block around it ($120 \times 80 - 60 \times 40\text{ mm}$) project together to form one complete $120 \times 80 = 9,600\text{ mm}^2$ top rectangle! 6. **Combined Top Footprint ($120 \times 80$):** `120 [ENTER] 80 [×] [Σ+]` ($n = 6,\; A = 9,600\text{ mm}^2$)

That same projection insight reveals how an extruded aluminum heat sink defeats Galileo's Square-Cube bottleneck (from our chapter opening). Consider a $100 \times 100\text{ mm}$ square base plate carrying $8$ vertical cooling fins, each $100\text{ mm}$ long, $35\text{ mm}$ tall, and $2\text{ mm}$ thick. We decompose the heat sink into four surface groups and accumulate them via `[Σ+]`:

- **8 Fin Top Tips:** $8 \times (100 \times 2) = 1,600\text{ mm}^2$
- **Exposed Valley Floor Between Fins:** $(100 \times 100) - 1,600 = 8,400\text{ mm}^2$
- **Base Flat Bottom:** $100 \times 100 = 10,000\text{ mm}^2$

Just as with the stepped machine casting above, notice that the $8$ fin tips ($1,600\text{ mm}^2$) plus the valley floor ($8,400\text{ mm}^2$) equal the original $10,000\text{ mm}^2$ top footprint—so extruding the $8$ fins adds their $16$ vertical side walls ($56,000\text{ mm}^2$), boosting total surface area from $20,000\text{ mm}^2$ to **$76,000.0\text{ mm}^2$** ($760.0\text{ cm}^2$, a $3.8\times$ thermal multiplier):

We can even evaluate Galileo's surface-to-volume ratio $A/V$ directly on a regular right square pyramid of base side $s = 12.0\text{ mm}$ and vertical altitude $h = 8.0\text{ mm}$. Notice how the half-base $s/2 = 6.0\text{ mm}$ and altitude $h = 8.0\text{ mm}$ form a $6\text{–}8\text{–}10$ Pythagorean right triangle on each face, giving slant height $l = \sqrt{8^2 + 6^2} = 10.0\text{ mm}$:
- **Total Surface Area:** $A = s^2 + 4\left(\frac{1}{2} s l\right) = 144 + 2(12)(10) = 384.0\text{ mm}^2$
- **Enclosed Volume:** $V = \frac{1}{3} s^2 h = \frac{1}{3}(144)(8) = 384.0\text{ mm}^3$
- **Surface-to-Volume Ratio:** $\frac{A}{V} = \frac{384.0\text{ mm}^2}{384.0\text{ mm}^3} = \mathbf{1.0000\text{ mm}^{-1}}$

Keying `8 [↰] [x²] 12 [ENTER] 2 [÷] [↰] [x²] [+] [√x] 2 [×] 12 [×] 12 [↰] [x²] [+] 12 [↰] [x²] 8 [×] 3 [÷] [÷]` returns **`1.0000`**. Why do the surface area and volume both equal $384$? Because for any polyhedron circumscribed around an inscribed sphere of radius $r_{\text{in}}$, decomposing the solid into pyramids from the incenter to each face proves that $V = \frac{1}{3} r_{\text{in}} A$, or $\frac{A}{V} = \frac{3}{r_{\text{in}}}$—and here the inscribed sphere has radius $r_{\text{in}} = 3.0\text{ mm}$!

## 6.5 Solid Mensuration: Classical 3D Volumes, Cavalieri's Principle & Curved Shells

The evaluation of three-dimensional solids in competitive contests and engineering stress analysis demands rapid, error-free reductions. The following master catalog pairs each classical geometry with its physical motivation and optimal RPN evaluation pipeline:

| 3D Solid Geometry | Analytical Volume Formula | Total External Surface Area Formula | Physical & Geometric Motivation |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **Rectangular Prism** | $V = l \cdot w \cdot h$ | $A = 2(lw + lh + wh)$ | Cartesian volume product; 6 orthogonal bounding faces. |
| **Right Circular Cylinder** | $V = \pi r^2 h$ | $A = 2\pi r^2 + 2\pi r h$ | Extrusion of circular base along normal axis $h$. |
| **Right Circular Cone** | $V = \frac{1}{3} \pi r^2 h$ | $A = \pi r^2 + \pi r \sqrt{r^2 + h^2}$ | Exactly $\frac{1}{3}$ of circumscribed cylinder (Eudoxus-Archimedes). |
| **Sphere** | $V = \frac{4}{3} \pi r^3$ | $A = 4\pi r^2$ | Surface area is derivative of volume with respect to radius $r$. |
| **Torus (Major $R$, minor $r$)** | $V = 2\pi^2 R r^2$ | $A = 4\pi^2 R r$ | **Pappus-Guldinus:** Centroid path ($2\pi R$) $\times$ disk area ($\pi r^2$) or perimeter ($2\pi r$). |
| **Frustum of Right Cone** | $V = \frac{1}{3} \pi h (R^2 + Rr + r^2)$ | $A = \pi(R^2 + r^2) + \pi(R + r)s$ | Truncated cone; factored in RPN via $(R+r)^2 - Rr$. |
| **Spherical Cap (height $h$)** | $V = \frac{1}{3} \pi h^2 (3r - h)$ | $A_{\text{dome}} = 2\pi r h$ | Archimedes' cylinder balance: sliced sphere disk integration. |
| **Spherical Zone (2 bases)** | $V = \frac{\pi h}{6}(3r_1^2 + 3r_2^2 + h^2)$ | $A_{\text{zone}} = 2\pi R h$ | Slice between two parallel cutting planes through a sphere. |
| **Ellipsoid** | $V = \frac{4}{3} \pi a b c$ | $A \approx 4\pi \left(\frac{(ab)^p + (ac)^p + (bc)^p}{3}\right)^{1/p}$ | Affine 3D stretch of sphere along 3 principal orthogonal axes. |
| **Paraboloid of Revolution** | $V = \frac{1}{2} \pi r^2 h$ | $A = \frac{\pi r}{6h^2} \left[(r^2 + 4h^2)^{3/2} - r^3\right]$ | Exactly $\frac{1}{2}$ of bounding cylinder (Archimedes' law of paraboloids). |
| **Cylindrical Ungula (Hoof)** | $V = \frac{2}{3} r^3 \tan\alpha$ | $A_{\text{curved}} = 2 r^2 \tan\alpha$ | Slicing cylinder by an inclined plane passing through base diameter. |
| **Universal Prismoidal Solid** | $V = \frac{h}{6}(A_{\text{top}} + 4A_{\text{mid}} + A_{\text{bot}})$ | Dependent on geometry | Simpson's 3D rule: exact for any solid whose area is a cubic polynomial in $z$. |
| **Regular Tetrahedron** | $V = \frac{\sqrt{2}}{12} a^3$ | $A = \sqrt{3} a^2$ | 4 equilateral triangular faces; self-dual Platonic solid. |
| **Regular Octahedron** | $V = \frac{\sqrt{2}}{3} a^3$ | $A = 2\sqrt{3} a^2$ | 8 equilateral triangular faces; dual of the cube. |
| **Regular Dodecahedron** | $V = \frac{15 + 7\sqrt{5}}{4} a^3$ | $A = 3\sqrt{25 + 10\sqrt{5}}\,a^2$ | 12 regular pentagonal faces; golden ratio $\phi$ geometry. |
| **Regular Icosahedron** | $V = \frac{5(3 + \sqrt{5})}{12} a^3$ | $A = 5\sqrt{3} a^2$ | 20 equilateral triangular faces; dual of the dodecahedron. |

For the master quick-reference tables of all 3D solid mensuration formulas, consult **[Appendix D: Section 8 (3D Solid Mensuration & Revolution Geometry)](sc32/appendix-d-constants-and-equations.md)**.

### 6.5.1 Cavalieri's Slice Principle, Conical Frustums & the Steinmetz Bicylinder

By Bonaventura Cavalieri's slice principle, any cone or pyramid whose cross-sectional area shrinks quadratically from base to apex as $A(z) = A_{\text{base}}(z/h)^2$ encloses exactly one-third the volume of its bounding prism or cylinder: $V = \frac{1}{3}A_{\text{base}}h$. For an aerodynamic transition nose cone with an elliptical base ($a = 24.0\text{ mm}$, $b = 15.0\text{ mm}$, so $A_{\text{base}} = \pi ab$) and vertical height $h = 50.0\text{ mm}$, the enclosed volume is:

$$V = \frac{1}{3} \pi a b h = \frac{\pi}{3} (24)(15)(50) = \frac{\pi}{3}(18000) = 6000\pi \approx \mathbf{18,849.5559\text{ mm}^3}$$

| Step | Keystroke | Register T | Register Z | Register Y | Register X | Notes & State Analysis |
| :---: | :--- | :---: | :---: | :---: | :---: | :--- |
| 1 | `24 [ENTER] 15 [×] 50 [×]` | $0.0000$ | $0.0000$ | $0.0000$ | $18000.0000$ | Product $a \cdot b \cdot h$ evaluated |
| 2 | `[↱] [π] [×] 3 [÷]` | $0.0000$ | $0.0000$ | $0.0000$ | **$18849.555922$** | Elliptic cone volume $V$ in mm³ |

Cavalieri's slice principle also unlocks one of the most surprising volumes in solid geometry: when two equal circular pipes of radius $r = 15.0\text{ mm}$ intersect at right angles (forming a groin vault in architecture or a cross-fitting in high-pressure piping), what is the volume and surface area of their common intersection—the **Steinmetz bicylinder**? Archimedes (in *The Method*) and 3rd-century Chinese mathematician Liu Hui (who called it the *Mouhefanggai*, or "two square umbrellas") discovered something astonishing: if you slice the bicylinder horizontally at any height $z$, the cross-section is a **square** of side $2\sqrt{r^2 - z^2}$, whereas the cross-section of an inscribed sphere of radius $r$ at the same height is a **circle** of area $\pi(r^2 - z^2)$. Because the ratio of the square's area to the circle's area is $\frac{4}{\pi}$ at every single slice, Cavalieri's principle guarantees that the total volume of the bicylinder is $\frac{4}{\pi}$ times the sphere's volume $\frac{4}{3}\pi r^3$—causing $\pi$ to cancel out completely!

$$V = \frac{4}{\pi}\left(\frac{4}{3}\pi r^3\right) = \frac{16}{3} r^3 = \frac{16}{3} (15^3) = \mathbf{18,000.0\text{ mm}^3}, \qquad A = 16 r^2 = 16(15^2) = \mathbf{3,600.0\text{ mm}^2}$$

Evaluating `16 [ENTER] 3 [÷] 15 [ENTER] 3 [yˣ] [×]` yields the exact rational volume **$18,000.0\text{ mm}^3$**, and `15 [↰] [x²] 16 [×]` gives the surface area **$3,600.0\text{ mm}^2$**.

What if a cone is sliced flat before reaching its apex? Consider an agricultural grain hopper (or rocket nozzle section) shaped as a **conical frustum**—a cone sliced by two parallel planes—with upper radius $R = 1.80\text{ m}$, lower discharge radius $r = 0.40\text{ m}$, and vertical height $h = 2.50\text{ m}$. Notice the geometric beauty of the frustum volume formula $V = \frac{h}{3}(\pi R^2 + \pi Rr + \pi r^2)$: it is the height $h$ multiplied by the average of three areas—the top circle $\pi R^2$, the bottom circle $\pi r^2$, and their **geometric mean** $\sqrt{(\pi R^2)(\pi r^2)} = \pi Rr$:

$$V = \frac{1}{3} \pi h (R^2 + R r + r^2) = \frac{2.5\pi}{3} (1.8^2 + 1.8(0.4) + 0.4^2) = \frac{2.5\pi}{3} (3.24 + 0.72 + 0.16) = \frac{2.5\pi}{3} (4.12) = \mathbf{10.7861\text{ m}^3}$$

Watch how `[↰] [LASTX]` in the sequence `1.8 [↰] [x²] 1.8 [ENTER] 0.4 [×] [+] 0.4 [↰] [x²] [+] [↱] [π] [×] 2.5 [×] 3 [÷]` lets you evaluate the entire hopper volume $V = \frac{1}{3}\pi h(R^2 + Rr + r^2)$ while typing `1.8` and `0.4` only once each: keying `1.8 [↰] [x²] [↰] [LASTX] 0.4 [×] [↰] [LASTX] [↰] [x²] [+] [+] [↱] [π] [×] 2.5 [×] 3 [÷]` forms $R^2 + Rr + r^2 = 4.12\text{ m}^2$ in Register $X$ and scales by $\frac{2.5\pi}{3}$ in a single stream to produce **`10.786134777`** (**$10.7861\text{ m}^3$**, or $10,786.1\text{ liters}$). You can also factor the parenthetical term as $(R+r)^2 - Rr$ via `R [ENTER] r [ENTER] [+] [↰] [x²] [↰] [LASTX] [x⇄y] [×] [-] h [×] [↱] [π] [×] 3 [÷]`, keeping every term inside the 4-register stack with zero register allocation.

### 6.5.2 Polyhedral Trusses & Hexagonal Fastener Mass Takeoffs

In structural machining and fastener design, regular polygons extrude into prismatic bars and bolt heads. Because any two concentric regular $n$-gons share the exact same shape factor $C_n$, the net cross-sectional area of a hollow polygonal bar always factors as $C_n(S^2 - s^2)$. For a regular hexagonal brass bar of outer side $S = 20.0\text{ mm}$ with a concentric hexagonal bore of inner side $s = 8.0\text{ mm}$ and length $L = 150.0\text{ mm}$ (where six equilateral triangles of area $\frac{\sqrt{3}}{4}s^2$ give the hexagon constant $C_6 = \frac{3\sqrt{3}}{2}$):

$$\text{Net Area } A_{\text{net}} = \frac{3\sqrt{3}}{2} (S^2 - s^2) = \frac{3\sqrt{3}}{2} (400 - 64) = 504\sqrt{3} \approx 872.9536\text{ mm}^2 \implies V_{\text{net}} = A_{\text{net}} L = \mathbf{130,943.04\text{ mm}^3}$$

Entering `20 [↰] [x²] 8 [↰] [x²] [-] 3 [√x] [×] 3 [×] 2 [÷] 150 [×]` evaluates $(S^2 - s^2) = 336.0\text{ mm}^2$, scales by $\frac{3\sqrt{3}}{2}$, and multiplies by $L = 150\text{ mm}$ to produce **$130,943.04\text{ mm}^3$**:

| Step | Keystroke | Register T | Register Z | Register Y | Register X | Notes & State Analysis |
| :---: | :--- | :---: | :---: | :---: | :---: | :--- |
| 1 | `20 [↰] [x²] 8 [↰] [x²] [-]` | $0.0000$ | $0.0000$ | $0.0000$ | $336.0000$ | Hexagonal span difference $(S^2 - s^2)$ |
| 2 | `3 [√x] [×] 3 [×] 2 [÷]` | $0.0000$ | $0.0000$ | $0.0000$ | $872.953607$ | Net hexagonal cross section $A_{\text{net}}$ in mm² |
| 3 | `150 [×]` | $0.0000$ | $0.0000$ | $0.0000$ | **$130943.041071$** | Prismatic void volume $V_{\text{net}} = A_{\text{net}} \cdot L$ in mm³ |

Similarly, for a solid steel hex bolt head of side $s = 10.0\text{ mm}$, height $h = 12.0\text{ mm}$, and steel density $\rho = 7.85\text{ g/cm}^3$ ($0.00785\text{ g/mm}^3$), the volume and mass of the bolt head follow directly from $A_{\text{hex}} = \frac{3\sqrt{3}}{2}s^2$:

$$A_{\text{hex}} = \frac{3\sqrt{3}}{2} s^2 = \frac{3\sqrt{3}}{2} (100) \approx 259.8076\text{ mm}^2 \implies V = A_{\text{hex}} h = 3,117.69\text{ mm}^3 = 3.11769\text{ cm}^3$$
$$\text{Mass } m = 3.11769\text{ cm}^3 \times 7.85\text{ g/cm}^3 = \mathbf{24.4739\text{ grams}}$$

On the stack, form the hexagon constant $3\sqrt{3}/2 \approx 2.598076$ via `3 [√x] [↰] [LASTX] [×] 2 [÷]` (using `[↰] [LASTX]` to recover $3$ after taking its square root), multiply by $s^2 = 100\text{ mm}^2$ (`10 [↰] [x²] [×]`) and height $h = 12\text{ mm}$ (`12 [×]`), and convert $\text{mm}^3$ to grams via `1000 [÷] 7.85 [×]` to obtain **$24.4739\text{ grams}$**.

In three-dimensional space-frame trusses, the simplest and stiffest of the five Platonic solids is the regular tetrahedron. Why does the volume of a regular tetrahedron of edge length $a = 50.0\text{ mm}$ have a factor of $\frac{\sqrt{2}}{12}$? You can inscribe a regular tetrahedron inside a cube of edge $a/\sqrt{2}$ by drawing the face diagonals connecting four alternating corners of the cube. Slicing off the four right-angled corner pyramids—each of volume $\frac{1}{6}\text{cube}$—leaves the central tetrahedron occupying $1 - \frac{4}{6} = \frac{1}{3}$ of the cube's volume, or $V = \frac{1}{3}(a/\sqrt{2})^3 = \frac{\sqrt{2}}{12}a^3$:

$$h = \sqrt{\frac{2}{3}} a \approx \mathbf{40.8248\text{ mm}}, \qquad A = \sqrt{3} a^2 \approx \mathbf{4,330.1270\text{ mm}^2}, \qquad V = \frac{\sqrt{2}}{12} a^3 = \frac{\sqrt{2}}{12} (125,000) \approx \mathbf{14,731.3913\text{ mm}^3}$$

For the enclosed volume, keying `2 [√x] 12 [÷] 50 [ENTER] 3 [yˣ] [×]` evaluates $\sqrt{2}/12 \approx 0.117851$ (`2 [√x] 12 [÷]`), cubes the edge length $a = 50\text{ mm}$ (`50 [ENTER] 3 [yˣ]` $\to 125,000$), and multiplies (`[×]`) to return **`14,731.39127`** (**$14,731.39\text{ mm}^3$**).

### 6.5.3 Spherical Caps, Lunes, Girard's Spherical Excess & Triaxial Asteroids

When aerospace textile engineers pattern the fabric gores of a hemispherical recovery parachute or a stratospheric weather balloon of radius $R = 25.0\text{ cm}$, each crescent-shaped panel bounded by two meridians separated by dihedral angle $\theta = 36.0^\circ$ is a **spherical lune**. Because $36.0^\circ$ is exactly one-tenth of a full $360^\circ$ revolution, the lune covers one-tenth of the sphere's total area $4\pi R^2$:

$$A_{\text{lune}} = 2 R^2 \theta_{\text{rad}} = 4\pi R^2 \left(\frac{\theta^\circ}{360^\circ}\right) = 4\pi(625) \left(\frac{36}{360}\right) = 2500\pi (0.1) = 250\pi \approx \mathbf{785.3982\text{ cm}^2}$$

| Step | Keystroke | Register T | Register Z | Register Y | Register X | Notes & State Analysis |
| :---: | :--- | :---: | :---: | :---: | :---: | :--- |
| 1 | `25 [↰] [x²] 4 [×] [↱] [π] [×]` | $0.0000$ | $0.0000$ | $0.0000$ | $7853.981634$ | Full sphere surface area $4\pi R^2$ in cm² |
| 2 | `36 [ENTER] 360 [÷]` | $0.0000$ | $0.0000$ | $7853.981634$ | $0.100000$ | Dihedral angle fraction $36^\circ / 360^\circ$ |
| 3 | `[×]` | $0.0000$ | $0.0000$ | $0.0000$ | **$785.398163$** | Spherical lune area $A_{\text{lune}}$ in cm² |

What if a region on a sphere is bounded by three great-circle arcs—a **spherical triangle**? On a flat sheet of paper, the interior angles of every triangle sum to exactly $180^\circ$ ($\pi\text{ rad}$), regardless of how big or small the triangle is. On a curved sphere of radius $R$, however, great-circle geodesics bow outward so that the interior angles $(\alpha, \beta, \gamma)$ of a spherical triangle *always* sum to more than $180^\circ$! In 1629, Dutch-French mathematician **Albert Girard** proved a stunning theorem (the ancestor of the Gauss-Bonnet theorem) by intersecting three pairs of spherical lunes: the **spherical excess** $E_{\text{rad}} = (\alpha + \beta + \gamma - 180^\circ)\frac{\pi}{180^\circ}$ is directly proportional to the triangle's surface area $A = R^2 E_{\text{rad}}$.

Suppose a geodetic survey network on Earth ($R = 6,371.0\text{ km}$) forms a continental spherical triangle with interior angles $\alpha = 82.5^\circ$, $\beta = 68.2^\circ$, and $\gamma = 44.7^\circ$. Let us find the enclosed planetary surface area:

$$\text{Spherical Excess } E = (\alpha + \beta + \gamma - 180^\circ) = (82.5^\circ + 68.2^\circ + 44.7^\circ) - 180^\circ = 195.4^\circ - 180^\circ = 15.4^\circ$$
$$E_{\text{rad}} = 15.4^\circ \times \frac{\pi}{180^\circ} \approx 0.268781\text{ rad} \implies A = R^2 E_{\text{rad}} = 6371^2 \times 0.268781 \approx \mathbf{10,911,102.5\text{ km}^2}$$

Summing the three angles on the stack, subtracting $180^\circ$, converting the $15.4^\circ$ spherical excess into radians, and multiplying by $R^2 = 6,371^2\text{ km}^2$ yields **$10,911,102.50\text{ km}^2$** (roughly the area of Europe):

| Step | Keystroke | Register T | Register Z | Register Y | Register X | Notes & State Analysis |
| :---: | :--- | :---: | :---: | :---: | :---: | :--- |
| 1 | `82.5 [ENTER] 68.2 [+] 44.7 [+]` | $0.0000$ | $0.0000$ | $0.0000$ | $195.4000$ | Interior angle sum $\alpha + \beta + \gamma$ in degrees |
| 2 | `180 [-]` | $0.0000$ | $0.0000$ | $0.0000$ | $15.4000$ | Spherical excess $E = 15.4^\circ$ |
| 3 | `[↱] [π] [×] 180 [÷]` | $0.0000$ | $0.0000$ | $0.0000$ | $0.268781$ | Excess in radians $E_{\text{rad}} \approx 0.268781\text{ rad}$ |
| 4 | `6371 [↰] [x²] [×]` | $0.0000$ | $0.0000$ | $0.0000$ | **$10911102.50$** | Spherical triangle area $A = R^2 E_{\text{rad}}$ in km² |

In a petrochemical refinery, volatile liquefied gases are stored inside spherical **Hortonsphere** tanks of radius $R = 4.0\text{ m}$ so that membrane tension is uniform in all directions. When an ultrasonic level sensor measures liquid depth $h = 1.5\text{ m}$ at the bottom of the sphere, what volume of liquid sits in the tank? Slicing the sphere into horizontal disks of radius $\sqrt{R^2 - (R-z)^2}$ and integrating from $z = 0$ to $h$ yields Archimedes' **spherical cap** formula:

$$V = \frac{1}{3} \pi h^2 (3R - h) = \frac{\pi (1.5^2)}{3} (3(4.0) - 1.5) = \frac{2.25\pi}{3} (10.5) = 0.75\pi \times 10.5 = \mathbf{24.7400\text{ m}^3}$$

Running `4 [ENTER] 3 [×] 1.5 [-] 1.5 [↰] [x²] [×] [↱] [π] [×] 3 [÷]` forms the factor $(3R - h) = 10.5\text{ m}$ via `4 [ENTER] 3 [×] 1.5 [-]`, recovers $h = 1.5\text{ m}$ from `LASTX` and squares it (`[↰] [LASTX] [↰] [x²] [×]`), and scales by `[↱] [π] [×] 3 [÷]` to deliver **`24.740042147`** (**$24.7400\text{ m}^3$**, or $24,740.0\text{ liters}$).

What if a celestial body is not a sphere at all, but an irregular asteroid stretched along three unequal axes? While the *volume* of a triaxial ellipsoid with semi-axes $(a, b, c)$ is simply $\frac{4}{3}\pi abc$, its *surface area*—just like the perimeter of an ellipse—has no closed-form expression in elementary functions. In 2004, Danish mathematician Knud Thomsen discovered that taking a power mean of the three projected semi-axis products $(ab, ac, bc)$ with exponent $p = 1.6075$ approximates the exact Legendre elliptic integral to within $1.06\%$ across all aspect ratios! Let us estimate the surface area of a potato-shaped asteroid modeled as a triaxial ellipsoid with semi-axes $a = 15.0\text{ km}$, $b = 10.0\text{ km}$, and $c = 6.0\text{ km}$:

$$p \approx 1.6075 \implies A \approx 4\pi \left(\frac{(ab)^p + (ac)^p + (bc)^p}{3}\right)^{1/p}$$

With projected semi-axis products $ab = 150$, $ac = 90$, and $bc = 60$, notice how `[↰] [LASTX]` lets you raise all three products to the power $p = 1.6075$ without re-typing the exponent: keying `150 [ENTER] 1.6075 [yˣ] 90 [↰] [LASTX] [yˣ] 60 [↰] [LASTX] [yˣ] [+] [+] 3 [÷] 1.6075 [1/x] [yˣ] 4 [×] [↱] [π] [×]` averages $3148.23 + 1384.98 + 721.74 = 5254.95 / 3 = 1751.65$, extracts the $1/1.6075$ root ($\to 104.16$), and scales by $4\pi$ to yield an asteroid surface area of **$1,308.90\text{ km}^2$** ($1308.8986\text{ km}^2$).

## 6.6 Analytic 3D Spatial Geometry: Distance, Centroid & Mass Moments of Inertia

Beyond static volumes and surface areas, three-dimensional structural and mechanical design requires spatial distance metrics, composite mass centroids, and rotational moments of inertia.

### 6.6.1 3D Spatial Euclidean Metric, Helical Coils & Direction Cosines

In three-dimensional Cartesian space $\mathbb{R}^3$, the straight-line distance between two coordinate stations $P_1(x_1, y_1, z_1)$ and $P_2(x_2, y_2, z_2)$ follows the 3D Pythagorean theorem:
$$d = \sqrt{(x_2 - x_1)^2 + (y_2 - y_1)^2 + (z_2 - z_1)^2}$$
On the SC-32, you evaluate this parenthesis-free by computing each coordinate difference, squaring it in place, and adding it to the running sum on the stack before extracting the square root:
`x2 [ENTER] x1 [-] [↰] [x²]  y2 [ENTER] y1 [-] [↰] [x²] [+]  z2 [ENTER] z1 [-] [↰] [x²] [+] [√x]`.

That 3D Pythagorean sum also unwraps helical and conical coils in the machine shop. Before winding a tapered conical compression spring (with base radius $R_1 = 30\text{ mm}$, top radius $R_2 = 10\text{ mm}$, axial height $h = 60\text{ mm}$, and $N = 6\text{ active coils}$), a spring maker must cut a straight spring-steel wire blank of length $L$. Unwrapping the conical helix into three orthogonal displacement components—total circumferential travel $2\pi N R_m$ at the mean radius $R_m = (R_1 + R_2)/2 = 20\text{ mm}$, vertical axial rise $h = 60\text{ mm}$, and radial inward taper $R_1 - R_2 = 20\text{ mm}$—turns the arc-length integral into a 3D Pythagorean norm:

$$L \approx \sqrt{(2\pi N R_m)^2 + h^2 + (R_1 - R_2)^2} = \sqrt{(2\pi \times 6 \times 20)^2 + 60^2 + 20^2} = \sqrt{753.98^2 + 3600 + 400} \approx \mathbf{756.63\text{ mm}}$$

Summing the three squared orthogonal displacements via `2 [↱] [π] [×] 6 [×] 20 [×] [↰] [x²] 60 [↰] [x²] [+] 30 [ENTER] 10 [-] [↰] [x²] [+] [√x]` returns **`756.6302`** (**$756.63\text{ mm}$**):

| Step | Keystroke | Register T | Register Z | Register Y | Register X | Notes & State Analysis |
| :---: | :--- | :---: | :---: | :---: | :---: | :--- |
| 1 | `2 [↱] [π] [×] 6 [×] 20 [×] [↰] [x²]` | $0.0000$ | $0.0000$ | $0.0000$ | $568489.2130$ | Developed circumferential metric $(2\pi N R_m)^2$ |
| 2 | `60 [↰] [x²] [+]` | $0.0000$ | $0.0000$ | $0.0000$ | $572089.2130$ | Accumulate axial rise component $h^2$ |
