| **Binary** | `[↰] [BASE] [BIN]` | `b` | `0` and `1` | `10000010010b` |

### 10.2.1 The Stack Preservation Invariant
Switching between base modes **never destroys, alters, or shifts the values in the operational stack ($X, Y, Z, T$)**. If Register $X$ holds `255` in Decimal mode, pressing `[↰] [BASE] [HEX]` instantly re-renders the register as `FFh`, pressing `[↰] [BASE] [OCT]` shows `377o`, and pressing `[↰] [BASE] [BIN]` reveals all eight asserted bits as `11111111b`. The underlying 36-bit integer word in the processor's registers never changes—only the radix lens through which you view and type it.

### 10.2.2 Direct Hexadecimal Digit Input (`A` through `F`) & Mid-Calculation Radix Mixing
When Hexadecimal mode (`[HEX]`) is active, the top row of primary scientific keys (Row 1, Columns 0 through 5) maps directly to the printed alpha legends $A$ through $F$: `[√x]` enters $\mathbf{A}$ ($10_{10}$), `[eˣ]` enters $\mathbf{B}$ ($11_{10}$), `[LN]` enters $\mathbf{C}$ ($12_{10}$), `[yˣ]` enters $\mathbf{D}$ ($13_{10}$), `[1/x]` enters $\mathbf{E}$ ($14_{10}$), and `[Σ+]` enters $\mathbf{F}$ ($15_{10}$). To enter the classic debugging magic number `0xDEADBEEF`, simply key `[yˣ] [1/x] [√x] [yˣ] [eˣ] [1/x] [1/x] [Σ+]`. Whenever you want to apply scientific functions (`[√x]`, `[LN]`, `[yˣ]`) to a hexadecimal value, switch back to Decimal mode (`[↰] [BASE] [DEC]`) first so the top-row keys resume their mathematical roles.

In computer science exams and embedded debugging sessions, expressions frequently mix bases—for instance, adding a hexadecimal base offset $3\text{A}7_{16}$ to an octal permission mask $452_8$ and reporting the result in decimal. Because the SC-32 preserves all four stack registers across base changes, you can switch radices right in the middle of a calculation without jotting down a single intermediate number: switch to Hex (`[↰] [BASE] [HEX]`) and enter the first operand via `3 [√x] 7 [ENTER]` ($3\text{A}7_{16} = 935_{10}$), switch directly to Octal (`[↰] [BASE] [OCT]`) and add the second operand via `452 [+]` so Register $X$ immediately sums both words in octal ($2261_8$), and then switch to Decimal (`[↰] [BASE] [DEC]`) to read the combined total **$1,201_{10}$** in Register $X$.

### 10.2.3 IPv4 Subnet Masks, Broadcast Boundaries & Hexadecimal Byte Alignment
Switching among `DEC`, `HEX`, `OCT`, and `BIN` becomes an immediate superpower when inspecting IPv4 subnets and network broadcast boundaries. Suppose a core router in a campus data center receives an IPv4 packet addressed to final host octet `205` on a `/28` VLAN interface (`255.255.255.240`). Because a `/28` mask reserves the top 4 bits of the final octet for the subnet prefix and leaves the bottom 4 bits for hosts, it partitions the 256-address octet into blocks of $2^{32-28} = 2^4 = 16$ addresses. Rather than converting `205` and `240` into binary strings by hand to bitwise-AND them ($205_{10} = 11001101_2$ and $240_{10} = 11110000_2$, so $205 \text{ AND } 240 = 11000000_2 = 192_{10}$), we can divide `205` by the block stride `16` via `[↱] [÷R]` to find which 16-address block it belongs to (quotient `12` in Register $X$, host offset `13` in Register $Y$) and multiply by `16` to snap directly to the `/28` subnet boundary. Working in `[DEC]` mode, keying `205 [ENTER] 16 [↱] [÷R] 16 [×]` snaps the octet directly to the aligned subnet boundary **`192`**:

| Step | Keystroke | Register T | Register Z | Register Y | Register X | Display |
| :---: | :--- | :---: | :---: | :---: | :---: | :--- |
| 01 | `205` | 0 | 0 | 0 | 205 | `205_` |
| 02 | `[ENTER]` | 0 | 0 | 205 | 205 | `205` |
| 03 | `16 [↱] [÷R]` | 0 | 0 | 13 | 12 | `12` |
| 04 | `16 [×]` | 0 | 0 | 13 | 192 | `192` |

Notice what happened in Step 03: `16 [↱] [÷R]` simultaneously placed the subnet block number (`12`) in Register $X$ and the host's relative offset within that subnet (`13`) in Register $Y$. Multiplying Register $X$ by `16` gives the aligned `/28` network ID (**`192`**), while Register $Y$ still holds the host number (`13`, since $192 + 13 = 205$)!

Why do network engineers prefer hexadecimal when scaling this up to a full 32-bit IPv4 address? Because every 8-bit octet (`0` to `255`) of an IPv4 dotted-quad address maps to a clean two-digit hexadecimal byte (`00h` to `FFh`). When you pack the workstation IPv4 address `192.168.10.45` into a single 32-bit hexadecimal integer (`C0A80A2Dh`), a `/24` subnet mask ($255.255.255.0 = \text{FFFFFF00h}$) has a block size of $2^{32-24} = 2^8 = 256_{10} = \text{100h}$:

| Field | Octet 1 (`192` / `C0h`) | Octet 2 (`168` / `A8h`) | Octet 3 (`10` / `0Ah`) | Octet 4 (`45` / `2Dh`) |
| :--- | :---: | :---: | :---: | :---: |
| **Host IP Bits** | `11000000` | `10101000` | `00001010` | `00101101` |
| **Subnet Mask (`/24`)** | `11111111` (Net) | `11111111` (Net) | `11111111` (Net) | `00000000` (Host) |
| **Aligned Network ID** | `11000000` (`192`) | `10101000` (`168`) | `00001010` (`10`) | `00000000` (`0`) |

In `[HEX]` mode, keying `C0A80A2D [ENTER] 100 [↱] [÷R] 100 [×]` extracts the `/24` network address **`C0A80A00h`** (`192.168.10.0`) while leaving the host offset (`2Dh`) in Register $Y$. Subtracting the `/24` netmask from the all-ones broadcast word via `FFFFFFFF [ENTER] FFFFFF00 [-]` isolates the wildcard mask **`FFh`** (`0.0.0.255`), and adding that wildcard mask to the aligned network address via `C0A80A00 [ENTER] FF [+]` produces the subnet broadcast address **`C0A80AFFh`** (`192.168.10.255`), leaving $2^{32 - 24} - 2 = 2^8 - 2 = 256 - 2 = \mathbf{254\text{ usable hosts}}$ (`192.168.10.1` to `192.168.10.254`):

| Step | Keystroke | Register T | Register Z | Register Y | Register X | Display |
| :---: | :--- | :---: | :---: | :---: | :---: | :--- |
| 01 | `C0A80A2D` | `0h` | `0h` | `0h` | `C0A80A2Dh` | `C0A80A2D_h` |
| 02 | `[ENTER]` | `0h` | `0h` | `C0A80A2Dh` | `C0A80A2Dh` | `C0A80A2Dh` |
| 03 | `100 [↱] [÷R]` | `0h` | `0h` | `2Dh` | `C0A80Ah` | `C0A80Ah` |
| 04 | `100 [×]` | `0h` | `0h` | `2Dh` | `C0A80A00h` | `C0A80A00h` |
| 05 | `FF [+]` | `0h` | `0h` | `2Dh` | `C0A80AFFh` | `C0A80AFFh` |

---

## 10.3 The 36-Bit Two's Complement Integer Architecture & Bitwise Register Control

In digital electronics, systems programming, firmware development, and network engineering, calculations operate directly upon discrete binary registers rather than continuous floating-point approximations. How does a finite ring of 36 binary switches represent both positive and negative numbers without needing a separate subtraction circuit?

Imagine a mechanical car odometer with nine hexadecimal wheels reading `000000000h`. If you drive forward one click (`+1`), the right wheel advances to `000000001h`. What happens if you roll the odometer *backward* one click from zero (`0 - 1`)? Every wheel rolls backward past `0` to `F`, leaving the display at `FFFFFFFFFh` (all 36 bits set to `1`). Notice what happens when you add `000000001h` to `FFFFFFFFFh`: every column carries into the next until the 37th bit spills off the left edge of the 36-bit register, leaving `000000000h`! Because $X + \text{FFFFFFFFFh} \equiv X - 1 \pmod{2^{36}}$, the bit pattern `FFFFFFFFFh` behaves identically to $-1$ inside an ordinary binary adder.

This odometer wrap-around is called **two's complement arithmetic**. Rather than dedicating all $2^{36}$ states to positive integers, we split the 36-bit number wheel in half at bit position 35 (the Most Significant Bit, or `MSB`):
- **Positive Half (`Bit 35 = 0`):** Walking clockwise from `000000000h` ($0$) up to `7FFFFFFFFh` ($+2^{35} - 1 = +34,359,738,367$) covers all non-negative integers.
- **Negative Half (`Bit 35 = 1`):** Taking one more step past `7FFFFFFFFh` flips Bit 35 to `1` at `800000000h`, which represents the most negative number ($-2^{35} = -34,359,738,368$). From there, counting upward through `800000001h`, $\dots$, `FFFFFFFFEh` ($-2$), and `FFFFFFFFFh` ($-1$) climbs steadily back toward `000000000h`. To negate any integer $X$ in two's complement, the processor simply inverts all 36 bits ($\sim X = \text{FFFFFFFFFh} - X$) and adds $1$.

| Bit Position | Field Designation | Meaning in 36-Bit Two's Complement |
| :---: | :---: | :--- |
| **Bit 35** | `MSB` / Sign Bit | `0` = Positive integer ($0$ to $+2^{35}-1$); `1` = Negative integer ($-2^{35}$ to $-1$) |
| **Bits 34–32** | Upper Headroom | Provides 4 full bits of positive headroom above standard 32-bit unsigned words |
| **Bits 31–0** | Standard 32-Bit Word | Holds full 32-bit unsigned addresses, IPv4 netmasks, and GPIO bitfields |

### 10.3.1 Why 36 Bits Solves the 32-Bit Signed Overflow Trap & Odometer Rollover Seams
On a conventional 32-bit signed calculator, Bit 31 is the sign bit. The moment you enter a 32-bit unsigned memory address or an IPv4 broadcast mask like `0xFFFFFFFF` ($4,294,967,295$), Bit 31 is `1`—so a 32-bit calculator misinterprets the address as $-1$ or throws a range error! Because the SC-32 places its sign bit four positions higher at **Bit 35**, any 32-bit unsigned value up to `0xFFFFFFFF` (`0FFFFFFFFh`) sits comfortably in Bits 31–0 with `0` in Bits 35–32. It remains strictly positive ($+4,294,967,295$) with four full bits of unsigned headroom to spare for carry flags, parity tags, and multi-word checksum accumulators. Values whose magnitude exceeds the 36-bit range ($+34,359,738,367$ or $-34,359,738,368$ in decimal entry) trigger the non-destructive `TOO BIG` annunciator rather than silently truncating digits.

We can inspect the two critical rollover seams of this 36-bit two's complement odometer directly on the stack in `[HEX]` mode. First, we load the largest positive signed 36-bit integer `7FFFFFFFFh` ($+2^{35} - 1 = +34,359,738,367_{10}$, where Bit 35 is `0` and Bits 34–0 are all `1`) and add `1` via `7FFFFFFFF [ENTER] 1 [+]` $\rightarrow$ `800000000h` ($-34,359,738,368_{10}$, the minimum negative bound). Second, we start at `0` and subtract `1` via `0 [ENTER] 1 [-]` $\rightarrow$ `FFFFFFFFFh` ($-1_{10}$) to watch the odometer roll backward across zero:

| Step | Keystrokes | Register T | Register Z | Register Y | Register X | Notes |
|:---|:---|:---|:---|:---|:---|:---|
| 01 | `7FFFFFFFF [ENTER]` | `0h` | `0h` | `7FFFFFFFFh` | `7FFFFFFFFh` | Load maximum signed positive 36-bit bound |
| 02 | `1 [+]` | `0h` | `0h` | `0h` | **`800000000h`** | Overflow rolls over to minimum negative bound |
| 03 | `0 [ENTER] 1 [-]` | `0h` | `0h` | `800000000h` | **`FFFFFFFFFh`** | Underflow to $-1_{10}$; all 36 bits set (`FFFFFFFFFh`) |

### 10.3.2 Bit-Field Extraction, Shifting & Masking on the RPN Stack

Why doesn't the SC-32 clutter its `BASE` menu with dedicated `AND`, `OR`, `XOR`, `SL`, and `SR` softkeys? Because in positional binary arithmetic, shifting a word left or right by $k$ bits is simply multiplying or dividing by $M = 2^k$, and splitting a hardware register at bit boundary $k$ is Euclidean division with remainder (`[↱] [÷R]`) *([Shannon, 1938](sc32/appendix-e-annotated-bibliography.md#cite-shannon1938))*!

When you divide a 36-bit integer $Y$ by a power of two $M = 2^k$ using `[↱] [÷R]`, the calculator cleaves the binary word cleanly at bit $k$ in a single keystroke:
* **Register `X` (Quotient $\lfloor Y / 2^k \rfloor$):** Receives the **upper bits** shifted right by $k$ positions ($Y \gg k$).
* **Register `Y` (Remainder $Y \bmod 2^k$):** Retains the **lower $k$ bits** masked off ($Y \ \& \ (2^k - 1)$).

| Bit-Field / Masking Operation | Mathematical Equivalent ($M = 2^k$) | SC-32 RPN Keystrokes (`HEX` / `DEC`) | Result Location |
| :--- | :---: | :--- | :--- |
| **Left Shift ($X \ll k$)** | $X \times 2^k$ | `X [ENTER] M [×]` | Shifted word in **`X`** |
| **Right Shift ($X \gg k$)** | $\lfloor X / 2^k \rfloor$ | `X [ENTER] M [÷]` (or `[↱] [÷R]`) | Upper bits in **`X`** |
| **Low-Bit Mask ($X \ \& \ (2^k - 1)$)** | $X \bmod 2^k$ | `X [ENTER] M [↱] [÷R] [x⇄y]` | Low $k$ bits in **`X`** |
| **High-Bit Alignment ($X \ \& \ \sim(2^k - 1)$)** | $\lfloor X / 2^k \rfloor \times 2^k$ | `X [ENTER] M [↱] [÷R] M [×]` | Aligned base in **`X`** |
| **Set Disjoint Bit $k$** | $X + 2^k$ | `X [ENTER] M [+]` | Updated word in **`X`** |
| **Clear Set Bit $k$** | $X - 2^k$ | `X [ENTER] M [-]` | Updated word in **`X`** |
| **32-Bit Unsigned Complement** | $\text{FFFFFFFF}_{16} - X$ | `FFFFFFFF [ENTER] X [-]` | Inverted mask in **`X`** |

Let's see how these positional powers of two control physical hardware pins on a microcontroller. Suppose you are bringing up a newly assembled prototype circuit board on the lab bench and need to illuminate a green status LED connected to GPIO Pin 5. A debugger readout shows that the 32-bit GPIO direction register (`GPIO_DIR`) currently holds `0x00001804` (Pins 2, 11, and 12 already configured as outputs, while Pin 5 is currently `0` for input). Because Bit 5 is currently `0`, asserting it via bitwise OR (`GPIO_DIR | (1 << 5)`) generates zero carry into neighboring bit positions—which means it is mathematically identical to adding Bit 5's positional weight $2^5 = 32_{10} = \text{20h}$:

| Register Stage | Binary Representation (Bits 15–0) | Hexadecimal Value |
| :--- | :---: | :---: |
| **Original Register** | `0001 1000 0000 0100` | `1804h` |
| **Bit 5 Weight ($2^5$)** | `0000 0000 0010 0000` | `0020h` |
| **Updated Register (`+`)** | `0001 1000 0010 0100` | **`1824h`** |

In `[HEX]` mode, keying `1804 [ENTER] 20 [+]` sets Bit 5 cleanly to produce **`1824h`**:

| Step | Keystroke | Register T | Register Z | Register Y | Register X | Display |
| :---: | :--- | :---: | :---: | :---: | :---: | :--- |
| 01 | `1804` | `0h` | `0h` | `0h` | `1804h` | `1804_h` |
| 02 | `[ENTER]` | `0h` | `0h` | `1804h` | `1804h` | `1804h` |
| 03 | `20` | `0h` | `0h` | `1804h` | `20h` | `20_h` |
| 04 | `[+]` | `0h` | `0h` | `0h` | `1824h` | `1824h` |

Similarly, to verify that a real-time timer interrupt is firing on schedule without halting the CPU, embedded engineers often strobe a "heartbeat" GPIO pin connected to an oscilloscope probe or external watchdog timer. Suppose the port output register currently holds `0x00000017` ($0001\,0111_2$, with Bits 0, 1, 2, and 4 asserted) and the heartbeat line is wired to Bit 2 (weight $2^2 = 4 = \text{4h}$). Because Bit 2 is known to be asserted (`1`) in `17h`, working in `[HEX]` mode and keying `17 [ENTER] 4 [-]` clears that single pulse bit without borrowing from neighboring columns to produce **`13h`**, and adding `4` back via `13 [ENTER] 4 [+]` (or `[↰] [LASTX] [+]`) drives the pin back high to restore **`17h`**.

That same borrow-free subtraction audits multi-bit status words in aerospace telemetry. Consider a spacecraft health-monitoring downlink that transmits a 16-bit subsystem status word `0x5F5A` while the nominal flight baseline status mask is `0x5A50`. Which status flags have newly asserted, and what is the **Hamming distance** (the number of differing bits) between the two words? In `[HEX]` mode, keying `5F5A [ENTER] 5A50 [-]` isolates the bit-difference mask **`50Ah`** ($0000010100001010_2$ in `[BIN]`), where Bits 1, 3, 8, and 10 are set—revealing a Hamming distance of **$4\text{ bits}$**. Why did simple subtraction work here? Whenever every asserted bit of the baseline mask `5A50h` is a subset of the active bits in `5F5Ah`, subtracting `5F5A [ENTER] 5A50 [-]` triggers zero borrows between binary columns and behaves identically to bitwise XOR (`^`), isolating the newly tripped fault flags `50Ah` in Register $X$. Switching to `[↰] [BASE] [BIN]` immediately displays the binary bit pattern $\mathbf{10100001010\text{b}}$ (bits 1, 3, 8, and 10 asserted; Hamming weight $w_H = \mathbf{4}$).

What if the bit-field we need sits right in the middle of a peripheral register? Hardware architects rarely waste an entire 32-bit register on a single setting; instead, they pack clock dividers, channel selectors, and enable flags into contiguous bit-fields inside a single control word. Suppose that while debugging an analog sensor driver, you read `0x3C6A` from a 16-bit Analog-to-Digital Converter (ADC) configuration register. According to the datasheet, Bits [7:4] (the upper nibble of the low byte) encode the ADC's bit-resolution setting ($0 \dots 15$, where `6h` selects 12-bit conversion mode). How do we slice Bits [7:4] out of the middle of `3C6Ah` into an isolated integer in Register $X$? First, dividing by $2^8 = \text{100h}$ via `[↱] [÷R]` trims away the upper byte (`3Ch`) and drops the lower byte (`6Ah`, Bits [7:0]) into Register $Y$; swapping `6Ah` into Register $X$ and dividing by $2^4 = \text{10h}$ shifts away Bits [3:0] (`Ah`), leaving Bits [7:4] (`6h`) standing alone:

| Extraction Stage | Binary Nibbles (Bits 15–0) | Hexadecimal Value |
| :--- | :---: | :---: |
| **ADC Configuration Register** | `0011 1100 0110 1010` | `3C6Ah` |
| **Lower Byte Remainder (`÷R 100h`)** | `0000 0000 0110 1010` | `006Ah` |
| **Right-Shifted Nibble (`÷ 10h`)** | `0000 0000 0000 0110` | `0006h` ($6_{10}$) |

In `[HEX]` mode, isolating the lower byte via modulo `0x100` (`3C6A [ENTER] 100 [↱] [÷R] [x⇄y]` $\rightarrow$ `6Ah`) and shifting right by 4 bits ($2^4 = 16 = \text{10h}$) via `6A [ENTER] 10 [÷]` extracts **`6h`**:

| Step | Keystroke | Register T | Register Z | Register Y | Register X | Display |
| :---: | :--- | :---: | :---: | :---: | :---: | :--- |
| 01 | `3C6A [ENTER]` | `0h` | `0h` | `3C6Ah` | `3C6Ah` | `3C6Ah` |
| 02 | `100 [↱] [÷R]` | `0h` | `0h` | `6Ah` | `3Ch` | `3Ch` |
| 03 | `[x⇄y]` | `0h` | `0h` | `3Ch` | `6Ah` | `6Ah` |
| 04 | `10 [÷]` | `0h` | `0h` | `3Ch` | `6h` | `6h` |

### 10.3.3 Multi-Field Bit Packing: RGB565 Framebuffers, Base64 Sextets & Endianness

Now let us run that bit-field slicing pipeline in reverse to *pack* three separate color channels into a single display word. To cut framebuffer RAM usage and SPI bus traffic by a third, embedded color LCD controllers commonly pack 24-bit TrueColor (`RGB888`, 8 bits per channel) into a 16-bit word (`RGB565`). Because the human retina's M-cones are most sensitive to green wavelengths, `RGB565` allocates 6 bits ($0\dots63$) to Green in the middle (`Bits 10–5`) and 5 bits ($0\dots31$) each to Red (`Bits 15–11`) and Blue (`Bits 4–0`). For the vibrant coral color `0xFF5733` ($R=255, G=87, B=51$), quantizing the three channels yields $\text{Red}_5 = \lfloor 255 \times 31 / 255 \rfloor = 31 = \text{1Fh}$, $\text{Green}_6 = \lfloor 87 \times 63 / 255 \rfloor = 21 = \text{15h}$, and $\text{Blue}_5 = \lfloor 51 \times 31 / 255 \rfloor = 6 = \text{06h}$, which assemble into $\text{Packed Word} = (R_5 \times 2^{11}) + (G_6 \times 2^5) + B_5$:

| Channel Allocation | Bit Positions | Binary Field | Shifted Hex Value |
| :--- | :---: | :---: | :---: |
| **Red (5-bit)** | Bits `15–11` | `11111` (`1Fh × 800h`) | `F800h` |
| **Green (6-bit)** | Bits `10–5` | `010101` (`15h × 20h`) | `02A0h` |
| **Blue (5-bit)** | Bits `4–0` | `00110` (`06h`) | `0006h` |
| **Combined RGB565 Word** | Bits `15–0` | `1111101010100110` | **`FAA6h`** |

In `[HEX]` mode, shifting the 5-bit Red channel left by 11 bits ($2^{11} = 800\text{h}$) via `1F [ENTER] 800 [×]` yields `F800h`, shifting the 6-bit Green channel left by 5 bits ($2^5 = 20\text{h}$) via `15 [ENTER] 20 [×]` yields `2A0h`, pressing `[+]` merges Red and Green into `FAA0h`, and adding the 5-bit Blue channel via `FAA0 [ENTER] 6 [+]` completes the packed 16-bit color word **`FAA6h`**:

| Step | Keystroke | Register T | Register Z | Register Y | Register X | Display |
| :---: | :--- | :---: | :---: | :---: | :---: | :--- |
| 01 | `1F [ENTER]` | `0h` | `0h` | `1Fh` | `1Fh` | `1Fh` |
| 02 | `800 [×]` | `0h` | `0h` | `0h` | `F800h` | `F800h` |
| 03 | `15 [ENTER]` | `0h` | `F800h` | `15h` | `15h` | `15h` |
| 04 | `20 [×]` | `0h` | `0h` | `F800h` | `2A0h` | `2A0h` |
| 05 | `[+]` | `0h` | `0h` | `0h` | `FAA0h` | `FAA0h` |
| 06 | `6 [+]` | `0h` | `0h` | `0h` | `FAA6h` | `FAA6h` |

Conversely, when a display controller or frame-capture analyzer reads a packed 16-bit RGB565 pixel back from video memory, a single `[↱] [÷R]` cascade unpacks all three color channels ($R_5, G_6, B_5$) onto the stack in one pass without re-typing the pixel word. Given the 16-bit RGB565 pixel `0xF38E` in `[HEX]` mode, keying the 9-token stream `F38E [ENTER] 800 [↱] [÷R] [x⇄y] 20 [↱] [÷R]` first cleaves `F38Eh` at bit 11 ($2^{11} = \text{800h}$) to isolate the 5-bit Red channel in Register $X$ and the lower 11-bit Green+Blue remainder in Register $Y$, then swaps that remainder into $X$ and cleaves at bit 5 ($2^5 = \text{20h}$)—leaving Red in Register $Z$ (`1Eh` $= 30_{10}$), Green in Register $X$ (`1Ch` $= 28_{10}$), and Blue in Register $Y$ (`Eh` $= 14_{10}$) simultaneously on the visible stack.

A closely related bit-packing problem arose when early internet mail systems (SMTP) and HTTP headers were designed around 7-bit printable ASCII text: transmitting raw binary files was a nightmare because routers interpreted byte values like `0x00` or `0x0A` as control characters. **Base64 encoding** solves this by welding every three 8-bit bytes ($3 \times 8 = 24\text{ bits}$) into a single 24-bit integer and slicing it into four 6-bit "sextets" ($4 \times 6 = 24\text{ bits}$, each ranging from $0$ to $63$), which map to the 64 safe printable characters `A–Z`, `a–z`, `0–9`, `+`, and `/`. Let's encode the classic 3-byte ASCII string `"Man"` (`0x4D`, `0x61`, `0x6E` $\implies$ 24-bit word `4D616Eh`) into its four 6-bit Base64 indices using slice divisors $2^{18} = \text{40000h}$, $2^{12} = \text{1000h}$, and $2^6 = \text{40h}$:

| Base64 Sextet | 6-Bit Binary Slice | Decimal Index | Base64 Character |
| :--- | :---: | :---: | :---: |
| **Sextet 1 (Bits 23–18)** | `010011` | `19` (`13h`) | **`T`** |
| **Sextet 2 (Bits 17–12)** | `010110` | `22` (`16h`) | **`W`** |
| **Sextet 3 (Bits 11–6)** | `000101` | `5` (`05h`) | **`F`** |
| **Sextet 4 (Bits 5–0)** | `101110` | `46` (`2Eh`) | **`u`** |

In `[HEX]` mode, slicing `4D616Eh` across the four 6-bit boundaries yields Sextet 1 via `4D616E [ENTER] 40000 [÷]` $\rightarrow$ **`13h`** ($19_{10} \implies \mathbf{T}$), Sextet 2 via `4D616E [ENTER] 40000 [↱] [÷R] [x⇄y] 1000 [÷]` $\rightarrow$ **`16h`** ($22_{10} \implies \mathbf{W}$), Sextet 3 via `4D616E [ENTER] 1000 [↱] [÷R] [x⇄y] 40 [÷]` $\rightarrow$ **`5h`** ($5_{10} \implies \mathbf{F}$), and Sextet 4 via `4D616E [ENTER] 40 [↱] [÷R] [x⇄y]` $\rightarrow$ **`2Eh`** ($46_{10} \implies \mathbf{u}$)—confirming that `"Man"` encodes to **`TWFu`**:

| Step | Keystrokes | Register T | Register Z | Register Y | Register X | Notes |
|:---|:---|:---|:---|:---|:---|:---|
| 01 | `4D616E [ENTER] 40000 [÷]` | `0h` | `0h` | `0h` | **`13h`** | Sextet 1: `4D616Eh >> 18 = 13h` ($19_{10} \implies \mathbf{T}$) |
| 02 | `4D616E [ENTER] 40000 [↱] [÷R] [x⇄y] 1000 [÷]` | `13h` | `13h` | `13h` | **`16h`** | Sextet 2: remainder `>> 12 = 16h` ($22_{10} \implies \mathbf{W}$) |
| 03 | `4D616E [ENTER] 1000 [↱] [÷R] [x⇄y] 40 [÷]` | `16h` | `16h` | `4D6h` | **`5h`** | Sextet 3: remainder `>> 6 = 5h` ($5_{10} \implies \mathbf{F}$) |
| 04 | `4D616E [ENTER] 40 [↱] [÷R] [x⇄y]` | `4D6h` | `5h` | `13585h` | **`2Eh`** | Sextet 4: lower 6-bit remainder = `2Eh` ($46_{10} \implies \mathbf{u}$) |

*(**Single-Entry `÷R` Cascade:** Because `[↱] [÷R]` preserves the lower remainder in $Y$ while placing the upper sextet in $X$, chaining `4D616E [ENTER] 40000 [↱] [÷R] [x⇄y] 1000 [↱] [÷R] [x⇄y] 40 [↱] [÷R]` unpacks all four Base64 indices across the four stack registers—`13h` in Register $T$, `16h` in Register $Z$, `2Eh` in Register $Y$, and `5h` in Register $X$—with `4D616E` keyed only once.)*

When multi-byte words move between a network wire and processor memory, they immediately encounter a famous architectural divide. In his classic 1980 computer-architecture essay *"On Holy Wars and a Plea for Peace"*, Danny Cohen borrowed the terms **Big-Endian** and **Little-Endian** from Jonathan Swift's *Gulliver's Travels* to describe the two rival ways computers order bytes in memory. Internet protocols transmit multi-byte integers in Big-Endian ("network byte order," most-significant byte first), whereas x86 and ARM Cortex processors store integers in Little-Endian (least-significant byte first). Let's reverse the 4-byte Big-Endian network word `0x12345678` into Little-Endian `0x78563412` on the stack using `[↱] [÷R]`, `[÷]`, `[×]`, and `[+]`:

| Byte Order | Byte 3 (MSB) | Byte 2 | Byte 1 | Byte 0 (LSB) |
| :--- | :---: | :---: | :---: | :---: |
| **Big-Endian (`12345678h`)** | `12h` | `34h` | `56h` | `78h` |
| **Shift Operation** | `>> 24` (`÷ 1000000h`) | `>> 8` (`÷ 100h`) | `<< 8` (`× 100h`) | `<< 24` (`× 1000000h`) |
| **Little-Endian (`78563412h`)** | `78h` | `56h` | `34h` | `12h` |

In `[HEX]` mode, we extract Byte 0 and shift it to Byte 3 via `12345678 [ENTER] 100 [↱] [÷R] [x⇄y] 1000000 [×]` $\rightarrow$ `78000000h`, extract Byte 1 and shift it to Byte 2 via `12345678 [ENTER] 10000 [↱] [÷R] [x⇄y] 100 [↱] [÷R] 10000 [×]` $\rightarrow$ `560000h`, extract Byte 2 and shift it to Byte 1 via `12345678 [ENTER] 1000000 [↱] [÷R] [x⇄y] 10000 [↱] [÷R] 100 [×]` $\rightarrow$ `3400h`, extract Byte 3 to Byte 0 via `12345678 [ENTER] 1000000 [÷]` $\rightarrow$ `12h`, and merge all four non-overlapping bytes via `[+] [+] [+]` to obtain **`78563412h`**:

| Step | Keystroke | Register T | Register Z | Register Y | Register X | Display |
| :---: | :--- | :---: | :---: | :---: | :---: | :--- |
| 01 | `78 [ENTER] 1000000 [×]` | `0h` | `0h` | `0h` | `78000000h` | `78000000h` |
| 02 | `56 [ENTER] 10000 [×]` | `0h` | `0h` | `78000000h` | `560000h` | `560000h` |
| 03 | `[+]` | `0h` | `0h` | `0h` | `78560000h` | `78560000h` |
| 04 | `34 [ENTER] 100 [×]` | `0h` | `0h` | `78560000h` | `3400h` | `3400h` |
| 05 | `[+]` | `0h` | `0h` | `0h` | `78563400h` | `78563400h` |
| 06 | `12` | `0h` | `0h` | `78563400h` | `12h` | `12h` |
| 07 | `[+]` | `0h` | `0h` | `0h` | `78563412h` | `78563412h` |

### 10.3.4 Mode-Locked Base Entry vs. Unified 36-Bit Word & Remainder Operations

Operating directly on 36-bit integer words across all four stack registers with simultaneous quotient-and-remainder division (`[↱] [÷R]`) eliminates the submenu radix conversions and manual remainder steps required on conventional algebraic calculators:

| Challenge / Metric | Conventional Algebraic Calculator (Infix) | Algebraic Strokes | SC-32 RPN Stack Method | SC-32 Strokes | Stack Advantage |

| **IPv4 Subnet Partitioning**: Split `192.168.10.45` (`C0A80A2Dh`) into `/24` network ID & host offset | Manual integer truncation: `int(C0A80A2D / 100)` followed by subtract-and-multiply remainder `C0A80A2D - Ans * 100` (28 strokes). Stack is invisible. | 28 | **Simultaneous Division with Remainder (`[↱] [÷R]`)**: Key `C0A80A2D ENTER 100 ÷R` (11 strokes). Network prefix in $X$, host offset in $Y$ immediately. | 11 | **60% fewer strokes + single-cycle quotient/remainder split** |

Stack history is discarded or obscured (26+ strokes). | 26 | **Native 36-Bit Base Engine**: Press `[↰] [BASE] [HEX]`, `[OCT]`, `[BIN]` (4 strokes). Requires repeated radix-256 entry and decimal-to-hex conversion. | 21 | **Positional RPN Pipeline (`[HEX]` mode)**: `FF [ENTER] 100 [×] 80 [+] 100 [×] 40 [+]` (12 strokes). ## 10.4 Protocol Checksums, Cryptographic Rotations & IEEE-754 Representation

Having mastered radix conversions, two's-complement bit-fields, and multi-byte packing, we now turn to three cornerstone problems in systems engineering: verifying internet packet checksums via end-around carry, rotating cryptographic state words without losing entropy, and unpacking fixed-point and IEEE-754 floating-point numbers *([IEEE, 2019](sc32/appendix-e-annotated-bibliography.md#cite-ieee754_2019))*.

### 10.4.1 RFC 1071 One's-Complement Checksums & Cryptographic Bit Rotations (`ROL`)

What if a transmission error flips bits inside an internet packet header? That brings us to why IPv4, TCP, and UDP packet headers use a 16-bit *one's complement* checksum (RFC 1071) rather than ordinary two's complement addition *([Knuth, 1997](sc32/appendix-e-annotated-bibliography.md#cite-knuth1997))*: one's complement addition with "end-around carry" is **endian-independent**, meaning that whether a router adds 16-bit words in Big-Endian or Little-Endian byte order, wrapping overflow carries from bit 16 back into bit 0 produces the exact same sum! Suppose summing the 16-bit words of an IPv4 header in a 32-bit accumulator yields $\text{Header Sum} = 2653\text{D}_{16}$. To fold the overflow carry bits ($> \text{FFFFh}$) back into the lower 16 bits and invert all bits for the wire checksum, we extract $\text{Carry} = \lfloor 2653\text{D}_{16} / 10000_{16} \rfloor = 2_{16}$ and $\text{Lower 16 Bits} = 2653\text{D}_{16} \bmod 10000_{16} = 653\text{D}_{16}$, fold them into $\text{Folded Sum} = 653\text{D}_{16} + 2_{16} = 653\text{F}_{16}$, and take the one's complement $\text{Checksum} = \text{FFFF}_{16} - 653\text{F}_{16} = \mathbf{9AC0}_{16} \ (39,616_{10})$. In `[HEX]` mode, loading the 32-bit accumulated header sum (`2653D [ENTER]`) and dividing by $2^{16} = \text{10000h}$ via `10000 [↱] [÷R]` places the upper carry (`2h`) in Register $X$ and the lower 16 bits (`653Dh`) in Register $Y$; pressing `[+]` folds the carry into the lower sum (`653Fh`), and subtracting from `FFFFh` via `FFFF [x⇄y] [-]` yields the one's complement checksum **`9AC0h`** ($39,616_{10}$ in `[DEC]`):

| Step | Keystroke | Register T | Register Z | Register Y | Register X | Display |
| :---: | :--- | :---: | :---: | :---: | :---: | :--- |
| 01 | `2653D [ENTER]` | `0h` | `0h` | `2653Dh` | `2653Dh` | `2653Dh` |
| 02 | `10000 [↱] [÷R]` | `0h` | `0h` | `653Dh` | `2h` | `2h` |
| 03 | `[+]` | `0h` | `0h` | `0h` | `653Fh` | `653Fh` |
| 04 | `FFFF` | `0h` | `0h` | `653Fh` | `FFFFh` | `FFFFh` |
| 05 | `[x⇄y]` | `0h` | `0h` | `FFFFh` | `653Fh` | `653Fh` |
| 06 | `[-]` | `0h` | `0h` | `0h` | `9AC0h` | `9AC0h` |

Notice how cleanly `[↱] [÷R]` executes the RFC 1071 end-around carry: dividing `2653Dh` by `10000h` ($2^{16}$) splits the upper carry (`2h`) into Register $X$ and the lower 16-bit word (`653Dh`) into Register $Y$ in one keystroke, so pressing `[+]` folds them together into `653Fh` immediately! What if adding that folded carry triggers a *second* overflow out of Bit 15? In corner-case network frames—for instance, when a 32-bit TCP pseudo-header accumulator reaches `0x1FFFF`—a single 16-bit fold `1FFFF [ENTER] 10000 [↱] [÷R] [+]` adds the upper carry `1h` to `FFFFh` and produces `10000h`, which itself carries into Bit 16! Applying a second end-around fold `10000 [↱] [÷R] [+]` reduces `10000h` to `1h`, and subtracting from the all-ones word `FFFFh` (`FFFF [x⇄y] [-]`) confirms the one's-complement wire checksum `FFFEh`.

That exact same end-around carry structure powers cryptographic ciphers. What if we want to permute bits inside a register without losing a single bit off the edge? In cryptographic hash functions (such as SHA-256 and ChaCha20), plain bit-shifts (`<<` or `>>`) are avoided because bits that slide off the edge of the register are lost forever, destroying information entropy. Instead, ciphers use **circular bit rotations** (`ROL` and `ROR`), where the bit pushed off the most-significant end wraps around and enters the least-significant end. To rotate the 8-bit byte `0x85` ($10000101_2$) left by 1 bit ($\implies 00001011_2 = \text{0Bh}$) in `[HEX]` mode using `[↱] [÷R]` at the 8-bit boundary $2^8 = \text{100h}$, we first shift left by 1 bit via `85 [ENTER] 2 [×]` $\rightarrow$ `10Ah`, split the 8-bit remainder (`0Ah` in $Y$) and overflow carry (`1h` in $X$) via `[↱] [÷R]` (`10A [ENTER] 100 [↱] [÷R]` $\rightarrow$ `1h`), and add the carry back into the least-significant bit via `10A [ENTER] 100 [↱] [÷R] [+]` $\rightarrow$ **`Bh`**:

| Step | Keystrokes | Register T | Register Z | Register Y | Register X | Notes |
|:---|:---|:---|:---|:---|:---|:---|
| 01 | `85 [ENTER] 2 [×]` | `0h` | `0h` | `0h` | **`10Ah`** | Shift byte left by 1 bit ($85\text{h} \times 2 = 10\text{Ah}$) |
| 02 | `100 [↱] [÷R]` | `0h` | `0h` | `Ah` | **`1h`** | Extract carry bit ($X=1\text{h}$) and rotated byte ($Y=\text{Ah}$) |
| 03 | `[+]` | `0h` | `0h` | `0h` | **`Bh`** | Add carry bit into LSB: $10\text{Ah} \bmod 100\text{h} + 1\text{h} = \text{Ah} + 1\text{h} = \text{Bh}$ |

> **Circular Bit Rotation (`ROL`) as a Meshing Gear Ring:** A circular left bit-rotation (`ROL 1`) is the binary equivalent of indexing a closed 256-state mechanical drum or **Planetary Geared Clock** ring gear by one step: multiplying by $2$ advances the state around the cylinder, `100 [↱] [÷R]` splits the wrap-around tooth carry (`1h` in Register $X$) from the in-range modulo-256 remainder (`Ah` in Register $Y$), and `[+]` feeds the wrapped bit back into Bit 0 so no information ever falls off the edge of the word.

### 10.4.2 Fixed-Point Clock Dividers & IEEE-754 Floating-Point Bit Layout

How does a physical serial port keep its bit-sampling clock locked onto an incoming waveform using integer hardware registers? Unlike SPI or I2C buses, an asynchronous UART serial link has no shared clock wire—the transmitter and receiver sample each bit using their own internal crystal oscillators. If their baud rates drift apart by more than $\sim 2\%$, the sampling strobe slips across a bit boundary by the 10th bit (the stop bit) and garbles the frame. To achieve sub-percent accuracy from a $f_{\text{clk}} = 150.0\text{ MHz}$ peripheral clock over an $8\times$ oversampling receiver, modern UART peripherals split the clock divider into a 16-bit integer register (`IBRD`) and a 6-bit fractional register (`FBRD`, counted in sixty-fourths, $1/64$):

$$\text{Baud Divider} = \frac{f_{\text{clk}}}{8 \times \text{Baud}} = \frac{150,000,000}{8 \times 115,200} = \frac{150,000,000}{921,600} \approx 162.760416667$$

In `[DEC]` and `[ALL]` display mode, keying `150000000 [ENTER] 8 [÷] 115200 [÷]` evaluates the exact floating-point baud divider **`162.760416667`**. Duplicating the divider and taking its integer part (`[ENTER] [↱] [PARTS] [IP]`) isolates `IBRD` = **`162`** (`0xA2`), while swapping back to the fractional part and scaling by $64$ (`[x⇄y] [↱] [PARTS] [FP] 64 [×] [↱] [PARTS] [IP]`) gives `FBRD` = **`48`** (or rounded via `[↰] [RND]`: **`49`**, `0x31`). With `IBRD = 162` and `FBRD = 49`, the actual baud rate is $150,000,000 / (8 \times (162 + 49/64)) = 150,000,000 / 1302.125 = \mathbf{115,196.3\text{ baud}}$, a timing error of just $(115196.3 - 115200) / 115200 \times 100\% = \mathbf{-0.0032\%}$:

| Step | Keystroke | Register T | Register Z | Register Y | Register X | Display |
| :---: | :--- | :---: | :---: | :---: | :---: | :--- |
| 01 | `150000000` | $0.00000000$ | $0.00000000$ | $0.00000000$ | $150000000.$ | `150000000._` |
| 02 | `[ENTER]` | $0.00000000$ | $0.00000000$ | $150000000.$ | $150000000.$ | `150000000._` |
| 03 | `8 [÷]` | $0.00000000$ | $0.00000000$ | $0.00000000$ | $18750000.0$ | `18750000._` |
| 04 | `115200 [÷]` | $0.00000000$ | $0.00000000$ | $0.00000000$ | $162.760417$ | `162.760417_` |
| 05 | `[ENTER]` | $0.00000000$ | $0.00000000$ | $162.760417$ | $162.760417$ | `162.760417_` |
| 06 | `[IP]` | $0.00000000$ | $0.00000000$ | $162.760417$ | $162.000000$ | `162._` |
| 07 | `[x⇄y] [FP]` | $0.00000000$ | $0.00000000$ | $162.000000$ | $0.76041667$ | `0.76041667_` |
| 08 | `64 [×]` | $0.00000000$ | $0.00000000$ | $162.000000$ | $48.6666667$ | `48.6666667_` |
| 09 | `[↰] [RND]` | $0.00000000$ | $0.00000000$ | $162.000000$ | $49.0000000$ | `49._` |

While fixed-point arithmetic locks the binary radix point at a fixed bit boundary (such as sixty-fourths), how does a processor pack a wide-ranging real number like $-6.25$ into a 32-bit binary register? William Kahan's **IEEE-754 single-precision (`binary32`) standard** writes the number in base-2 scientific notation, $(-1)^S \times 2^{E - 127} \times (1.\text{Mantissa}_2)$. Because every normalized non-zero binary number starts with a leading `1.` before the radix point, the hardware doesn't even store that leading `1`—it hides it ("the implicit leading bit") and uses all 23 low bits (`Bits 22–0`) for the fractional mantissa, 8 middle bits (`Bits 30–23`, biased by $+127$) for the exponent $E$, and 1 top bit (`Bit 31`) for the sign $S$. For $-6.25_{10}$, the magnitude is $6.25_{10} = 4 + 2 + 0.25 = 110.01_2 = 1.1001_2 \times 2^2$, so the negative sign sets $S = \mathbf{1}$, the biased exponent is $E = 2 + 127 = 129_{10} = 10000001_2 = \mathbf{81h}$, and the 23-bit fractional mantissa after the hidden `1.` is $M = 10010000000000000000000_2 = \mathbf{480000h}$, assembling into the 32-bit word `1 10000001 10010000000000000000000` = **`0xC0C80000`**. Watch how two chained `[↱] [÷R]` divisions in `[HEX]` mode—first by $2^{23} = \text{800000h}$ and then by $2^8 = \text{100h}$ (`C0C80000 [ENTER] 800000 [↱] [÷R] 100 [↱] [÷R]`)—unpack all three IEEE-754 fields of `C0C80000h` directly onto Registers $Z$ (`480000h`), $Y$ (`81h`, Biased Exponent $E=129_{10}$), and $X$ (`1h`, Sign $S=1$):

| Step | Keystroke | Register T | Register Z | Register Y | Register X | Display |
| :---: | :--- | :---: | :---: | :---: | :---: | :--- |
| 01 | `C0C80000 [ENTER]` | `0h` | `0h` | `C0C80000h` | `C0C80000h` | `C0C80000h` |
| 02 | `800000 [↱] [÷R]` | `0h` | `0h` | `480000h` | `181h` | `181h` |
| 03 | `100 [↱] [÷R]` | `0h` | `480000h` | `81h` | `1h` | `1h` |
| 04 | `[↰] [BASE] [DEC]` | 0 | 4718592 | 129 | 1 | `1` |
| 05 | `[x⇄y] 127 [-]` | 4718592 | 4718592 | 1 | 2 | `2` |

From those three registers, we read off the Sign Bit $S = 1$ (negative), the Biased Exponent $E = \text{81h}$ ($129_{10} \implies e = 129 - 127 = \mathbf{2}$), and the Fractional Mantissa $M = \text{480000h}$ ($\frac{4,718,592}{2^{23}} = 0.5625 = \frac{9}{16}$), reconstructing $(-1)^1 \times 2^2 \times (1 + 0.5625) = -4 \times 1.5625 = \mathbf{-6.25}$.

When scientific software upgrades from 32-bit `float` to 64-bit `double` (`binary64`), IEEE-754 widens the biased exponent from 8 bits (bias $127$) to **11 bits** (bias $1023$) and expands the fractional mantissa from 23 bits to **52 bits** (with the top 20 mantissa bits stored in the upper 32-bit word). For the double-precision float value $-13.375_{10}$, the magnitude is $13.375_{10} = 8 + 4 + 1 + 0.25 + 0.125 = 1101.011_2 = 1.101011_2 \times 2^3$, giving Sign $S = 1$, Biased Exponent $3 + 1023 = 1026_{10} = 10000000010_2 = \mathbf{402h}$, and 52-bit fractional mantissa $101011000000\dots0_2$, which assemble into **`0xC02AC00000000000`** (with high 32-bit word `0xC02AC000`). In William Kahan's IEEE-754 binary64 format, that upper 32-bit word packs the 1-bit sign, the 11-bit excess-1023 exponent, and the top 20 bits of the 52-bit significand. Working in `[HEX]` mode and chaining two modular divisions (`C02AC000 [ENTER] 100000 [↱] [÷R] 800 [↱] [÷R]`)—first `100000 [↱] [÷R]` ($2^{20}$) to drop the 20-bit significand fraction `AC000h` into Register $Y$, then `800 [↱] [÷R]` ($2^{11}$) on the upper 12 bits—places the unpacked fields across three adjacent stack registers in one pass: Sign $S = \mathbf{1}$ (`1h`) in $X$, Biased Exponent $E = \mathbf{\text{402h}}$ ($1026_{10} \implies e = 1026 - 1023 = \mathbf{3}$) in $Y$, and upper significand bits `AC000h` ($\frac{704,512}{2^{20}} = 0.671875 = \frac{43}{64}$) in $Z$, reconstructing $(-1)^1 \times 2^3 \times (1 + 0.671875) = -8 \times 1.671875 = \mathbf{-13.375}$.

Returning to Decimal floating-point mode (`[↰] [BASE] [DEC]`) after inspecting integer bit-fields restores the full IEEE-754 dynamic range for combinatorial state-space and algorithmic complexity analysis (`[↱] [PROB]` menu: `[Cn,r]`, `[Pn,r]`, `[↰] [x!]`, `[RAND]`). For example, when auditing permutation state spaces such as $12! = 479,001,600$ in `[DEC]` mode, keying `12 [↱] [PROB] [↰] [x!]` evaluates the exact factorial in Register $X$ while saving $n = 12$ in `[↰] [LASTX]`; recovering $n = 12$ from `[↰] [LASTX]` to evaluate James Stirling's asymptotic approximation $\sqrt{2\pi n}(n/e)^n \approx 475,687,486.47$ and dividing on the stack immediately confirms that the ratio $n! / \text{Stirling}(n)$ matches the first-order Stirling correction factor $e^{1/(12n)} \approx \mathbf{1.00697}$ without re-typing `12`.

## 10.5 Summary & Looking Ahead

Operating across a 36-bit two's complement integer architecture preserves multi-level stack register values intact across Hexadecimal, Decimal, Octal, and Binary modes. Modular integer division via `[↱] [÷R]`—returning the quotient in $X$ and remainder in $Y$—combines with word-length masking, modular reduction, and powers-of-two arithmetic to configure microcontroller registers, construct IPv4 CIDR subnet masks, pack and extract RGB color channels, and analyze telemetry bit disparities alongside discrete combinatorics ($nPr$, $nCr$, $n!$) and pseudorandom seeding.

From discrete bits and memory registers, the positional mathematics of radix scaling extends directly into quantitative economics and capital valuation. Notice the structural isomorphism as we cross into **Part IV (Applied STEM, Finance & Visual Modeling)**: **just as positional base-2 and base-16 arithmetic weights each column of the Place Value Cubes tray by a constant radix power $b^k$, financial time-value-of-money weights each cash flow across time by an exponential compounding or discount power $(1 + i)^{-k}$.** That means the exact same Horner polynomial nesting (`(a·b + c)·b + d`) that packed hexadecimal bytes in this chapter will discount multi-year corporate cash-flow streams in a single pass. In **[Chapter 11: Financial Mathematics & Time Value of Money (TVM)](sc32/11-financial-tvm.md)**, you will master both direct stack annuity formulas and the SC-32's dedicated five-variable compound interest solver ($N, I\%YR, PV, PMT, FV$) to calculate mortgage amortization schedules, net present value (NPV), internal rate of return (IRR), and real-world capital flows.

# Chapter 11: Financial Mathematics, Executive Analytics & TVM

## 11.1 William Kahan and the Base-Preserving Percentage Invariant (`[↱] [%]`, `[↱] [%CHG]`)

Beyond digits in a bank ledger, **money represents stored human time and labor**. 

When an engineer signs an employment contract, an entrepreneur secures an equipment lease, or a family signs a 30-year home mortgage, the mathematics of compound interest dictates whether that labor compounds into generational freedom or evaporates into perpetual interest debt.

In the late 1970s, UC Berkeley Professor and future Turing Award laureate **William M. Kahan** examined how commercial handheld calculators implemented financial percentage keys.

On almost every algebraic calculator of the era, the percentage key was **destructive**. Suppose you were billing a corporate client for $\$150.00$ of engineering consulting, plus an $8.25\%$ state sales tax:

$$\text{Algebraic keystrokes: } 150 \ [\times] \ 8.25 \ [\%] \quad \Longrightarrow \quad \text{Displays } 12.38$$

The moment you pressed `[↱] [%]`, the calculator **overwrote your $\$150.00$ base amount**. To find the invoice total ($\$162.38$), you had to either manually re-enter $\$150.00$, write it down on scratch paper, or rely on a separate memory key (`M+`). If the client asked to test an alternative $9.5\%$ tax rate, you had to start over from scratch.

In 1979, writing in the *Hewlett-Packard Journal* *([Kahan, 1979](sc32/appendix-e-annotated-bibliography.md#cite-kahan1979))*, Kahan formalized what is now known in numerical computing as the **Kahan Percentage Invariant**: a percentage operator must be **non-destructive and dyadic**, replacing Register $X$ with the percentage amount while preserving the base amount frozen in Register $Y$:

$$X \longleftarrow \frac{Y \times X}{100}, \qquad Y \longleftarrow Y \quad (\text{Preserved frozen on the stack})$$

On the StackCalc SC-32, your base amount *never* disappears. When you key in `150 [ENTER] 8.25 [↱] [%]`, Register $X$ displays `12.38` (the tax amount) while Register $Y$ silently holds `150.00` (the base invoice). Want the total invoice? Just tap `[+]` to obtain `$162.38`. Need a discount subtracted instead? Tap `[-]` to obtain `$137.62`. And if the client asks to test an alternative rate, tap `[↰] [LASTX] [x⇄y]` or key the new rate against the preserved base without re-entering a single digit of the original invoice.

![Active RPN Calculation on Transflective LCD](../assets/manuals/screenshots/sc32_tvm_mortgage.png)
*Figure 11.1: The SC-32 transflective display executing multi-variable financial calculations with continuous stack preservation.*

![StackCalc SC-32 Pure Black Craftsmanship Edition](../assets/renders/sc32-craftsmanship-pureblack.png)
*Figure 11.2: The SC-32 precision aluminum chassis and tactile key switches, engineered for fatigue-free boardroom and field accounting.*

In high-stakes corporate boardrooms, private equity deal evaluations, commercial contract negotiations, and dynamic field estimation, computational latency disrupts quantitative decision-making. When an executive using an algebraic calculator attempts to evaluate compound financial relationships, they are forced to mentally manage parenthesis depth, worry about operator precedence, and store intermediate results into disjointed memory keys (`M+`, `MR`, `STO 1`). Reverse Polish Notation eliminates this parenthetical bookkeeping *([HP, 1982](sc32/appendix-e-annotated-bibliography.md#cite-hp15c1982))*: the four-level operational stack acts as a visual, transparent ledger where operands are staged, intermediate results are automatically preserved, and dyadic operations consume inputs with zero syntax errors. To format currency outputs rounded to cents while retaining full 64-bit internal precision, set the display mode to two decimal places (`[FIX] 2`) via `[↰] [DISP]` $\to$ `[FIX]` $\to$ `2`.

### 11.1.1 Cash-Flow Sign Conventions, Register Allocation & Tactile Financial Models
Every financial calculation on the SC-32 models a physical cash ledger: money leaving your pocket (investments, loan principal outlays, savings deposits) carries a negative sign (`[+/-]`), while money entering your pocket (loan proceeds, coupon inflows, maturity payouts) carries a positive sign. On the 4-level stack, each register serves as an explicit working account—Register $X$ holds the active adjustment or tax delta, Register $Y$ preserves the pre-tax invoice or principal baseline intact, Register $Z$ accumulates multi-tier reserves, and the dedicated five-variable `[↰] [TVM]` solver links those cash flows directly to compound discounting and amortization equations.

Three physical manipulative models turn the core concepts of quantitative finance into tangible geometry on your desk:
1. **Simple vs. Compound Growth (Counting Tiles & Prime Factor Blocks):** Simple interest ($FV = PV(1 + N i)$) merely docks a constant number of new $19.0 \times 19.0\text{ mm}$ **Counting Tiles** onto the end of a row each period. Compound interest ($FV = PV(1 + i)^N$), by contrast, scales the entire rectangular array in two dimensions so that *prior interest tiles generate new interest tiles of their own*—and with the **Prime Factor Blocks**, each doubling of capital adds one full $7.00\text{ mm}$ Blue $[2]$ block to your wealth tower.
2. **Percentages & Basis Points (Place Value Cubes Decimal Tray):** Switching the **Place Value Cubes** tray to its engraved decimal face (`1 • 0.1 | 0.01 | 0.001`) makes financial rate scaling transparent: moving two slots right of the unit post (`•`) into the hundredths socket (`0.01`) represents $1\% = 0.01$, while a single institutional **basis point** ($1\text{ bp} = 0.01\% = 0.0001$) is one hundredth of the `0.01` percent slot.
3. **Present-Value Discounting & Bond Duration (84 mm Fraction Towers):** Why is a dollar promised 10 or 20 years in the future worth less than a dollar in your hand today? Line up the **84 mm Fraction Towers** in decreasing height order ($1 = 84.0\text{ mm}$ today at $t=0$, down through $\frac{1}{2} = 42.0\text{ mm}$, $\frac{1}{3} = 28.0\text{ mm}$, and $\frac{1}{4} = 21.0\text{ mm}$ at distant horizons). Dividing a future cash flow $FV$ by $(1 + i)^N$ physically compresses its present-value tower height according to how far in the future it arrives—and **Macaulay Duration** (analyzed under **Bond Pricing, Duration & Discounted Cash-Flow Analysis** later in this chapter) is literally the horizontal center-of-mass fulcrum where those discounted cash-flow towers balance along the timeline.

### 11.1.2 The Base-Preserving Percentage Operator (`[↱] [%]`), Chain Discounts & Gross Margin

On standard commercial calculators, pressing the percentage key is fraught with peril: some models merely divide the active entry by 100, others multiply by the previous operand, and nearly all overwrite the base operand in the process. Worse still, keying `100 + 8% =` on many algebraic pocket calculators literally computes $100 + 0.08 = 100.08$!

On the StackCalc SC-32, the **Percentage Function (`[↱] [%]`)** is an invariant dyadic operator adhering strictly to William Kahan's non-destructive specification:

$$\text{Calculation: } \quad X \leftarrow \frac{Y \times X}{100}, \quad Y \leftarrow Y \text{ (Preserved)}, \quad \text{Lift} \leftarrow \text{TRUE}$$

| Register | State After Keying `[Base] [ENTER] [Rate] [↱] [%]` | Executive Function |
| :---: | :--- | :--- |
| **Register $Y$** | Base Amount (Preserved frozen in $Y$) | Base remains intact for subsequent total, discount, or alternative trial |
| **Register $X$** | Computed Percentage Amount: $(Y \times X) / 100$ | Tax, tip, commission, or margin dollar value |

Because the base amount remains frozen in Register $Y$ while the dollar percentage appears in Register $X$, you see *both* numbers on the screen before deciding what to do with them. On our opening $\$150.00$ invoice at $8.25\%$ tax, keying `150 [ENTER] 8.25 [↱] [%]` places $\$12.38$ in Register $X$ while holding $\$150.00$ in Register $Y$; pressing `[+]` yields $\$162.38$ in a single stroke, and keying `100 [ENTER] 8 [↱] [%]` on a $\$100.00$ baseline places the exact dollar amount ($\mathbf{8}$) in $X$ while freezing $100.00$ in $Y$.

Let's see how this base-preserving ledger works across real commercial transactions. Suppose a procurement officer is signing off on an enterprise server hardware order subtotaling $\$18,450.00$ in a jurisdiction with an $8.25\%$ state sales tax. Rather than multiplying by $0.0825$ and losing the subtotal, we use `[↱] [%]` in `[FIX] 2` display mode so that both the tax liability and the pre-tax base remain visible on the stack: keying `18450 [ENTER] 8.25 [↱] [%]` places the tax amount $X = \mathbf{\$1,522.13}$ below the preserved base $Y = \$18,450.00$, and pressing `[+]` immediately sums the total invoice to **`$19,972.13`**:

| Step | Keystroke | Register T | Register Z | Register Y | Register X | Display |
| :---: | :--- | :---: | :---: | :---: | :---: | :--- |
| 01 | `18450 [ENTER]` | 0.00 | 0.00 | 18450.00 | 18450.00 | `18450.00_` |
| 02 | `8.25 [↱] [%]` | 0.00 | 0.00 | 18450.00 | 1522.13 | `1522.13` |
| 03 | `[+]` | 0.00 | 0.00 | 0.00 | 19972.13 | `19972.13` |

Now flip the scenario to the other side of the negotiating table: an enterprise software license carries a list price of $\$85,000.00$, and the procurement team negotiates a $17.5\%$ volume discount, requiring both the dollar concession for the discount line item and the net invoice payable. Because `[↱] [%]` replaces Register $X$ with $(Y \times X)/100$ while leaving the base contract amount untouched in Register $Y$, keying `85000 [ENTER] 17.5 [↱] [%]` in `[FIX] 2` mode displays the negotiated dollar concession ($X = \mathbf{\$14,875.00}$) alongside the $\$85,000.00$ list price in $Y$, and pressing `[-]` immediately yields the net invoice payable (**`$70,125.00`**, $X = \mathbf{70125.00}$).

What happens when a retailer stacks *two* percentage markdowns in succession—advertising a "$30\%$ seasonal sale plus an extra $15\%$ VIP coupon" on a $\$280.00$ designer jacket? A casual shopper might add $30\% + 15\% = 45\%$ off, expecting to pay $\$154.00$—but successive percentage markdowns compound multiplicatively against the reduced subtotal rather than additively! Keying `280 [ENTER] 30 [↱] [%]` followed by `[-]` deducts the initial $30\%$ markdown $(\$84.00)$ to leave the sale price $(\$196.00)$ in Register $X$, and chaining `15 [↱] [%] [-]` applies the $15\%$ VIP coupon $(\$29.40)$ against that reduced base to yield $\mathbf{\$166.60}$—an effective combined discount of $1 - (0.70)(0.85) = 40.5\%$.

Even outside the boardroom, keeping intermediate subtotals live on the four-level stack turns multi-way dinner splits into effortless one-pass calculations. Suppose eight colleagues dine out together and receive a grand total bill of $\$480.00$, where three of the eight guests shared two reserve bottles of wine totaling $\$96.00$ while everyone shared the food equally. How much should the wine drinkers and non-drinkers each pay? Deducting the wine tab via `480 [ENTER] 96 [-]` isolates the shared food bill $(\$384.00)$, and `8 [÷]` establishes the per-guest food share $(\$48.00)$ in Register $X$. Computing the per-drinker wine allocation via `96 [ENTER] 3 [÷]` places $\$32.00$ in $X$ while the $\$48.00$ food share waits in $Y$, so `[+]` resolves the wine-drinker total ($X = \mathbf{\$80.00}$) alongside **`$48.00`** for non-wine guests.

Consider next one of the most expensive mistakes in retail and hardware manufacturing: confusing **Markup** (profit divided by *cost*) with **Gross Margin** (profit divided by *selling price*). Suppose a hardware product has a landed bill-of-materials cost of $C = \$60.00$, and the board mandates a **$40.0\%$ Gross Margin** on retail sales. An amateur might fall into the markup trap of adding $40\%$ on top of $\$60.00$ (`60 [ENTER] 40 [↱] [%] [+]` $\rightarrow$ **`\$84.00`**), which yields $\$24.00$ of profit on an $\$84.00$ price tag—only $\$24.00 / \$84.00 = 28.57\%$ gross margin! Under true gross margin pricing, if gross profit takes $40\%$ of the selling price, then the $\$60.00$ cost must represent the remaining $1 - 0.40 = 60\%$ of the selling price ($\text{Price} = \frac{\text{Cost}}{1 - \text{Margin}}$), which `60 [ENTER] 1 [ENTER] 0.40 [-] [÷]` resolves to **`\$100.00`**:

| Step | Keystrokes | Register T | Register Z | Register Y | Register X | Notes |
|:---|:---|:---|:---|:---|:---|:---|
| 01 | `60 [ENTER] 40 [↱] [%]` | 0.00 | 0.00 | 60.00 | 24.00 | 40% markup on \$60.00 cost: \$24.00 |
| 02 | `[+]` | 0.00 | 0.00 | 0.00 | 84.00 | Flawed markup price: \$84.00 (28.57% margin) |
| 03 | `60 [ENTER] 1 [ENTER]` | 84.00 | 60.00 | 1.00 | 1.00 | True margin pricing: stage cost \$60 in $Z$ and 1.00 in $Y$ |
| 04 | `.40 [-]` | 84.00 | 84.00 | 60.00 | 0.60 | 1 - 0.40 = 0.60 margin complement; \$60.00 drops to $Y$ |
| 05 | `[÷]` | 84.00 | 84.00 | 84.00 | 100.00 | True gross margin retail price: \$100.00 |

### 11.1.3 Period-over-Period Growth (`[↱] [%CHG]`), Cross-Metric Elasticity & Multi-Year CAGR

Corporate revenue growth, cost expansion, and quarterly margin velocity are measured by relative percentage change:

$$\%CHG = \frac{\text{New Value} - \text{Old Value}}{\text{Old Value}} \times 100$$

On the SC-32, the **Percent Change Function (`[↱] [%CHG]`)** is executed via Right Shift `[↱]` followed by `[%CHG]` using the natural chronological order **Old Value `[ENTER]` New Value `[↱] [%CHG]`**:

| Register | State Before `[↱] [%CHG]` | State After `[↱] [%CHG]` | Executive Role |
| :---: | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **Register $Y$** | Old Value (Baseline) | Old Value (Preserved in $Y$) | Allows instant variance check: `[x⇄y] [↰] [LASTX] [x⇄y] [-]` |
| **Register $X$** | New Value (Current) | $\frac{\text{New} - \text{Old}}{\text{Old}} \times 100$ | Relative rate of expansion/contraction (%) |
| **`LASTX`** | Previous operand | New Value | Retained for delta calculations |

Just like `[↱] [%]`, `[↱] [%CHG]` is non-destructive: the Old Value stays anchored in Register $Y$ and the New Value is saved in `LASTX`, so you can immediately recover the absolute dollar variance ($\text{New} - \text{Old}$) by pressing `[x⇄y] [↰] [LASTX] [x⇄y] [-]`.

The computational superiority of the RPN stack shines when we compare growth rates across two competing operating lines (**comparative multi-metric corporate analytics**). Suppose an executive is evaluating a software portfolio company whose **Annual Recurring Revenue (ARR)** grew from $\$12.0\text{M}$ to $\$15.6\text{M}$ ($+30.00\%$), while **Customer Acquisition Cost (CAC)** expanded from $\$2.4\text{M}$ to $\$2.88\text{M}$ ($+20.00\%$). Two questions immediately arise at the board table:
1. **The ARR vs. CAC Growth Spread ($\Delta \text{ARR}\% - \Delta \text{CAC}\%$):** By how many percentage points did revenue growth outpace acquisition cost growth?
2. **The Growth Elasticity Ratio ($\Delta \text{ARR}\% \div \Delta \text{CAC}\%$):** How many percentage points of top-line revenue growth did each percentage point of acquisition spending buy?

Watch how the 4-level stack lets us compute the ARR percentage change via `12 [ENTER] 15.6 [↱] [%CHG]` ($\rightarrow 30.00$) followed by the CAC percentage change via `2.4 [ENTER] 2.88 [↱] [%CHG]` ($\rightarrow 20.00$). Dropping the old baseline out of the way (`[x⇄y] [R↓]`) aligns revenue growth ($Y = 30.00$) and acquisition cost growth ($X = 20.00$) side-by-side on the stack, where pressing `[-]` yields the **`+10.00%`** growth spread and keying `30 [ENTER] 20 [÷]` computes the **`1.5`** growth elasticity multiplier:

| Step | Keystroke | Register T | Register Z | Register Y | Register X | Display |
| :---: | :--- | :---: | :---: | :---: | :---: | :--- |
| 01 | `12 [ENTER] 15.6 [↱] [%CHG]` | 0.00 | 0.00 | 12.00 | 30.00 | `30.00` |
| 02 | `2.4 [ENTER] 2.88 [↱] [%CHG]` | 12.00 | 30.00 | 2.40 | 20.00 | `20.00` |
| 03 | `[x⇄y]` | 12.00 | 30.00 | 20.00 | 2.40 | `2.40` |
| 04 | `[R↓]` | 2.40 | 12.00 | 30.00 | 20.00 | `20.00` |
| 05 | `[-]` | 2.40 | 2.40 | 12.00 | 10.00 | `10.00` |

When multi-year growth is measured from initial investment to final exit, we move from single-period `%CHG` to the geometric **Compound Annual Growth Rate (CAGR)**. Suppose a venture capital fund invests $\$14.0\text{M}$ into an industrial robotics startup at Series A, and the company exits via acquisition for $\$88.5\text{M}$ exactly $n = 5\text{ years}$ later. The total multiple on invested capital is $88.5 / 14.0 = 6.32\times$, and taking the fifth root (`5 [1/x] [yˣ]`) of that terminal wealth ratio and subtracting $1$ gives the exact geometric mean annual return, $\text{CAGR} = (88.5 / 14.0)^{1/5} - 1$. Keying `88.5 [ENTER] 14.0 [÷] 5 [1/x] [yˣ] 1 [-] 100 [×]` evaluates the terminal multiple, raises it to the $1/5$ power, subtracts $1$, and scales by $100$ to reveal a compound annual growth rate of **`44.60%`**:

| Step | Keystroke | Register T | Register Z | Register Y | Register X | Display |
| :---: | :--- | :---: | :---: | :---: | :---: | :--- |
| 01 | `88.5 [ENTER]` | 0.00 | 0.00 | 88.50 | 88.50 | `88.50_` |
| 02 | `14.0 [÷]` | 0.00 | 0.00 | 0.00 | 6.32 | `6.32` |
| 03 | `5 [1/x]` | 0.00 | 0.00 | 6.32 | 0.20 | `0.20` |
| 04 | `[yˣ]` | 0.00 | 0.00 | 0.00 | 1.45 | `1.45` |
| 05 | `1 [-]` | 0.00 | 0.00 | 0.00 | 0.45 | `0.45` |
| 06 | `100 [×]` | 0.00 | 0.00 | 0.00 | 44.60 | `44.60` |

Conversely, when exponential compounding works *against* uninvested cash via inflation, even a gentle annual CPI rate quietly erodes purchasing power over decades: what will $\$100,000$ of uninvested cash buy in today's constant dollars after 20 years of $3.2\%$ average annual inflation ($PV = 100,000 / (1.032)^{20}$)? Deflating nominal currency by the cumulative CPI price-level factor $(1 + \pi)^{20}$ via `100000 [ENTER] 1.032 [ENTER] 20 [yˣ] [÷]` ($1.87756$ in the denominator) reveals that $3.2\%$ annual inflation erodes $\$100,000$ to **`53260.60`** ($\mathbf{\$53260.60}$) in constant-dollar purchasing power—cutting purchasing power nearly in half and shrinking an $84.0\text{ mm}$ 1-Whole purchasing-power column in the **84 mm Fraction Towers** down to nearly the $42.0\text{ mm}$ ($\frac{1}{2}$) block. That same sub-period compounding explains why a credit card or commercial revolving line quoted at a nominal $18.5\%$ APR compounded monthly ($m = 12$) actually charges a noticeably higher **Effective Annual Rate ($\text{EAR} = (1 + r_{\text{nom}}/m)^m - 1$)**: by exploiting `[↰] [LASTX]` to recover the compounding frequency $m = 12$ after dividing the nominal rate, you can evaluate $\text{EAR} = (1 + 0.185/12)^{12} - 1$ while typing `12` only once—keying `0.185 [ENTER] 12 [÷] [↰] [LASTX] [x⇄y] 1 [+] [x⇄y] [yˣ] 1 [-] 100 [×]` places the periodic rate $0.015417$ in $X$, recalls $12$ into $Y$, raises $1.015417^{12}$, and scales to reveal an effective annual yield of $\mathbf{20.15\%}$ ($165\text{ bps}$ above the stated APR).

## 11.2 The Five-Variable Time Value of Money Engine (`[↰] [TVM]`) & Cash-Flow Sign Conventions

Beyond single-sum percentages and growth ratios, all commercial banking, corporate bonds, and mortgages rest on the 5-variable Time Value of Money (TVM) equation:

$$PV + PMT \left[ \frac{1 - (1 + i)^{-N}}{i} \right] + FV (1 + i)^{-N} = 0$$

Consider what happens when an analyst tries to evaluate the monthly mortgage annuity payment manually from the closed-form equation on an algebraic textbook calculator:

$$PMT = PV \cdot \frac{i(1 + i)^N}{(1 + i)^N - 1} \quad \Longrightarrow \quad \mathrm{PV} \times ((I / 1200) \times (1 + I / 1200)^N) / ((1 + I / 1200)^N - 1)$$

Notice the vulnerabilities: $(I / 1200)$ must be recomputed or stored in scratch memory three separate times; five levels of open parentheses must remain balanced in working memory; and a single missing closing parenthesis triggers a syntax error or a silent erroneous amortization table.

On the StackCalc SC-32, you can either evaluate that closed form from the inside out in seconds (computing $G = (1 + i)^N$ once, duplicating with `[ENTER]`, and forming $G / (G - 1)$ with zero parentheses), or invoke the onboard **Five-Variable Time Value of Money (TVM) Engine** accessed via Left Shift `[↰]` followed by `[TVM]` on the multi-action `[x∥y]` key (Row 7, Column 3):

| TVM Variable | LFU Softkey | Actuarial Description | Computational Units |
| :---: | :---: | :--- | :--- |
| **$N$** | `[N]` | Total number of compounding periods | Integer or fractional periods |
| **$I\%YR$** | `[I%YR]` | Periodic interest rate per compounding period | Percent per period (e.g. `6.5` for 6.5%/yr or `6.75/12` for monthly) |
| **$PV$** | `[PV]` | Present value (initial loan principal or investment) | Currency ($) |
| **$PMT$** | `[PMT]` | Periodic annuity payment amount | Currency ($ per period) |
| **$FV$** | `[FV]` | Future value (final balloon balance or accumulated savings) | Currency ($) |

### 11.2.1 The Master Actuarial TVM Equation & Hybrid Analytical-Bisection Engine
All five financial variables are bound together by a single conservation law—the universal compound interest annuity equation:

$$PV + PMT \left[ \frac{1 - (1 + i)^{-N}}{i} \right] (1 + i \cdot S) + FV (1 + i)^{-N} = 0$$

where $i = \frac{I\%YR}{100}$ is the periodic interest rate per compounding period stored in `[I%YR]`, $N$ is the total number of compounding periods stored in `[N]`, and $S = 0$ for End-of-Period payments (Ordinary Annuity, the default for loans and mortgages) or $S = 1$ for Beginning-of-Period payments (Annuity Due, the standard for equipment leases and tuition, flagged by the `BEGIN` annunciator and toggled via `[↰] [TVM] [BEG/END]`).

When you store any four of the five TVM variables and press the fifth softkey, the SC-32 solves for the unknown variable automatically. Four of the five variables have exact $\mathcal{O}(1)$ analytical closed-form solutions, with a smooth zero-interest limit ($a_{\overline{N}|i} = \frac{1 - (1+i)^{-N}}{i} \to N$ whenever $|i| < 10^{-14}$):
* **Solving for `FV`:** $FV = -\frac{PV + PMT \cdot (1 + i \cdot S) \cdot a_{\overline{N}|i}}{(1+i)^{-N}}$
* **Solving for `PV`:** $PV = -PMT \cdot (1 + i \cdot S) \cdot a_{\overline{N}|i} - FV(1+i)^{-N}$
* **Solving for `PMT`:** $PMT = -\frac{PV + FV(1+i)^{-N}}{(1 + i \cdot S) \cdot a_{\overline{N}|i}}$
* **Solving for `N`:** Inverted analytically via natural logarithms:
  $$N = -\frac{\ln\!\left(\frac{\text{PMT}_{\text{adj}} - i \cdot FV}{\text{PMT}_{\text{adj}} + i \cdot PV}\right)}{\ln(1 + i)}, \qquad \text{PMT}_{\text{adj}} = PMT(1 + i \cdot S)$$
  (which simplifies cleanly to $N = -(PV + FV)/PMT$ when $|i| < 10^{-14}$).
* **Solving for `I%YR` (240-Interval Scan + 100-Iteration Bisection):** Because the polynomial $f(i) = PV + PMT(1 + i \cdot S)a_{\overline{N}|i}(i) + FV(1+i)^{-N} = 0$ has no closed-form algebraic inverse for $i$ when $N > 4$ (by the Abel-Ruffini theorem!), the SC-32 runs a two-stage numerical root finder: first, it sweeps **240 uniform subintervals** across $i \in [-0.9999, +10.0]$ ($-99.99\%$ to $+1000\%$ per period) to bracket the sign change $f(a) \cdot f(b) \le 0$; second, it refines that bracket across up to **100 bisection steps** until $|f(\text{mid})| < 10^{-12}$ or $(b - a)/2 < 10^{-13}$, returning $I\%YR = 100 \cdot i$ to full 64-bit precision.

### 11.2.2 Why Cash-Flow Sign Discipline Works Like Conservation of Energy
Notice that the right-hand side of the master TVM equation is **zero**. Think of your wallet—or a corporate treasury account—as a physical control volume in thermodynamics or a circuit node in Kirchhoff's Current Law:
- **Cash Inflows ($+$) are Positive:** Any cash flowing *into* your hands (the $\$350,000$ loan wire you receive at mortgage closing, the $\$27.50$ semi-annual coupon check from a bond, or the final maturity payout at the end of a CD) is entered as a **positive** number.
- **Cash Outflows ($-$) are Negative (`[+/-]`):** Any cash flowing *out* of your pocket (the $\$925.00$ purchase price you pay to buy a bond, the monthly $\$2,270.09$ mortgage check you mail to the bank, or a balloon payoff at the end of a commercial note) is entered as a **negative** number using `[+/-]`.

When every future payment and final balance is discounted back to the present moment ($t = 0$), the inflows and outflows must balance to zero. That immediately explains why entering all positive numbers ($PV = +1000, PMT = +50, FV = +1000$) causes the TVM solver to halt with `ERROR 5` (Code 08): physically, a transaction where you only receive money and never pay anything out cannot balance to zero at any real interest rate! Likewise, always make sure your time period $N$ and periodic rate $I\%YR$ share the same time unit: for a 30-year monthly mortgage ($N = 360\text{ months}$), divide the annual nominal rate ($6.75\%$) by $12$ (`6.75 [ENTER] 12 [÷] [I%YR]` $\to 0.5625\%/\text{month}$) before storing it—otherwise `6.75 [I%YR]` would model a loan charging $6.75\%$ interest *every single month* ($81\%\text{ APR}$)!

### 11.2.3 Residential Mortgages, Amortization Crossover & Accelerated Payoff

Few financial calculations are more eye-opening than turning the five-variable `[↰] [TVM]` engine onto the true 30-year cost of a fixed residential mortgage. Suppose a family borrows $PV = +\$350,000.00$ (cash inflow received at closing) on a 30-year fixed mortgage ($N = 30 \times 12 = 360\text{ months}$, $FV = \$0.00$) at an annual nominal rate of $6.75\%$ APR (monthly periodic rate $i = 6.75\% / 12 = 0.5625\%$). After clearing TVM registers (`[↰] [CLEAR] [CLALL]`), store $N = 360$ (`30 [ENTER] 12 [×] [N]`), monthly periodic rate $I\%YR = 0.5625\%$ (`6.75 [ENTER] 12 [÷] [I%YR]`), principal $PV = \$350,000$, and $FV = \$0$. Pressing `[PMT]` solves the monthly payment (**`-$2,270.09`**), multiplying by `360 [×]` yields total lifetime payments (**`-$817,233.60`**), and adding the original principal `350000 [+]` isolates total lifetime interest (**`-$467,233.60`**—more than $1.33\times$ the price of the house itself!):

| 02 | `.5625 [I%YR]` | 0.00 | 0.00 | 360.00 | 0.56 | `0.56` |

| 04 | `0 [FV]` | 360.00 | 0.56 | 350000.00 | 0.00 | `0.00` |
| 05 | `[PMT]` | 360.00 | 0.56 | 350000.00 | -2270.09 | `-2270.09` |

| 07 | `350000 [+]` | 0.56 | 0.56 | 350000.00 | -467233.60 | `-467233.60` |

> **5-Variable `[↰] [TVM]` Solver vs. Closed-Form Stack Annuity with `[↰] [LASTX]`:**
> Every mortgage payment can be verified via the dedicated 5-variable `[↰] [TVM]` registers or directly from the closed-form compound-factor equation $PMT = PV \cdot \frac{i}{1 - (1+i)^{-N}}$ on the stack:
>
> * **At $6.75\%$ APR ($i = 0.005625$/month):** **Dedicated `[↰] [TVM]` Registers:** key `360 [N] .5625 [I%YR] 350000 [PV] 0 [FV] [PMT]` $\implies \mathbf{-\$2,270.09}$. **Direct Stack Closed Form:** key `1 [ENTER] .005625 [+] 360 [+/-] [yˣ] 1 [x⇄y] [-] .005625 [x⇄y] [÷] 350000 [×]` $\implies \mathbf{\$2,270.09}$.
> * **Rate-Comparison Check at $6.50\%$ APR ($i = 0.065/12$/month):** **Dedicated `[↰] [TVM]` Registers:** key `360 [N] 6.5 [ENTER] 12 [÷] [I%YR] 350000 [PV] 0 [FV] [PMT]` $\implies \mathbf{-\$2,212.24}$. **Direct Stack Closed Form with `[↰] [LASTX]`:** compute $1 + i$ and $(1+i)^{360}$ once via `.065 [ENTER] 12 [÷] [ENTER] 1 [+] 360 [yˣ] [ENTER] 1 [-] [÷] [×] 350000 [×]` $\implies \mathbf{\$2,212.24}$—immediately confirming that a $25\text{ bp}$ ($0.25\%$) rate reduction saves $\$57.85/\text{month}$ ($\$20,826$ over 30 years).

Why does your loan balance barely budge during the early years of that 30-year mortgage? Because each month, the bank first charges rent on the entire remaining debt ($I_1 = PV \times i$) and only applies whatever is left over of your monthly check ($P_1 = |PMT| - I_1$) toward reducing principal. On our $\$350,000$ mortgage at $0.5625\%/\text{month}$ ($PMT = -\$2,270.09$), Month 1 interest consumes $350,000 \times 0.005625 = \mathbf{\$1,968.75}$ ($86.7\%$ of the payment), leaving just $\$2,270.09 - \$1,968.75 = \mathbf{\$301.34}$ ($13.3\%$ of the payment) to reduce principal and nudging the remaining balance to $\$350,000 - \$301.34 = \mathbf{\$349,698.66}$. In fact, as the amortization schedule and stack trace below illustrate, the monthly principal reduction $P_k$ does not overtake the monthly interest charge $I_k$ until **Month 237**—nearly twenty years into the loan!

| Month | Remaining Balance | Monthly Payment | Interest ($I_k$) | Principal ($P_k$) | Equity % | Notes |
| :---: | :--- | :---: | :---: | :---: | :---: | :--- |
| **1** | $\$349,698.66$ | $\$2,270.09$ | $\$1,968.75$ | $\$301.34$ | $0.09\%$ | $86.7\%$ of payment goes to interest |
| **237** | $\$199,642.18$ | $\$2,270.09$ | $\$1,130.71$ | $\$1,139.38$ | $42.96\%$ | **Amortization Crossover:** $P_k > I_k$ |
| **360** | $\$0.00$ | $\$2,270.09$ | $\$12.70$ | $\$2,257.39$ | $100.00\%$ | Final payoff; $\$467,233.60$ total interest |

| 04 | `350000 [x⇄y] [-]` | 0.00 | 0.00 | 0.00 | 349698.66 | `349698.66` |

Why does that amortization crossover happen specifically around Month 237? Because on any level-payment loan of $N$ periods at periodic rate $i$, the principal portion of payment $k$ is $P_k = |PMT|(1 + i)^{-(N - k + 1)}$, which means $P_k$ reaches exactly half of the total payment $|PMT|$ (and therefore overtakes the interest half $I_k$) when $(1 + i)^{N - k + 1} = 2$, or $N - k + 1 = \frac{\ln 2}{\ln(1 + i)}$. On our 30-year ($N = 360$) mortgage at monthly rate $i = 0.005625$ ($6.75\%$ APR), evaluating `2 [LN] 1.005625 [LN] [÷] 361 [x⇄y] [-]` directly on the stack confirms the exact continuous crossover point $k = \mathbf{237.43}$ (so Month **238** is the first full payment where principal reduction strictly exceeds interest).

Now imagine standing at a residential open house where a prospective buyer is hesitant about that 30-year ($360\text{-month}$) commitment on the $\$350,000.00$ mortgage at $6.75\%$ APR ($PMT = -\$2,270.09/\text{mo}$). Because $86.7\%$ of early payments go to interest, any extra principal added each month attacks the loan balance directly! We can show the buyer in seconds what happens if they add just **$\$250.00/\text{month}$** in extra principal ($PMT = -\$2,520.09/\text{mo}$) and solve for the new payoff term `[N]` via `6.75 [ENTER] 12 [÷] [I%YR] 350000 [PV] 0 [FV] 2520.09 [+/-] [PMT] [N]`, which drops the repayment horizon to **`270.93` months** ($22.6\text{ years}$):

| 01 | `6.75 [ENTER] 12 [÷] [I%YR]` | 0.00 | 0.00 | 0.00 | 0.56 | Monthly rate i = 0.5625% |
| 02 | `350000 [PV] 0 [FV]` | 0.00 | 0.56 | 350000.00 | 0.00 | Store PV = \$350,000.00, FV = \$0.00 |

| 04 | `[N]` | 0.56 | 350000.00 | 0.00 | 270.93 | Accelerated repayment: 270.93 months |

Adding $\$250/\text{month}$ eliminates **$89\text{ monthly payments}$ ($7.4\text{ years}$)** and saves **$\$134,474.66$** in lifetime interest.

## 11.3 Bond Pricing, Duration & Discounted Cash-Flow Analysis (`NPV`, `IRR`)

Moving from loans and mortgages into institutional capital markets, we now apply the TVM solver, Horner polynomial discounting, and Brent's root-finder (`[↱] [SOLVE]`) to price corporate bonds, measure interest-rate duration sensitivity, value operating businesses via Discounted Cash Flow (DCF), and size quantitative trading positions.

### 11.3.1 Fixed-Income Bond Yield to Maturity (YTM) & Macaulay Duration

Storing four TVM variables and solving for the fifth (`N`, `I%YR`, `PV`, `PMT`, `FV`) under strict cash-flow sign conventions prices corporate and Treasury bonds directly. Suppose an investor buys a 10-year corporate bond ($N = 20$ semi-annual periods) with a $\$1,000.00$ par value ($FV = +\$1,000.00$) and a $5.5\%$ annual coupon paid semi-annually ($PMT = +\$27.50$ every six months) at a discounted market price of $\$925.00$ ($PV = -\$925.00$ cash outflow today). What is the bond's annualized **Yield to Maturity (YTM)**? Storing $N, PV, PMT,$ and $FV$ and pressing `[I%YR]` invokes the 240-interval bisection solver to find the semi-annual yield $i = 3.2666\%$, which we double (`2 [×]`) to obtain the bond-equivalent annual yield $\text{YTM} = \mathbf{6.53\%}$:

| Step | Keystroke | Register T | Register Z | Register Y | Register X | Display |
| :---: | :--- | :---: | :---: | :---: | :---: | :--- |
| 01 | `20 [N]` | 0.00 | 0.00 | 0.00 | 20.00 | `20.00` |
| 02 | `925 [+/-] [PV]` | 0.00 | 0.00 | 20.00 | -925.00 | `-925.00` |
| 03 | `27.50 [PMT]` | 0.00 | 20.00 | -925.00 | 27.50 | `27.50` |
| 04 | `1000 [FV]` | 20.00 | -925.00 | 27.50 | 1000.00 | `1000.00` |
| 05 | `[I%YR]` | 20.00 | -925.00 | 27.50 | 3.27 | `3.27` |
| 06 | `2 [×]` | -925.00 | -925.00 | 27.50 | 6.53 | `6.53` |

What about the interest-rate sensitivity of a multi-year bond? Why does a 3-year coupon bond behave like a slightly shorter-than-3-year zero-coupon bond when interest rates move? Because you receive part of your cash back early in Years 1 and 2 via the coupon payments! In 1938, economist Frederick Macaulay defined **Macaulay Duration ($D$)** as the present-value-weighted average time until a bond's cash flows arrive, and dividing by $(1 + y)$ gives **Modified Duration ($D^*$)**, which measures the percentage change in bond price per $1\%$ change in yield. For a 3-year $8.0\%$ annual coupon bond trading at par ($\$1,000.00$) with yield $y = 8.0\%$:

$$\text{Macaulay Duration } D = \frac{1 \times 80/1.08 + 2 \times 80/1.08^2 + 3 \times 1080/1.08^3}{1000} = \mathbf{2.783\text{ years}}, \qquad D^* = \frac{D}{1 + y} = \frac{2.783}{1.08} = \mathbf{2.577\text{ years}}$$

Physically, if you dock three present-value **84 mm Fraction Towers** at $t = 1, 2, 3\text{ years}$ proportional to the discounted cash flows ($\$74.07$, $\$68.59$, and $\$857.34$), Macaulay Duration $D = 2.783\text{ years}$ is the exact center-of-mass pivot point where the timeline balances, and a $100\text{ bps}$ ($1.0\%$ on the `0.01` hundredths socket of the **Place Value Cubes** tray) rise in market interest rates causes approximately a $2.58\%$ decline in bond price:

| :---: | :--- | :---: | :---: | :---: | :---: | :--- |
| 01 | `80 [ENTER] 1.08 [÷]` | 0.00 | 0.00 | 0.00 | 74.0741 | `74.07` |
| 02 | `80 [ENTER] 1.08 [ENTER] 2 [yˣ] [÷] 2 [×] [+]` | 74.07 | 74.07 | 74.07 | 211.2483 | `211.25` |
| 03 | `1080 [ENTER] 1.08 [ENTER] 3 [yˣ] [÷] 3 [×] [+]` | 211.25 | 211.25 | 211.25 | 2783.2648 | `2783.26` |
| 04 | `1000 [÷]` | 211.25 | 211.25 | 211.25 | 2.7833 | `2.7833` |
| 05 | `1.08 [÷]` | 211.25 | 211.25 | 211.25 | 2.5771 | `2.5771` |

### 11.3.2 Corporate DCF Valuation, Uneven Cash-Flow IRR & Quantitative Risk

When valuing an entire operating business rather than a fixed-coupon bond, an investment banking analyst discounts projected free cash flows (FCF) back to the present. Suppose a precision manufacturing firm is projected to generate free cash flows of $\$10\text{M}, \$12\text{M}, \$15\text{M},$ and $\$18\text{M}$ over the next 4 years, discounted at a weighted average cost of capital (WACC) of $10\%$, and at the end of Year 4 the business is valued at a terminal exit multiple of $12\times$ Year 4 FCF ($12 \times 18 = \$216\text{M}$), bringing the total Year 4 cash flow to $18 + 216 = \$234\text{M}$:

$$\text{Enterprise Value} = \frac{10}{1.10} + \frac{12}{1.10^2} + \frac{15}{1.10^3} + \frac{234}{1.10^4}$$

Discounting and accumulating the four annual inflows term-by-term via `10 [ENTER] 1.1 [÷] 12 [ENTER] 1.1 [↰] [x²] [÷] [+] 15 [ENTER] 1.1 [ENTER] 3 [yˣ] [÷] [+] 234 [ENTER] 1.1 [ENTER] 4 [yˣ] [÷] [+]` yields an enterprise valuation of **`190.10313503`** ($\mathbf{\$190.11\text{M}}$):
