### D.4.9 Section 9: Contest Financial Mathematics, Amortization & TVM

Equations E.73–E.77 summarize closed-form compound-interest recipes for ordinary annuities, loan amortization payments, sinking funds, and perpetuities.

**Equation E.73 — Present Value of an Ordinary Annuity:**
$$PV = PMT \left[ \frac{1 - (1 + i)^{-N}}{i} \right]$$
With parameters Periodic payment $PMT$, rate per period $i$, total periods $N$.
Sum of discounted future cash flow geometric series. Determines loan balances, actuarial pension reserves, and bond valuation.  
On the stack, key in `1 [ENTER] i [+] N [+/-] [yˣ] 1 [x⇄y] [-] i [÷] PMT [×]`.
For the benchmark case ($PMT = 500\text{ USD}, i = 0.005$ ($6\%$ APR monthly), $N = 36\text{ months}$), this evaluates to **`16,429.62`** $\text{USD}$.

---

**Equation E.74 — Future Value of an Ordinary Annuity:**
$$FV = PMT \left[ \frac{(1 + i)^N - 1}{i} \right]$$
With parameters Periodic savings deposit $PMT$, rate per period $i$, total periods $N$.
Compound growth accumulation of periodic deposits. Solves retirement nest-egg and university savings goals.  
On the stack, key in `1 [ENTER] i [+] N [yˣ] 1 [-] i [÷] PMT [×]`.
For the benchmark case ($PMT = 250\text{ USD}, i = 0.006$ ($7.2\%$ APR monthly), $N = 60\text{ months}$), this evaluates to **`17,984.66`** $\text{USD}$.

---

**Equation E.75 — Loan Amortization Periodic Payment:**
$$PMT = PV \left[ \frac{i}{1 - (1 + i)^{-N}} \right]$$
With parameters Principal loan amount $PV$, interest rate per period $i$, total payment periods $N$.
Capital recovery factor: inverts annuity PV to find fixed monthly installment liquidating principal and interest.  
On the stack, key in `1 [ENTER] i [+] N [+/-] [yˣ] 1 [x⇄y] [-] i [x⇄y] [÷] PV [×]`.
For the benchmark case ($PV = 25,000\text{ USD}, i = 0.0045$ ($5.4\%$ APR monthly), $N = 48\text{ months}$), this evaluates to **`579.98`** $\text{USD}$.

---

**Equation E.76 — Sinking Fund Periodic Savings Payment:**
$$PMT = FV \left[ \frac{i}{(1 + i)^N - 1} \right]$$
With parameters Target future balance $FV$, interest rate per period $i$, total saving periods $N$.
Periodic contribution required to accumulate a predetermined future balloon payment or capital equipment replacement fund.  
On the stack, key in `1 [ENTER] i [+] N [yˣ] 1 [-] i [x⇄y] [÷] FV [×]`.
For the benchmark case (Target $FV = 50,000\text{ USD}, i = 0.005$ ($6\%$ APR monthly), $N = 120\text{ months}$), this evaluates to **`305.10`** $\text{USD}$.

---

**Equation E.77 — Flat & Growing Perpetuities:**
$$PV_{\text{flat}} = \frac{PMT}{i}, \quad PV_{\text{growing}} = \frac{PMT}{i - g}$$
With parameters Annual dividend payment $PMT$, discount rate $i$, constant dividend growth rate $g$ ($i > g$).
Gordon growth model; sum of infinite geometric cash flow series with continuous compounding. Dictates preferred stock and endowment valuations.  
The stack evaluation sequences are:
- Flat: `PMT [ENTER] i [÷]`  
- Growing: `PMT [ENTER] i [ENTER] g [-] [÷]`  
For the benchmark case ($PMT = 1,200\text{ USD/yr}, i = 0.06, g = 0.02$), this evaluates to Flat Perpetuity = **`20,000.00`** $\text{USD}$; Growing Perpetuity = **`30,000.00`** $\text{USD}$.

### D.4.10 Section 10: Chemistry, Electrochemistry, Chemical Kinetics & Biochemistry

Equations E.78–E.85 cover aqueous acid-base equilibria, Nernst electrochemical potentials, Arrhenius and Michaelis-Menten kinetics, and spectrophotometric absorbance.

**Equation E.78 — pH & Hydronium Ion Activity:**
$$\text{pH} = -\log_{10}[\text{H}_3\text{O}^+], \quad [\text{H}_3\text{O}^+] = 10^{-\text{pH}}$$
With parameters $[\text{H}_3\text{O}^+]$ (molar hydronium ion concentration, $\text{mol/L}$).
Sørensen logarithmic acidity scale compressing 14 orders of magnitude of aqueous proton activity into a linear 0–14 bench index.  
On the stack, key in `H3O [↰] [LOG] [+/-]` (Inverse: `pH [+/-] [↰] [10ˣ]`).
For the benchmark case ($[\text{H}_3\text{O}^+] = 3.50 \times 10^{-5}\text{ mol/L}$ (`3.5 [E] 5 [+/-] [↰] [LOG] [+/-]`)), this evaluates to **`4.4559`**.

---

**Equation E.79 — Henderson–Hasselbalch Buffer Equilibrium:**
$$\text{pH} = \text{p}K_a + \log_{10}\left(\frac{[\text{A}^-]}{[\text{HA}]}\right)$$
With parameters $\text{p}K_a = -\log_{10} K_a$ (acid dissociation constant), $[\text{A}^-]$ (conjugate base molarity), $[\text{HA}]$ (weak acid molarity).
Governs blood bicarbonate homeostasis ($\text{pH } 7.40$) and analytical laboratory buffer capacity against strong acid/base perturbations.  
On the stack, key in `[A⁻] [ENTER] [HA] [÷] [↰] [LOG] pKa [+]`.
For the benchmark case (Acetate buffer with $\text{p}K_a = 4.76, [\text{A}^-] = 0.25\text{ M}, [\text{HA}] = 0.15\text{ M}$), this evaluates to **`4.9818`**.

---

**Equation E.80 — Nernst Electrochemical Cell Potential:**
$$E_{\text{cell}} = E^\circ_{\text{cell}} - \frac{R T}{n F} \ln Q$$
With parameters $E^\circ_{\text{cell}}$ (standard cell potential, $\text{V}$), $R = 8.31446\text{ J/(mol}\cdot\text{K)}$, $T$ (temperature, $\text{K}$), $n$ (moles of electrons transferred), $F = 96,485.3\text{ C/mol}$, $Q$ (reaction quotient).
Links Gibbs free energy driving force ($\Delta G = -n F E_{\text{cell}}$) to real-time reactant/product activity ratios in galvanic batteries and biological ion channels.  
On the stack, key in `8.31446 [ENTER] T [×] n [÷] 96485.3 [÷] Q [LN] [×] E0 [x⇄y] [-]`.
For the benchmark case (Daniell $\text{Zn/Cu}$ cell: $E^\circ = 1.100\text{ V}, T = 298.15\text{ K}, n = 2, Q = 0.050$), this evaluates to **`1.1385`** $\text{V}$.

---

**Equation E.81 — Arrhenius Chemical Reaction Rate Constant:**
$$k = A \exp\left(-\frac{E_a}{R T}\right)$$
With parameters $A$ (pre-exponential collision frequency factor, $\text{s}^{-1}$), $E_a$ (activation energy barrier, $\text{J/mol}$), $R = 8.31446\text{ J/(mol}\cdot\text{K)}$, $T$ (absolute temperature, $\text{K}$).
Boltzmann thermal fraction of molecular collisions possessing sufficient kinetic energy to surmount the transition-state activation barrier.  
On the stack, key in `Ea [ENTER] 8.31446 [÷] T [÷] [+/-] [eˣ] A [×]`.
For the benchmark case ($A = 1.25 \times 10^{11}\text{ s}^{-1}, E_a = 75,000\text{ J/mol}, T = 350.0\text{ K}$), this evaluates to **`0.7937`** $\text{s}^{-1}$.

---

**Equation E.82 — Michaelis–Menten Enzyme Saturation Kinetics:**
$$v_0 = \frac{V_{\max}[S]}{K_m + [S]}$$
With parameters $V_{\max}$ (maximum turnover velocity), $[S]$ (substrate concentration), $K_m$ (Michaelis constant: substrate concentration at $0.5\,V_{\max}$).
Hyperbolic saturation of catalytic active sites; transitions from first-order kinetics ($v_0 \approx \frac{V_{\max}}{K_m}[S]$) at low $[S]$ to zero-order saturation ($v_0 \to V_{\max}$) at high $[S]$.  
On the stack, key in `Vmax [ENTER] S [×] Km [ENTER] S [+] [÷]`.
For the benchmark case ($V_{\max} = 140.0\text{ }\mu\text{M/min}, [S] = 15.0\text{ mM}, K_m = 5.0\text{ mM}$), this evaluates to **`105.0000`** $\mu\text{M/min}$.

---

**Equation E.83 — Beer–Lambert Spectrophotometric Absorbance:**
$$A = \varepsilon \ell c = -\log_{10}\left(\frac{I}{I_0}\right)$$
With parameters $\varepsilon$ (molar absorptivity, $\text{L}\cdot\text{mol}^{-1}\cdot\text{cm}^{-1}$), $\ell$ (optical cuvette path length, $\text{cm}$), $c$ (molar concentration, $\text{mol/L}$), $I/I_0$ (transmittance $T$).
Differential photon attenuation through an absorbing solution; fundamental calibration equation for UV-Vis spectrophotometry and pulse oximetry.  
On the stack, key in `eps [ENTER] l [×] c [×]` (Transmittance $T = I/I_0$: `A [+/-] [↰] [10ˣ]`).
For the benchmark case (NADH assay at $340\text{ nm}$: $\varepsilon = 6,220\text{ L}\cdot\text{mol}^{-1}\cdot\text{cm}^{-1}, \ell = 1.00\text{ cm}, c = 8.50 \times 10^{-5}\text{ M}$), this evaluates to $A =$ **`0.5287`** ($T = 29.60\%$).

---

**Equation E.84 — Clausius–Clapeyron Vapor Pressure Scaling:**
$$P_2 = P_1 \exp\left[\frac{\Delta H_{\text{vap}}}{R}\left(\frac{1}{T_1} - \frac{1}{T_2}\right)\right]$$
With parameters $P_1, P_2$ (saturation vapor pressures), $\Delta H_{\text{vap}}$ (molar enthalpy of vaporization, $\text{J/mol}$), $R = 8.31446\text{ J/(mol}\cdot\text{K)}$, $T_1, T_2$ (absolute temperatures, $\text{K}$).
Governs phase-boundary equilibrium slope ($dP/dT = \Delta H / (T \Delta V)$) for vacuum distillation, autoclave sterilization, and atmospheric meteorology.  
On the stack, key in `T1 [1/x] T2 [1/x] [-] dH [×] 8.31446 [÷] [eˣ] P1 [×]`.
For the benchmark case (Water: $P_1 = 23.76\text{ Torr}$ at $T_1 = 298.15\text{ K}$, find $P_2$ at $T_2 = 323.15\text{ K}$ ($\Delta H_{\text{vap}} = 43,990\text{ J/mol}$)), this evaluates to **`93.7330`** $\text{Torr}$.

---

**Equation E.85 — Debye–Hückel Solution Ionic Strength:**
$$I = \frac{1}{2}\sum_{i=1}^n c_i z_i^2$$
With parameters $c_i$ (molar concentration of ion species $i$, $\text{mol/L}$), $z_i$ (integer charge valency of ion $i$).
Measures total electrostatic shielding density in electrolyte solutions; multivalent ions ($z_i = \pm 2, \pm 3$) weight quadratically via `[↰] [x²]`.  
On the stack, key in `z1 [↰] [x²] c1 [×] z2 [↰] [x²] c2 [×] [+] 2 [÷]`.
For the benchmark case ($0.10\text{ M }\text{MgCl}_2$ solution ($c_{\text{Mg}^{2+}} = 0.10\text{ M}, z_1 = +2$; $c_{\text{Cl}^-} = 0.20\text{ M}, z_2 = -1$)), this evaluates to **`0.3000`** $\text{mol/L}$.

---

### D.4.11 Section 11: Probability, Statistics, Quality Control & Information Theory

Equations E.86–E.93 address discrete probability distributions, Gaussian confidence intervals, Bayesian inference, Six Sigma capability indices, and Shannon channel capacity.

**Equation E.86 — Binomial Probability Mass Function:**
$$P(X = k) = \binom{n}{k} p^k (1 - p)^{n - k}$$
With parameters $n$ (independent Bernoulli trials), $k$ (exact number of successes), $p$ (single-trial success probability).
Exact discrete probability of observing $k$ successes in $n$ trials using the `PROB` menu `[Cn,r]` combinatorics softkey.  
On the stack, key in `n [ENTER] k [Cn,r] p [ENTER] k [yˣ] [×] 1 [ENTER] p [-] n [ENTER] k [-] [yˣ] [×]`.
For the benchmark case ($n = 10\text{ wafer dies}, k = 3\text{ defects}, p = 0.25$), this evaluates to **`0.2503`** ($25.0282\%$).

---

**Equation E.87 — Poisson Rare-Event Arrival Probability:**
$$P(X = k) = \frac{\lambda^k e^{-\lambda}}{k!}$$
With parameters $\lambda$ (mean arrival rate per interval), $k$ (observed event count in interval).
Limiting law of rare independent events: radioactive Geiger-counter clicks, optical shot noise photons, and packet switch arrivals.  
On the stack, key in `lam [ENTER] k [yˣ] lam [+/-] [eˣ] [×] k [↰] [x!] [÷]`.
For the benchmark case ($\lambda = 4.2\text{ photons/ms}, k = 3\text{ photons}$), this evaluates to **`0.1852`** ($18.5165\%$).

---

**Equation E.88 — Gaussian Standard $z$-Score & Confidence Interval Half-Width:**
$$z = \frac{x - \mu}{\sigma}, \quad E = z_{\alpha/2}\frac{s}{\sqrt{n}}$$
With parameters $x$ (observation), $\mu$ (population mean), $\sigma$ (standard deviation), $s$ (sample SD from `[sx]`), $n$ (sample size), $z_{\alpha/2}$ ($1.9600$ for $95\%$ CI; $2.5758$ for $99\%$ CI).
Normalizes measurements into dimensionless standard deviation units and bounds the sampling error of the sample mean $\bar{x} \pm E$.  
The stack evaluation sequences are:
- $z$-Score: `x [ENTER] mu [-] sigma [÷]`  
- $95\%$ CI Margin $E$: `s [ENTER] n [√x] [÷] 1.96 [×]`  
For the benchmark case ($s = 8.40\text{ MPa}, n = 49\text{ tensile specimens}, z_{\alpha/2} = 1.96$), this evaluates to Margin of Error $E =$ **`2.3520`** $\text{MPa}$.

---

**Equation E.89 — Bayes' Theorem Diagnostic Posterior Probability:**
$$P(A \mid B) = \frac{P(B \mid A)P(A)}{P(B \mid A)P(A) + P(B \mid A')P(A')}$$
With parameters $P(A)$ (prior prevalence), $P(B \mid A)$ (true-positive sensitivity), $P(B \mid A')$ (false-positive rate), $P(A') = 1 - P(A)$.
Updates prior belief with conditional likelihood evidence; critical in medical diagnostics, radar target classification, and spam filtering.  
On the stack, key in `PBA [ENTER] PA [×] [ENTER] PBnotA [ENTER] PnotA [×] [+] [÷]`.
For the benchmark case ($P(A) = 0.01$ prevalence, sensitivity $P(B \mid A) = 0.99$, false-positive rate $P(B \mid A') = 0.05$ ($P(A') = 0.99$)), this evaluates to **`0.1667`** ($16.67\%$ posterior probability).

---

**Equation E.90 — Six Sigma Process Capability Index ($C_{pk}$):**
$$C_{pk} = \min\left(\frac{\text{USL} - \bar{x}}{3s},\; \frac{\bar{x} - \text{LSL}}{3s}\right)$$
With parameters $\text{USL}, \text{LSL}$ (upper/lower engineering specification limits), $\bar{x}$ (process mean via `[x̄]`), $s$ (process standard deviation via `[sx]`).
Measures how many $3\sigma$ half-widths fit between the shifted process center $\bar{x}$ and the nearest tolerance wall ($C_{pk} \ge 1.33$ required for $4\sigma$ manufacturing).  
On the stack (Upper side), key in `USL [ENTER] xbar [-] 3 [÷] s [÷]`.
For the benchmark case (CNC shaft diameter: $\text{USL} = 10.050\text{ mm}, \text{LSL} = 9.950\text{ mm}, \bar{x} = 10.010\text{ mm}, s = 0.010\text{ mm}$), this evaluates to **`1.3333`**.

---

**Equation E.91 — Shannon Information Entropy (Base-2 Bits):**
$$H(X) = -\sum_{i=1}^m p_i \log_2 p_i = -\frac{1}{\ln 2}\sum_{i=1}^m p_i \ln p_i$$
With parameters $p_i$ (symbol probability distribution with $\sum p_i = 1$).
Fundamental theoretical lower bound on average lossless compression bits per symbol across a noisy or noiseless communication source.  
On the stack (Binary source $p, 1-p$), key in `p [ENTER] [LN] [×] 1 [ENTER] p [-] [ENTER] [LN] [×] [+] 2 [LN] [÷] [+/-]`.
For the benchmark case (Biased binary telemetry source with $p_1 = 0.75, p_2 = 0.25$), this evaluates to **`0.8113`** $\text{bits/symbol}$.

---

**Equation E.92 — Shannon–Hartley Channel Capacity Law:**
$$C = B \log_2\left(1 + \frac{S}{N}\right) = \frac{B \ln(1 + S/N)}{\ln 2}$$
With parameters $B$ (channel bandwidth, $\text{Hz}$), $S/N$ (linear signal-to-noise power ratio; from $\text{SNR}_{\text{dB}}$ via `SNR_dB 10 [÷] [↰] [10ˣ]`).
Maximum error-free information bit rate transmissible over an additive white Gaussian noise (AWGN) radio or optical channel.  
On the stack, key in `SNR [ENTER] 1 [+] [LN] 2 [LN] [÷] B [×]`.
For the benchmark case ($B = 20.0\text{ MHz}$ Wi-Fi channel with linear $S/N = 31.0$ ($14.91\text{ dB}$)), this evaluates to **`100.0000`** $\text{Mbps}$.

---

**Equation E.93 — M/M/1 Queueing Utilization, Queue Length & Latency:**
$$\rho = \frac{\lambda}{\mu}, \quad L = \frac{\lambda}{\mu - \lambda}, \quad W = \frac{1}{\mu - \lambda}$$
With parameters $\lambda$ (mean Poisson arrival rate, $\text{req/s}$), $\mu$ (mean exponential service rate, $\text{req/s}$, with $\mu > \lambda$).
Little's Law ($L = \lambda W$) and Markovian birth-death steady state for CPU packet schedulers, database connection pools, and toll plazas.  
On the stack (Mean system occupancy $L$), key in `lam [ENTER] mu [ENTER] lam [-] [÷]` (Mean latency $W$: `mu [ENTER] lam [-] [1/x]`).
For the benchmark case ($\lambda = 45.0\text{ req/s}, \mu = 60.0\text{ req/s}$), this evaluates to $L =$ **`3.0000`** $\text{requests}$; $W =$ **`0.0667`** $\text{s}$ ($66.7\text{ ms}$).

---

### D.4.12 Section 12: Structural Mechanics, Semiconductor Electronics, RF & Computer Engineering

Equations E.94–E.100 span shaft torsion, structural beam deflection, axial Hookean strain, semiconductor diode junctions, op-amp feedback, RF path loss, and parallel computing speedup.

**Equation E.94 — Cylindrical Shaft Torsional Shear Stress & Angle of Twist:**
$$\tau_{\max} = \frac{T r}{J}, \qquad \theta = \frac{T L}{G J}, \qquad J = \frac{\pi r^4}{2}$$
With parameters $T = 450\text{ N}\cdot\text{m}$ (applied torque), $r = 0.025\text{ m}$ (shaft radius), $L = 1.20\text{ m}$ (length), $G = 79.3\times 10^9\text{ Pa}$ (shear modulus of steel), and polar moment of inertia $J = \frac{\pi (0.025)^4}{2} = 6.1359\times 10^{-7}\text{ m}^4$: on the stack, key in `0.025 [↰] [x²] [↰] [x²] [↱] [π] [×] 2 [÷] 450 [x⇄y] [÷] 0.025 [×]` to obtain $\tau_{\max} = \mathbf{1.8335\times 10^7}\text{ Pa}$ ($18.33\text{ MPa}$), and `[↰] [LASTX] [÷] 1.2 [×] 79.3 [E] 9 [÷]` for $\theta = \mathbf{0.01110}\text{ rad}$ ($0.636^\circ$).

---

**Equation E.95 — Cantilever & Simply Supported Beam Tip Deflection:**
$$\delta_{\text{cantilever}} = \frac{F L^3}{3 E I}, \quad \delta_{\text{simple}} = \frac{F L^3}{48 E I}$$
With parameters $F$ (point load, $\text{N}$), $L$ (beam span, $\text{m}$), $E$ (Young's modulus, $\text{Pa}$), $I$ (cross-sectional second moment of area, $\text{m}^4$).
Euler–Bernoulli double integration of bending moment $M(x) = E I \, d^2w/dx^2$; note the cubic sensitivity ($L^3$) to beam span.  
On the stack (Cantilever), key in `L [ENTER] 3 [yˣ] F [×] 3 [÷] E [÷] I [÷]`.
For the benchmark case ($F = 5,000\text{ N}, L = 2.0\text{ m}, E = 200 \times 10^9\text{ Pa}, I = 4.0 \times 10^{-6}\text{ m}^4$), this evaluates to **`0.0167`** $\text{m}$ ($16.67\text{ mm}$).

---

**Equation E.96 — Hooke's Law Axial Stress, Strain & Elastic Elongation:**
$$\sigma = \frac{F}{A}, \quad \varepsilon = \frac{\Delta L}{L_0}, \quad \Delta L = \frac{F L_0}{A E}$$
With parameters $F$ (axial tensile force, $\text{N}$), $L_0$ (unstrained length, $\text{m}$), $A$ (cross-sectional area, $\text{m}^2$), $E$ (Young's modulus, $\text{Pa}$).
Linear elastic constitutive law ($\sigma = E \varepsilon$) for tie rods, suspension cables, and bolted preload joints.  
On the stack, key in `F [ENTER] L0 [×] A [÷] E [÷]`.
For the benchmark case (Steel tie rod: $F = 45,000\text{ N}, L_0 = 2.50\text{ m}, A = 3.00 \times 10^{-4}\text{ m}^2, E = 200 \times 10^9\text{ Pa}$), this evaluates to $\Delta L =$ **`0.001875`** $\text{m}$ ($1.875\text{ mm}$; axial stress $\sigma = 150.0\text{ MPa}$).

---

**Equation E.97 — Shockley Semiconductor Diode Current-Voltage Law:**
$$I_D = I_S \left[\exp\left(\frac{V_D}{n V_T}\right) - 1\right]$$
With parameters $I_S$ (reverse saturation current, $\text{A}$), $V_D$ (forward bias voltage, $\text{V}$), $n$ (ideality factor, $1.0\text{–}2.0$), $V_T = k_B T / q \approx 0.02585\text{ V}$ at $300\text{ K}$.
Carrier diffusion across a $p$-$n$ junction depletion barrier; inside-out RPN evaluation avoids parentheses around the exponential argument.  
On the stack, key in `VD [ENTER] n [÷] VT [÷] [eˣ] 1 [-] IS [×]`.
For the benchmark case (Silicon junction diode: $I_S = 1.0 \times 10^{-12}\text{ A}, V_D = 0.650\text{ V}, n = 1.0, V_T = 0.02585\text{ V}$), this evaluates to **`0.0835`** $\text{A}$ ($83.47\text{ mA}$).

---

**Equation E.98 — Operational Amplifier Closed-Loop Gain & $-3\text{ dB}$ Bandwidth:**
$$A_{v,\text{non}} = 1 + \frac{R_f}{R_g}, \quad A_{v,\text{inv}} = -\frac{R_f}{R_{\text{in}}}, \quad f_{-3\text{dB}} = \frac{\text{GBWP}}{A_{v,\text{non}}}$$
With parameters $R_f$ (feedback resistor, $\Omega$), $R_g$ or $R_{\text{in}}$ (input ground resistor, $\Omega$), $\text{GBWP}$ (gain-bandwidth product, $\text{Hz}$).
Negative feedback trades open-loop gain for precision closed-loop linearity and extended closed-loop bandwidth $f_{-3\text{dB}}$.  
On the stack (Non-Inverting Gain & Bandwidth), key in `Rf [ENTER] Rg [÷] 1 [+] GBWP [x⇄y] [÷]`.
For the benchmark case ($R_f = 90\text{ k}\Omega, R_g = 10\text{ k}\Omega, \text{GBWP} = 10.0\text{ MHz}$), this evaluates to $A_{v,\text{non}} =$ **`10.0000`** ($20.0\text{ dB}$); $f_{-3\text{dB}} =$ **`1.0000`** $\text{MHz}$.

---

**Equation E.99 — Friis Free-Space RF Path Loss ($\text{FSPL}$):**
$$\text{FSPL}_{\text{dB}} = 20\log_{10}\left(\frac{4\pi d f}{c}\right)$$
With parameters $d$ (line-of-sight range, $\text{m}$), $f$ (carrier frequency, $\text{Hz}$), $c = 2.99792458 \times 10^8\text{ m/s}$.
Spherical inverse-square wave-front spreading ($1/(4\pi d^2)$) combined with effective isotropic receiving aperture ($\lambda^2 / 4\pi$) for satellite and microwave link budgets.  
On the stack, key in `4 [↱] [π] [×] d [×] f [×] 2.99792458 [E] 8 [÷] [↰] [LOG] 20 [×]`.
For the benchmark case ($d = 1,000\text{ m}$ ($1\text{ km}$), $f = 2.40 \times 10^9\text{ Hz}$ ($2.4\text{ GHz}$ ISM band)), this evaluates to **`100.0460`** $\text{dB}$.

---

**Equation E.100 — Amdahl's Law Multiprocessor Speedup & CMOS Dynamic Power:**
$$S(N) = \frac{1}{(1 - p) + \frac{p}{N}}, \quad P_{\text{dyn}} = \alpha C V_{DD}^2 f$$
With parameters $p$ (parallelizable workload fraction), $N$ (processor core count); $\alpha$ (switching activity), $C$ (load capacitance, $\text{F}$), $V_{DD}$ (supply rail, $\text{V}$), $f$ (clock frequency, $\text{Hz}$).
Shows why serial bottlenecks $(1-p)$ cap parallel scaling at $1/(1-p)$ and why voltage scaling ($V_{DD}^2$) dominates microprocessor thermal design power.  
The stack evaluation sequences are:
- Amdahl Speedup $S(N)$: `p [ENTER] N [÷] 1 [ENTER] p [-] [+] [1/x]`  
- CMOS Dynamic Power $P_{\text{dyn}}$: `VDD [↰] [x²] alpha [×] C [×] f [×]`  
For the benchmark case ($p = 0.90$ ($90\%$ parallel code), $N = 16\text{ cores}$), this evaluates to $S(16) =$ **`6.4000`** $\times$ speedup (asymptotic ceiling $S(\infty) = 10.0\times$).

## D.5 Specialized RPN Idioms & Stack Optimization Patterns

Fluency on the SC-32 comes from recognizing recurring mathematical forms and applying dedicated hardware keys to minimize button presses and eliminate redundant variable stores.

### D.5.1 The Harmonic Mean Idiom (`[x∥y]`)
The SC-32 provides a dedicated primary key **`[x∥y]`** which calculates:
$$X = \frac{X \cdot Y}{X + Y} = \frac{1}{\frac{1}{X} + \frac{1}{Y}}$$
In algebraic calculators, entering a reciprocal sum requires 12 to 16 keystrokes with fractions and parentheses. On the SC-32, it takes exactly **one keystroke**:
* **Parallel Resistors:** $R_{\text{eq}} = R_1 \parallel R_2 \parallel R_3$ $\rightarrow$ `R1 [ENTER] R2 [x∥y] R3 [x∥y]`.
* **Series Capacitors:** $C_{\text{eq}} = C_1 \parallel C_2$ $\rightarrow$ `C1 [ENTER] C2 [x∥y]`.
* **Thin Lens Optics:** Focal length $f = d_o \parallel d_i$ $\rightarrow$ `do [ENTER] di [x∥y]`.
* **Spring Series Compliance:** $k_{\text{eq}} = k_1 \parallel k_2$ $\rightarrow$ `k1 [ENTER] k2 [x∥y]`.
* **Reduced Mass in Two-Body Problem:** $\mu = m_1 \parallel m_2$ $\rightarrow$ `m1 [ENTER] m2 [x∥y]`.

### D.5.2 The Difference-of-Squares Idiom
When evaluating expressions of the form $a^2 - b^2$ (such as Pythagorean legs $b = \sqrt{c^2 - a^2}$ or numerical aperture $NA = \sqrt{n_1^2 - n_2^2}$):
* **Traditional RPN:** `c [↰] [x²] a [↰] [x²] [-] [√x]` (6 keystrokes).
* **Stack Factoring Alternative:** `c [ENTER] a [ENTER] [+] [↰] [LASTX] c [x⇄y] [-] [×] [√x]`. When numbers are large multi-digit values, entering them once and using `[x⇄y]` and `[↰] [LASTX]` avoids re-typing.

### D.5.3 Constant Factor Replication in Register T
When evaluating a formula with a repeated scalar factor $K$ across multiple variables (e.g. converting several values from feet to meters using $0.3048$, or multiplying items by sales tax $1.0825$):
1. Load the constant into the stack: `1.0825 [ENTER] [ENTER] [ENTER]` (fills $X, Y, Z, T$).
2. Enter Price 1: `10 [×]` $\rightarrow$ Displays result $10.825$. Register $T$ drops to $Z$ and replicates $1.0825$ in $T$!
3. Enter Price 2: `[CLx] 25 [×]` $\rightarrow$ Displays $27.0625$. Register $T$ continues to supply $1.0825$ indefinitely without ever touching memory registers!

## D.6 Numerical Root-Finding (`[↱] [SOLVE]`) & Quadrature (`[↱] [∫]`) Function Selector

As detailed in [Chapter 7](sc32/07-polynomials-brent-solver.md) and [Chapter 8](sc32/08-calculus-romberg-quadrature.md), the StackCalc SC-32 provides numerical root-finding via Richard Brent's hybrid inverse-quadratic/secant/bisection algorithm (**`[↱] [SOLVE]`**, Right Shift `[↱]` + `[7]`) and adaptive Romberg numerical integration (**`[↱] [∫]`**, Right Shift `[↱]` + `[8]`). Both engines evaluate either **user-defined postfix expressions** stored in Equation Mode (**`[↱] [EQN]`**, Right Shift `[↱]` + `[STO]`) or **six built-in benchmark templates ($f_0$ through $f_5$)** with Register $Z$ parameter passing:

### D.6.1 SC-32 Numerical Root-Finding & Quadrature Workflows

1. **User-Defined Postfix Equations (`[↱] [EQN]` Mode):** Press `[↱]` + `[STO]` (`[↱] [EQN]`) to enter or select a custom RPN expression in variable `X` (for example, `X SQ 2 -` for $f(x) = x^2 - 2$). Exit to the stack, load the bracket or integration limits $[a, b]$ into Registers $Y$ and $X$ (`a [ENTER] b`), and press `[↱] [SOLVE]` (`[↱]` + `[7]`) or `[↱] [∫]` (`[↱]` + `[8]`) to solve or integrate the active equation directly.
2. **Built-In Benchmark Templates ($f_0$–$f_5$):** When no custom equation is active (or when selecting a built-in test function), pressing `[↱] [SOLVE]` (`[↱]` + `[7]`) or `[↱] [∫]` (`[↱]` + `[8]`) accesses the 6-template function selector:
   * `0`: $f_0(x) = x^2 - c$ (where constant $c$ is read from Register $Z$)
   * `1`: $f_1(x) = \cos(x) - x$ (transcendental fixed-point benchmark)
   * `2`: $f_2(x) = \sin(x)$ (trigonometric waveform quadrature)
   * `3`: $f_3(x) = e^{-x^2}$ (Gaussian error-function bell curve)
   * `4`: $f_4(x) = x^3 - 2x - 5$ (Wallis's classical cubic benchmark)
   * `5`: $f_5(x) = \ln(x) - 1$ (Euler natural-base root benchmark)
3. **Execute Brent Root-Finder (`[↱] [SOLVE]`):** Place parameter $c$ in Register $Z$ (if using $f_0$), lower bracket $a$ in Register $Y$, and upper bracket $b$ in Register $X$, then invoke `[↱] [SOLVE]` (for the active `[↱] [EQN]` expression or followed by template digit `0`–`5`). The converged root $x^*$ is returned in Register $X$, the previous iterate in Register $Y$, and residual $f(x^*)$ in Register $Z$.
4. **Execute Romberg Quadrature (`[↱] [∫]`):** Place lower integration limit $a$ in Register $Y$ and upper limit $b$ in Register $X$, then invoke `[↱] [∫]` (for the active `[↱] [EQN]` expression or followed by template digit `0`–`5`). The definite integral $\int_a^b f(x)\,dx$ is returned in Register $X$ with the Richardson truncation error estimate in Register $Y$.

### D.6.2 Benchmark Example: Parabolic Area & Root Verification with Template $f_0(x) = x^2 - c$
To evaluate $\int_0^4 x^2 \, dx = \left[\frac{x^3}{3}\right]_0^4 = 21.3333$ (with $c = 0$ in Register $Z$):
1. Clear stack and load $c = 0$ into $Z$, lower limit $a = 0$ into $Y$, and upper limit $b = 4$ into $X$: `0 [ENTER] 0 [ENTER] 4`
2. Press `[↱] [∫] 0` (selects template $f_0(x) = x^2 - 0$).
3. The transflective screen converges via Romberg Richardson extrapolation and returns **`21.3333`** in Register $X$ (multiply by `3 [×]` for $\int_0^4 3x^2\,dx = 64.0000$).

## D.7 Storing Physical Constants in Registers A–Z

While pure mathematical invariants ($\pi$ via `[↱] [π]` and $e$ via `1 [eˣ]`) are permanently hardcoded in firmware, empirical 2022 CODATA physical constants (such as the Planck constant $h = 6.62607015 \times 10^{-34}\text{ J}\cdot\text{s}$, speed of light $c = 2.99792458 \times 10^8\text{ m/s}$, elementary charge $e = 1.602176634 \times 10^{-19}\text{ C}$, molar gas constant $R = 8.314462618\text{ J/(mol}\cdot\text{K)}$, and Avogadro constant $N_A = 6.02214076 \times 10^{23}\text{ mol}^{-1}$) are keyed explicitly via `[E]` or stored into the 26 non-volatile global letter registers (`[STO] A` through `[STO] Z`) for instant single-key recall (`[RCL] C`, `[RCL] H`, `[RCL] R`). Computing physical benchmarks with 4-level stack traces ensures that experimental calculations and textbook derivations match standard reference tables to full floating-point precision without compounding rounding errors.

---

## D.8 Numerical Boundary Conditions & Singularity Guards

* **Scientific Exponent Entry Syntax:** Never press `[×] 10 [yˣ]` to enter scientific notation; doing so pushes an extra operand onto the stack and consumes two stack levels. Always use the dedicated **`[E]`** (Exponent) key:
  * **Correct:** `1.602176634 [E] 19 [+/-]` (enters a single number into Register $X$).
  * **Incorrect:** `1.602176634 [ENTER] 10 [ENTER] 19 [+/-] [yˣ] [×]` (consumes four stack registers and risks stack overflow).
* **Trigonometric Angular Modes in Physical Laws:** Physical formulas involving wave motion, optics, and projectile trajectories require the matching angular mode:
  * **Geometric and Surveying Formulas (Snell's Law, Law of Cosines, Great Circle):** Require Degrees mode (`[↰] [MODES] [DEG]`).
  * **Analytical Calculus and Fourier Syntheses (Pendulum Period, Harmonic Oscillations):** Require Radians mode (`[↰] [MODES] [RAD]`).
  Check the `DEG` or `RAD` annunciator at the top of the display before starting a trigonometric sequence.
* **Mathematical Singularity and Boundary Handling:**
  * **Division by Zero ($x / 0$):** Halts execution and displays `DIVIDE BY 0` (Code 01). Press `[C]` or `[<-]` to clear the error and restore the prior stack state.
  * **Square Root of a Negative Number ($\sqrt{-x}$):** Displays `INVALID DATA` (Code 02) in Real mode; in Complex mode ([↰] [CMPLX]), returns the pure imaginary result $i\sqrt{x}$ across $(Y, X)$.
  * **Logarithm of a Non-Positive Number ($\ln(0)$ or $\ln(-x)$):** Displays `DIVIDE BY 0` (for $\ln 0$) or `INVALID DATA` (for $\ln(-x)$).

# Appendix E: Primary Sources & Annotated Further Reading Guide

The architecture of the StackCalc SC-32 does not exist in isolation. It represents the conscious convergence of more than a century of research across mathematical logic, stack-oriented computer organization, numerical error analysis, human-factors engineering, and scientific instrument craftsmanship.

While the historical narratives of William Hewlett's 1972 Palo Alto pocket calculator challenge, John Napier's 1614 logarithms, Cody and Waite's range-reduction polynomials, Eratosthenes' geodesy, Carl Friedrich Gauss's 1801 orbital recovery of Ceres, and Claude Shannon's 1937 Boolean switching algebra have been woven directly into the chapters of this book, this appendix provides an annotated guide to the primary historical, mathematical, and engineering literature cited throughout the volume.

---

## E.1 Annotated Literature & Thematic Reading Pathways

### E.1.1 Foundations of Logic & Computer Architecture

<a id="cite-lukasiewicz1924"></a>
**[lukasiewicz1924] Jan Łukasiewicz (1924)** — *Oznaczenie bez nawiasów (Parenthesis-Free Notation)*. *Komunikaty Polskiego Towarzystwa Matematycznego, Vol. 1, pp. 1–6*.
> **Annotation:** Introduces parenthesis-free prefix and postfix notation, demonstrating that operator position alone uniquely determines evaluation order without grouping symbols.  
> **Cited in Chapters:** [Ch 02](sc32/02-rpn-stack-dynamics.md), [Foreword](sc32/index.md)

<a id="cite-shannon1938"></a>
**[shannon1938] Claude E. Shannon (1938)** — *A Symbolic Analysis of Relay and Switching Circuits*. *Transactions of the American Institute of Electrical Engineers, Vol. 57, No. 12, pp. 713–723*.
> **Annotation:** Proves that Boolean algebra directly models physical electromechanical relays, establishing the foundation of binary arithmetic and digital logic gates.  
> **Cited in Chapters:** [Ch 10](sc32/10-computer-science-bases.md)

<a id="cite-burks1954"></a>
**[burks1954] Arthur W. Burks, Don W. Warren & Jesse B. Wright (1954)** — *An Analysis of a Logical Machine Using Parenthesis-Free Notation*. *Mathematical Tables and Other Aids to Computation, Vol. 8, No. 46, pp. 53–57*.
> **Annotation:** Formalizes Polish parenthesis-free postfix notation for electronic digital computers, laying the theoretical foundation for hardware-evaluated operational stacks.  
> **Cited in Chapters:** [Ch 02](sc32/02-rpn-stack-dynamics.md), [Foreword](sc32/index.md)

<a id="cite-hamblin1957"></a>
**[hamblin1957] Charles Leonard Hamblin (1957)** — *An Addressless Computer*. *The Australian Journal of Science, Vol. 20, No. 4, pp. 111–123*.
> **Annotation:** Pioneers the push-down operational stack in computer hardware, demonstrating that a zero-address computer architecture eliminates memory traffic and register allocation overhead.  
> **Cited in Chapters:** [Ch 02](sc32/02-rpn-stack-dynamics.md), [Foreword](sc32/index.md)

<a id="cite-dijkstra1961"></a>
**[dijkstra1961] Edsger W. Dijkstra (1961)** — *Making a Translator for ALGOL 60*. *Mathematisch Centrum, Amsterdam, Netherlands*.
> **Annotation:** Details the Shunting-Yard algorithm, proving the hidden buffering debt and parenthesis parsing overhead imposed by infix notation.  
> **Cited in Chapters:** [Ch 02](sc32/02-rpn-stack-dynamics.md)

<a id="cite-knuth1997"></a>
**[knuth1997] Donald E. Knuth (1997)** — *The Art of Computer Programming, Volume 1: Fundamental Algorithms*. *Addison-Wesley, Reading, MA*.
> **Annotation:** The monumental reference on sequential stack allocation, LIFO queue dynamics, combinatorics, and exact algorithm analysis.  
> **Cited in Chapters:** [Ch 02](sc32/02-rpn-stack-dynamics.md), [Ch 10](sc32/10-computer-science-bases.md)

### E.1.2 Corvallis Silicon & Handheld Architecture

<a id="cite-cochran1972"></a>
**[cochran1972] David S. Cochran (1972)** — *Algorithms and Hardware for the HP-35*. *Hewlett-Packard Journal, Vol. 23, No. 10, pp. 10–14*.
> **Annotation:** Documents the 4-register XYZT stack, serial bit-slice silicon architecture, CORDIC transcendental algorithms, and T-register constant replication.  
> **Cited in Chapters:** [Ch 01](sc32/01-craftsmanship-hardware.md), [Ch 02](sc32/02-rpn-stack-dynamics.md), [Foreword](sc32/index.md)

<a id="cite-hewlett1972"></a>
**[hewlett1972] William R. Hewlett (1972)** — *The Idea of a Personal Scientific Calculator*. *Hewlett-Packard Journal, Vol. 23, No. 10, pp. 2–4*.
> **Annotation:** Documents Bill Hewlett's shirt-pocket challenge to his Corvallis engineering team, conceiving the HP-35 as an electronic slide rule.  
> **Cited in Chapters:** [Ch 01](sc32/01-craftsmanship-hardware.md), [Ch 02](sc32/02-rpn-stack-dynamics.md), [Foreword](sc32/index.md)

<a id="cite-nelsonppc"></a>
**[nelsonppc] Richard J. Nelson (1974)** — *PPC Journal (formerly 65 Notes)*. *Personal Programmable Calculator Club, Santa Ana, CA*.
> **Annotation:** Pioneering user-group forensic engineering publications demanding absolute register transparency and synthetic programming capabilities.  
> **Cited in Chapters:** *Foundational reference & curriculum background*

<a id="cite-nelson1974"></a>
**[nelson1974] Richard J. Nelson (1974)** — *PPC Journal (formerly 65 Notes)*. *Personal Programmable Calculator Club, Santa Ana, CA*.
> **Annotation:** Pioneering user-group forensic engineering publications demanding absolute register transparency and synthetic programming capabilities.  
> **Cited in Chapters:** *Foundational reference & curriculum background*

<a id="cite-crowley1979"></a>
**[crowley1979] William L. Crowley (1979)** — *Inside the HP-41C: Architecture of an Alphanumeric Handheld Computer*. *Hewlett-Packard Journal, Vol. 30, No. 12, pp. 3–11*.
> **Annotation:** Introduces continuous CMOS memory, alphanumeric display segments, user key reassignment, and expandable peripheral architectures.  
> **Cited in Chapters:** *Foundational reference & curriculum background*

<a id="cite-hamrick1980"></a>
**[hamrick1980] Kathy B. Hamrick (1980)** — *The History of Reverse Polish Notation*. *The Two-Year College Mathematics Journal, Vol. 11, No. 5, pp. 317–326*.
> **Annotation:** Traces the historical evolution of Polish notation from abstract Warsaw mathematical logic to Corvallis handheld scientific computing.  
> **Cited in Chapters:** *Foundational reference & curriculum background*

<a id="cite-evett1983"></a>
**[evett1983] Eric A. Evett, Charles M. Fraser & Leonard J. Miller (1983)** — *Scientific Handheld Calculator with Extension Capabilities*. *Hewlett-Packard Journal, Vol. 34, No. 5, pp. 3–14*.
> **Annotation:** Establishes the split-stack complex number convention, matrix solver algorithms, and continuous memory architecture of the HP-15C Voyager.  
> **Cited in Chapters:** *Foundational reference & curriculum background*

### E.1.3 Numerical Stability & Scientific Algorithms

<a id="cite-cardano1545"></a>
**[cardano1545] Gerolamo Cardano (1545)** — *Artis Magnae, Sive de Regulis Algebraicis (The Great Art, or The Rules of Algebra)*. *Johannes Petreius, Nuremberg*.
> **Annotation:** Publishes the depressed cubic reduction and radical root formulas discovered by Scipione del Ferro and Niccolò Tartaglia, along with the first appearance of casus irreducibilis complex intermediates.  
> **Cited in Chapters:** [Ch 07](sc32/07-polynomials-brent-solver.md)

<a id="cite-napier1614"></a>
**[napier1614] John Napier (1614)** — *Mirifici Logarithmorum Canonis Descriptio*. *Andrew Hart, Edinburgh*.
> **Annotation:** The invention of logarithms, transforming laborious multi-digit multiplication into addition and doubling the working lifespan of astronomers.  
> **Cited in Chapters:** [Ch 03](sc32/03-algebra-transcendentals.md)

<a id="cite-descartes1637"></a>
**[descartes1637] René Descartes (1637)** — *La Géométrie (Appendix to Discours de la méthode)*. *Jan Maire, Leiden*.
> **Annotation:** Unifies Euclidean geometry and symbolic algebra via coordinate axes, laying the foundation for analytic geometry and function plotting.  
> **Cited in Chapters:** [Ch 12](sc32/12-function-scatter-plotting.md)

<a id="cite-galilei1638"></a>
**[galilei1638] Galileo Galilei (1638)** — *Discorsi e Dimostrazioni Matematiche, intorno à due nuoue scienze (Dialogues Concerning Two New Sciences)*. *Louis Elsevier, Leiden*.
> **Annotation:** Establishes the geometric Square-Cube Law governing surface-area-to-volume scaling in structural mechanics and biological thermoregulation, as well as the isochronous law of the pendulum.  
> **Cited in Chapters:** [Ch 06](sc32/06-geometry-surface-area.md)

<a id="cite-gauss1809"></a>
**[gauss1809] Carl Friedrich Gauss (1809)** — *Theoria Motus Corporum Coelestium in Sectionibus Conicis Solem Ambientium*. *Perthes and Besser, Hamburg*.
> **Annotation:** Introduces the Method of Least Squares and the Gaussian Normal error distribution, recovering the lost celestial orbit of Ceres.  
> **Cited in Chapters:** [Ch 09](sc32/09-statistics-curve-fitting.md)

<a id="cite-steinmetz1893"></a>
**[steinmetz1893] Charles Proteus Steinmetz (1893)** — *Complex Quantities and Their Use in Electrical Engineering*. *Proceedings of the International Electrical Congress, Chicago, August 21–25, 1893, pp. 33–74, New York*.
> **Annotation:** Landmark paper introducing complex phasor representation (Z = R + jX) to alternating-current analysis, reducing differential equations to complex arithmetic.  
> **Cited in Chapters:** [Ch 05](sc32/05-complex-numbers-phasors.md)

<a id="cite-richardson1911"></a>
**[richardson1911] Lewis Fry Richardson (1911)** — *The Approximate Arithmetical Solution by Finite Differences of Physical Problems Involving Differential Equations*. *Philosophical Transactions of the Royal Society of London, Series A, Vol. 210, pp. 307–357*.
> **Annotation:** Formulates Richardson extrapolation (deferred approach to the limit), canceling lowest-order error terms in numerical approximations.  
> **Cited in Chapters:** *Foundational reference & curriculum background*

<a id="cite-colebrook1939"></a>
**[colebrook1939] Cyril F. Colebrook (1939)** — *Turbulent Flow in Pipes, with Particular Reference to the Transition Region between the Smooth and Rough Pipe Laws*. *Journal of the Institution of Civil Engineers, Vol. 11, No. 4, pp. 133–156*.
> **Annotation:** Establishes the implicit non-linear Colebrook-White Darcy friction factor equation for turbulent pipe hydraulics, requiring numerical root finding.  
> **Cited in Chapters:** [Ch 07](sc32/07-polynomials-brent-solver.md)

<a id="cite-romberg1955"></a>
**[romberg1955] Werner Romberg (1955)** — *Vereinfachte numerische Integration*. *Det Kongelige Norske Videnskabers Selskab Forhandlinger, Vol. 28, No. 7, pp. 30–36*.
> **Annotation:** Applies triangular Richardson extrapolation to composite trapezoidal approximations, canceling successive Euler-Maclaurin error terms for rapid convergence.  
> **Cited in Chapters:** [Ch 08](sc32/08-calculus-romberg-quadrature.md), [Ch 12](sc32/12-function-scatter-plotting.md)

<a id="cite-bellman1957"></a>
**[bellman1957] Richard Bellman (1957)** — *Dynamic Programming*. *Princeton University Press, Princeton, NJ*.
> **Annotation:** Introduces the principle of optimality and dynamic programming, structuring complex multi-stage computational problems.  
> **Cited in Chapters:** *Foundational reference & curriculum background*

<a id="cite-brent1973"></a>
**[brent1973] Richard P. Brent (1973)** — *Algorithms for Minimization without Derivatives*. *Prentice-Hall, Englewood Cliffs, NJ*.
> **Annotation:** Synthesizes bisection, secant, and inverse quadratic interpolation into an unconditionally stable numerical root finder converging to 10⁻¹² precision.  
> **Cited in Chapters:** [Ch 07](sc32/07-polynomials-brent-solver.md), [Ch 08](sc32/08-calculus-romberg-quadrature.md), [Ch 12](sc32/12-function-scatter-plotting.md)

<a id="cite-kahan1979"></a>
**[kahan1979] William M. Kahan (1979)** — *Personal Calculator Has Key to Solve Any Equation f(x) = 0*. *Hewlett-Packard Journal, Vol. 30, No. 12, pp. 20–26*.
> **Annotation:** Establishes the non-destructive base-preserving percentage invariant and foundational floating-point error bounds for handheld solvers.  
> **Cited in Chapters:** [Ch 08](sc32/08-calculus-romberg-quadrature.md), [Ch 11](sc32/11-financial-tvm.md), [Foreword](sc32/index.md)

<a id="cite-cody1980"></a>
**[cody1980] William J. Cody & William Waite (1980)** — *Software Manual for the Elementary Functions*. *Prentice-Hall, Englewood Cliffs, NJ*.
> **Annotation:** The definitive treatise on extended-precision range reduction for transcendentals, preserving 53 bits of IEEE-754 mantissa across large arguments.  
> **Cited in Chapters:** [Ch 03](sc32/03-algebra-transcendentals.md)

<a id="cite-golub1996"></a>
**[golub1996] Gene H. Golub & Charles F. Van Loan (1996)** — *Matrix Computations*. *Johns Hopkins University Press, Baltimore, MD*.
> **Annotation:** The standard treatise on matrix decomposition, singular value decomposition, least-squares solvers, and floating-point stability.  
> **Cited in Chapters:** *Foundational reference & curriculum background*

### E.1.4 Breakout Mathematics & Scientific Nonfiction

<a id="cite-sartorius1856"></a>
**[sartorius1856] Wolfgang Sartorius von Waltershausen (1856)** — *Gauss zum Gedächtniss*. *S. Hirzel, pp. 12–13, Leipzig*.
> **Annotation:** Primary biographical source recording young Carl Friedrich Gauss's arithmetic series solution in J.G. Büttner's Brunswick classroom and his Low German exclamation 'Ligget se!' ('There it lies!').  
> **Cited in Chapters:** *Foundational reference & curriculum background*

<a id="cite-gardner1959"></a>
**[gardner1959] Martin Gardner (1959)** — *The Scientific American Book of Mathematical Puzzles and Diversions*. *Simon & Schuster, New York*.
> **Annotation:** Pioneered popular mathematical recreations, flexagons, hexaflexagons, and spatial puzzles that celebrate mathematical play.  
> **Cited in Chapters:** *Foundational reference & curriculum background*

<a id="cite-singh1997"></a>
**[singh1997] Simon Singh (1997)** — *Fermat's Enigma: The Epic Quest to Solve the World's Greatest Mathematical Problem*. *Walker & Company, New York*.
> **Annotation:** Captures the three-century human quest to prove Fermat's Last Theorem, conveying the passion and stakes of mathematical discovery.  
> **Cited in Chapters:** *Foundational reference & curriculum background*

<a id="cite-ifrah2000"></a>
**[ifrah2000] Georges Ifrah (2000)** — *The Universal History of Numbers: From Prehistory to the Invention of the Computer*. *John Wiley & Sons, New York*.
> **Annotation:** Comprehensive historical account of tally stones, Mesopotamian sexagesimal accounting, Egyptian hieroglyphic numerals, and the independent invention of zero and positional place value in India and Mesoamerica.  
> **Cited in Chapters:** *Foundational reference & curriculum background*

<a id="cite-cleomedes2004"></a>
**[cleomedes2004] Cleomedes (trans. Alan C. Bowen & Robert B. Todd) (2004)** — *Cleomedes' Lectures on Astronomy: A Translation of The Heavens*. *University of California Press, Berkeley, CA*.
> **Annotation:** Preserves the primary classical account (Book I, Chapter 7) of Eratosthenes of Cyrene's geometric measurement of the Earth's circumference using solstice shadows at Syene and Alexandria.  
> **Cited in Chapters:** [Ch 04](sc32/04-trig-vectors-polar.md)

<a id="cite-strogatz2012"></a>
**[strogatz2012] Steven Strogatz (2012)** — *The Joy of x: A Guided Tour of Math, from One to Infinity*. *Eamon Dolan / Houghton Mifflin Harcourt, Boston*.
> **Annotation:** Opens every mathematical section with everyday curiosity and intuitive aha-moments, showing how mathematical beauty connects to human experience.  
> **Cited in Chapters:** [Ch 02](sc32/02-rpn-stack-dynamics.md)

<a id="cite-ellenberg2014"></a>
**[ellenberg2014] Jordan Ellenberg (2014)** — *How Not to Be Wrong: The Power of Mathematical Thinking*. *Penguin Press, New York*.
> **Annotation:** Exposes common cognitive biases, non-linear scaling traps, and statistical survivorship fallacies with conversational wit.  
> **Cited in Chapters:** [Ch 02](sc32/02-rpn-stack-dynamics.md), [Foreword](sc32/index.md)

<a id="cite-munroe2014"></a>
**[munroe2014] Randall Munroe (2014)** — *What If?: Serious Scientific Answers to Absurd Hypothetical Questions*. *Houghton Mifflin Harcourt, Boston*.
> **Annotation:** Applies order-of-magnitude dimensional analysis, physics Fermi approximations, and creative mathematical modeling to wild scenarios.  
> **Cited in Chapters:** *Foundational reference & curriculum background*

<a id="cite-macaulay2016"></a>
**[macaulay2016] David Macaulay (2016)** — *The Way Things Work Now*. *HMH Books for Young Readers, Boston*.
> **Annotation:** Visualizes mechanical physical mechanisms and gear systems through step-by-step illustrations, inspiring the SC-6 tactile manipulative studio design.  
> **Cited in Chapters:** *Foundational reference & curriculum background*

<a id="cite-parker2019"></a>
**[parker2019] Matt Parker (2019)** — *Humble Pi: A Comedy of Maths Errors*. *Riverhead Books, New York*.
> **Annotation:** Explores famous engineering catastrophes and numerical bugs caused by round-off errors, integer overflows, and unit conversion failures.  
> **Cited in Chapters:** [Ch 02](sc32/02-rpn-stack-dynamics.md), [Ch 05](sc32/05-complex-numbers-phasors.md)

<a id="cite-strogatz2019"></a>
**[strogatz2019] Steven Strogatz (2019)** — *Infinite Powers: How Calculus Reveals the Secrets of the Universe*. *Eamon Dolan / Houghton Mifflin Harcourt, Boston*.
> **Annotation:** Illuminates numerical integration, derivatives, and continuous change from Archimedes to modern spacecraft trajectory navigation.  
> **Cited in Chapters:** [Foreword](sc32/index.md)

### E.1.5 Pedagogy, Cognitive Science & Manipulatives

<a id="cite-polya1945"></a>
**[polya1945] George Pólya (1945)** — *How to Solve It: A New Aspect of Mathematical Method*. *Princeton University Press, Princeton, NJ*.
> **Annotation:** Defines the heuristic problem-solving framework (Understand, Plan, Carry Out, Look Back), aligned with step-by-step RPN stack inspection.  
> **Cited in Chapters:** *Foundational reference & curriculum background*

<a id="cite-miller1956"></a>
**[miller1956] George A. Miller (1956)** — *The Magical Number Seven, Plus or Minus Two: Some Limits on Our Capacity for Processing Information*. *Psychological Review, Vol. 63, No. 2, pp. 81–97*.
> **Annotation:** Identifies the 7 ± 2 item capacity limit of human short-term working memory, validating the 4-register stack as the optimal cognitive span.  
> **Cited in Chapters:** [Ch 01](sc32/01-craftsmanship-hardware.md), [Ch 02](sc32/02-rpn-stack-dynamics.md), [Foreword](sc32/index.md)

<a id="cite-bruner1966"></a>
**[bruner1966] Jerome S. Bruner (1966)** — *Toward a Theory of Instruction*. *Harvard University Press, Cambridge, MA*.
> **Annotation:** Establishes the developmental progression from physical action to visual imagery and symbolic notation underpinning the StackCalc manipulative studios and display modes.  
> **Cited in Chapters:** *Foundational reference & curriculum background*

<a id="cite-sweller1988"></a>
**[sweller1988] John Sweller (1988)** — *Cognitive Load During Problem Solving: Effects on Learning*. *Cognitive Science, Vol. 12, No. 2, pp. 257–285*.
> **Annotation:** Establishes Cognitive Load Theory, demonstrating that parentheses and operator precedence buffering in algebraic calculators impose extraneous cognitive load.  
> **Cited in Chapters:** [Ch 01](sc32/01-craftsmanship-hardware.md), [Ch 02](sc32/02-rpn-stack-dynamics.md), [Foreword](sc32/index.md)

**[ccssm2010] National Governors Association Center for Best Practices & Council of Chief State School Officers (2010)** — *Common Core State Standards for Mathematics*. *National Governors Association & CCSSO, Washington, DC*.
> **Annotation:** The foundational curriculum standards framework governing K-12 operations, algebraic thinking, number sense, and geometry in US classrooms.

<a id="cite-horowitz2015"></a>
**[horowitz2015] Paul Horowitz & Winfield Hill (2015)** — *The Art of Electronics*. *Cambridge University Press, Cambridge, UK*.
> **Annotation:** The definitive hardware design treatise, establishing the master-practitioner voice, rule-of-thumb heuristics, and parallel resistance shortcuts.  
> **Cited in Chapters:** [Ch 05](sc32/05-complex-numbers-phasors.md), [Ch 08](sc32/08-calculus-romberg-quadrature.md), [Ch 13](sc32/13-applied-stem-case-studies.md), [Foreword](sc32/index.md)

**[ieee754_2019] IEEE Computer Society (2019)** — *IEEE Standard for Floating-Point Arithmetic*. *Institute of Electrical and Electronics Engineers, Piscataway, NJ*.
> **Annotation:** The international standard governing 64-bit double-precision floating-point arithmetic, subnormal representation, and arithmetic exceptions.

## E.2 Continuing the Exploration

From Jan Łukasiewicz's 1924 parenthesis-free logic to the four-register operational stack on your desk, every algorithm and physical manipulative in this volume shares a single goal: making mathematical structure visible, tactile, and immediate. To revisit the opening engineering narrative of this volume, return to the **[Prologue: Why Think in the Stack?](sc32/index.md)**, or explore interactive web simulators, 3D-printable studio manipulative files, and ongoing hardware build logs at **[stackcalc.io](https://stackcalc.io)**.
